<!-- file: README.md -->

# UIDirector

Runs your Screens, Popups & Overlays. One root, one way back, one queue.

UIDirector is a navigation layer for uGUI. Views are prefabs under one persistent root, opened by typed keys that carry their argument and result types, and `ShowAsync` completes with a result that says how the view ended instead of throwing. Screens keep a history stack, popups share a backdrop, system overlays block input, one back rule decides what a back press does, and an optional priority queue presents notices one at a time.

## Requirements

| | |
|---|---|
| Unity | 6000.0 or newer. |
| [UniTask](https://github.com/Cysharp/UniTask) | Required. Install it before this package; a package installed from a git URL cannot declare it as a dependency. |
| `com.unity.ugui` 2.0.0 | Required. It is declared as a dependency, so a git install brings it in when your manifest does not list it. It includes TextMesh Pro, which the samples use. |
| Addressables (`com.unity.addressables`) | Optional, for views loaded by address. |
| DOTween | Optional, for `TweenTransition` and your own transitions on DOTween. |
| Zenject or Extenject | Optional, for injecting services into views. |
| Input System (`com.unity.inputsystem`) | Optional. `BackInput` reads the back key from it when it is installed and active, and from the legacy input manager otherwise. |

## Install

Install UniTask first. In the Package Manager open the **+** menu, choose **Add package from git URL**
(newer editors label it **Install package from git URL**) and enter:

```
https://github.com/Cysharp/UniTask.git?path=src/UniTask/Assets/Plugins/UniTask
```

UniTask documents its other install routes in its own README. Then add UIDirector the same way:

```
https://github.com/ecanakli/UnityUIDirector.git#v0.1.1
```

Or add both lines to the `dependencies` of `Packages/manifest.json` (the order does not matter):

```json
"com.cysharp.unitask": "https://github.com/Cysharp/UniTask.git?path=src/UniTask/Assets/Plugins/UniTask",
"com.ecanakli.uidirector": "https://github.com/ecanakli/UnityUIDirector.git#v0.1.1"
```

Always install a tag. Without `#v0.1.1` the install tracks the default branch.

### Then, depending on your setup

- **Your code is in assembly definitions.** Reference `Ecanakli.UIDirector` and `UniTask`. Add
  `Ecanakli.UIDirector.Addressables` to use `AddressablesViewProvider` from code,
  `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DOTween` (with `DOTween.dll` and the define constraint, see
  [DOTween](Documentation~/DOTween.md)) to use `TweenTransition`, and
  `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection.Zenject` plus `Zenject` for `NavigatorInstaller`. Every type
  is in the namespace `Ecanakli.UIDirector` except `NavigatorInstaller`
  (`Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection`). Code outside assembly definitions needs no reference.
- **Addressables.** The integration compiles by itself when `com.unity.addressables` is installed.
  There is nothing to switch on. See [Assets and Addressables](Documentation~/Assets-and-Addressables.md).
- **DOTween.** The integration compiles when the `DOTWEEN` define is present, which DOTween's own setup
  panel sets, or when a UPM package named `com.demigiant.dotween` is installed. If neither is true but
  the DOTween assembly is in the project, choose `Tools/UIDirector/DOTween Integration` once. See
  [DOTween](Documentation~/DOTween.md).
- **Zenject under `Assets/`.** Choose `Tools/UIDirector/Zenject Integration` once; it sets a scripting
  define on every build target, so commit `ProjectSettings` afterwards. **Extenject as a UPM package,
  9.0.0 or newer:** the integration turns itself on. See [Zenject](Documentation~/Zenject.md).

## Getting started in 5 minutes

Six steps. Every block of code below is copied from the Basic Usage sample (see
[Samples](#samples)), which compiles. The code is the scenario of its Settings screen: it asks
"Reset settings" ("All settings return to their defaults.") in a confirm popup and acts on the answer.

The blocks leave out the `using` lines. Add the ones a file needs: `Ecanakli.UIDirector` for every
package type, `Cysharp.Threading.Tasks` where `UniTask` or `Forget` appears, `System.Threading` for
`CancellationToken`, `TMPro` for `TMP_Text`, and `UnityEngine` and `UnityEngine.UI` for `SerializeField`
and `Button`. The sample's own files sit in the namespace `Ecanakli.UIDirector.Samples.BasicUsage`, which
already reaches `Ecanakli.UIDirector`; your files need the `using` line. The argument types the blocks
pass around (`ConfirmArgs`, `ItemArgs`, `RenameArgs`, `ToastArgs`) are plain structs you write yourself.
In the sample they are in `ViewArgs.cs`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ViewArgs.cs -->
```csharp
/// <summary>What the confirm popup shows.</summary>
public readonly struct ConfirmArgs
{
    public readonly string Title;
    public readonly string Message;

    public ConfirmArgs(string title, string message)
    {
        Title = title;
        Message = message;
    }
}

/// <summary>Which item the detail screen shows.</summary>
public readonly struct ItemArgs
{
    public readonly string ItemId;

    public ItemArgs(string itemId)
    {
        ItemId = itemId;
    }
}

/// <summary>The item to rename and its current title.</summary>
public readonly struct RenameArgs
{
    public readonly string ItemId;
    public readonly string CurrentTitle;

    public RenameArgs(string itemId, string currentTitle)
    {
        ItemId = itemId;
        CurrentTitle = currentTitle;
    }
}

/// <summary>The one line a toast shows.</summary>
public readonly struct ToastArgs
{
    public readonly string Message;

    public ToastArgs(string message)
    {
        Message = message;
    }
}
```

### 1. Create the root

Choose `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root`. It creates a canvas with a `ViewRoot` and a `BackInput`,
and an `EventSystem` when the scene has none. Without an `EventSystem` views show but receive no
clicks ([UIDIRECTOR116](Documentation~/Troubleshooting.md#uidirector116)). With `Initialize On Awake`
left on, the root initializes itself in `Awake` with the three default layers and `ViewRoot.Navigator`
is ready from then on. The Basic Usage sample turns `Initialize On Awake` off and initializes the root
in code, because its toast row sits on a layer that only code can declare (step 5). Details are in
[Root canvas](Documentation~/Root-Canvas.md).

### 2. Describe the views and name them

Create a catalog with `Assets > Create > UIDirector/View Catalog`, add one row per view prefab (an id,
the prefab, the layer it opens on) and drag the catalog into the `Catalogs` list of the root. A view
prefab has a `ViewHost` and one view component on its root. Then give every row a typed key, in one
static class marked `[ViewKeys]`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppViews.cs -->
```csharp
[ViewKeys]
public static class AppViews
{
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Home = ViewKey.Create("home");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Library = ViewKey.Create("library");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ItemArgs, NoResult> ItemDetail = ViewKey.Create<ItemArgs>("item-detail");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Settings = ViewKey.Create("settings");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ConfirmArgs, bool> Confirm = ViewKey.Create<ConfirmArgs, bool>("confirm");
    public static readonly ViewKey<RenameArgs, string> Rename = ViewKey.Create<RenameArgs, string>("rename");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Saving = ViewKey.Create("saving");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ToastArgs, NoResult> Toast = ViewKey.Create<ToastArgs>("toast");
}
```

`Confirm` takes a `ConfirmArgs` and answers with a `bool`; `Home` takes nothing and answers nothing.
The compiler checks what you pass in and what you read out. Run `Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs`
to check keys and rows against each other before you press Play. See
[Catalogs and keys](Documentation~/Catalogs-and-Keys.md).

### 3. Write the confirm popup

A view derives from `ViewBehaviour<TArgs, TResult>`. `OnOpen` receives the arguments and a scope; what
you bind to the scope is removed when the open ends, so there is no `OnDisable` and no
`RemoveListener`. `Complete(value)` closes the popup and answers:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ConfirmView.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class ConfirmView : ViewBehaviour<ConfirmArgs, bool>
{
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _title;
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _message;
    [SerializeField] private Button _accept;
    [SerializeField] private Button _decline;

    protected override void OnOpen(ConfirmArgs args, ViewScope open)
    {
        _title.text = args.Title;
        _message.text = args.Message;

        // The package removes both listeners when this open ends.
        open.Bind(_accept.onClick, Accept);
        open.Bind(_decline.onClick, Refuse);
    }

    private void Accept()
    {
        Complete(true);
    }

    private void Refuse()
    {
        Complete(false);
    }
}
```

The popup's row sits on the built-in `popups` layer: modal, with a shared backdrop, and it takes back.
See [View authoring](Documentation~/View-Authoring.md) and
[Popups and backdrop](Documentation~/Popups-and-Backdrop.md).

### 4. Open it from a screen and read the answer

`ShowAsync` opens a view and completes with a `ViewResult<bool>`. It does not throw for anything that
happens to the view: a back press, a tap on the backdrop, a refusal and an ended owner all arrive as a
result without a value. The token passed with every open is its **owner**; when it is cancelled the view
ends. Here the owner is the token of the screen's open scope, so the popup cannot outlive the screen:

The Reset button starts the check in the screen's open scope, which runs it with the scope's token:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private void OnResetClicked()
{
    OpenScope.Run(ConfirmResetAsync);
}
```

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private async UniTask ConfirmResetAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // The owner is this screen's scope token: the popup cannot outlive the screen.
    var answer = await Navigator.ShowAsync(
        AppViews.Confirm,
        new ConfirmArgs("Reset settings", "All settings return to their defaults."),
        ct,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.reset", RejectWhenBusy = true });

    // Refused at once instead of waiting behind a view that is still opening.
    if (answer.Rejected == RejectReason.Busy)
    {
        _status.text = "Busy, try again.";
        return;
    }

    // Back, backdrop and a closed screen all end with no value, so this line also guards the screen.
    if (!answer.HasValue || !answer.Value)
        return;

    _settings.ResetToDefaults();
    _status.text = "Settings were reset.";

    // The toast outlives this screen, so the root owns it.
    Navigator.Open(
        AppViews.Toast,
        new ToastArgs("Settings were reset."),
        Navigator.RootToken,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.reset" });
}
```

Always check `HasValue` before you read `Value`: for a `bool` result the default is `false`, which looks
like an answer. The last call is the other way to open a view: `Open` returns a handle at once and does
not wait. The root owns the toast because it must outlive the screen that asked for it. More in
[Opening and results](Documentation~/Opening-and-Results.md).

### 5. Initialize the root and open the first screen

The toast row of the catalog sits on a layer named `toasts`. The three default layers do not include
it, so the sample declares it in code:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppLayers.cs -->
```csharp
// Above the system layer, no history, no back and no input shield: a toast never blocks a tap.
public static readonly ViewLayer Toasts = new ViewLayer("toasts", 3, ViewLayerRules.None);
```

A layer declared in code reaches the root through `ViewRootSetup.ExtraLayers`, which only `Initialize`
accepts. That is why the sample turns `Initialize On Awake` off and initializes the root in its own
`Awake`. Turn it off on your root too before you call `Initialize`: a root that already initialized
itself throws `InvalidOperationException` on a second initialization. Without this call the `toast` row is refused at registration
([UIDIRECTOR109](Documentation~/Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109)) and opening the toast ends as not
shown. The other `ViewRootSetup` members are covered in
[Add a layer of your own](Documentation~/Root-Canvas.md#add-a-layer-of-your-own):

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
_viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup
{
    Inject = InjectServices,
    ErrorHandler = OnViewError,
    ExtraLayers = new[] { AppLayers.Toasts }
});
_navigator = _viewRoot.Navigator;
```

Then open the first screen. The root's token as owner means the screen ends only when the root does:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
private void Start()
{
    // Owned by the root, so Home ends only when the root does.
    _navigator.Open(AppViews.Home, _navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "boot" });
}
```

`_navigator` is `ViewRoot.Navigator`. A screen opens on the `screens` layer, which is a stack and the
back history; opening an id that is already in the stack returns to it. See
[Navigation and back](Documentation~/Navigation-and-Back.md).

### 6. Route back

`Back()` is the single back rule. It returns `true` when something handled the press and `false` when
nothing did:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/LibraryView.cs -->
```csharp
// The other screens use a ViewButton set to Back; this one shows the call.
private void GoBack() => Navigator.Back();
```

`BackInput`, which the root menu added, calls `Back()` on the Escape key once the root is initialized. On the bottom screen `Back()`
returns `false` and closes nothing; `BackInput` then raises `Unhandled`, and the game decides. The sample
listens and asks to quit with the same confirm popup:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// No removal needed: the bootstrap and the root live and die together.
_backInput.Unhandled.AddListener(OnBackUnhandled);
```

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
private void OnBackUnhandled()
{
    // A Unity event cannot await; the quit answer is read inside.
    ConfirmQuitAsync().Forget();
}

private async UniTaskVoid ConfirmQuitAsync()
{
    var answer = await _navigator.ShowAsync(
        AppViews.Confirm,
        new ConfirmArgs("Quit", "Close the application?"),
        _navigator.RootToken,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "back.root" });

    if (!answer.HasValue || !answer.Value)
        return;
```

A yes then calls `Application.Quit()`, and in the editor it stops Play Mode.

Press Play and open `Window > UIDirector` to watch the layers, the requests and the input shield live.
To see every request in the Console, add an observer: the sample's `ViewEventLog` prints one `[views]`
line per event (see [Events and analytics](Documentation~/Events-and-Analytics.md)). A message
tagged `UIDIRECTOR1xx` is explained in [Troubleshooting](Documentation~/Troubleshooting.md).

## Samples

Import them from the Package Manager: select **UIDirector**, open the **Samples** tab and press
**Import**. Each sample has its own README with the setup steps and a list of things to try. Every
sample scene has no Event System on purpose, because the right input module depends on your project's
input handling; the sample creates one when Play starts. Basic Usage, Queue Usage, Addressables Usage,
DOTween Usage and Zenject Usage all use TextMesh Pro, so import its Essential Resources once with
`Window > TextMeshPro > Import TMP Essential Resources`; the texts stay blank until then.

| Sample | Needs | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| [Basic Usage](Samples~/BasicUsage/README.md) | The core only, TextMesh Pro Essential Resources | A confirm popup with a result, three screens with back, a system overlay, a custom layer and transition, events and errors |
| [Queue Usage](Samples~/QueueUsage/README.md) | The core only, TextMesh Pro Essential Resources | A priority queue for popups: startup notices, a gate that denies, a hold while a flow runs, a feature catalog added at run time |
| [Addressables Usage](Samples~/AddressablesUsage/README.md) | `com.unity.addressables`, and the two prefabs marked addressable (a menu item does it) | Views loaded by address, a preload lease and trimming kept instances |
| [DOTween Usage](Samples~/DOTweenUsage/README.md) | DOTween, with the integration active | `TweenTransition` on a popup and a custom transition built on DOTween |
| [Zenject Usage](Samples~/ZenjectUsage/README.md) | Zenject or Extenject with the integration active, and a Scene Context you add yourself | The navigator bound in a SceneContext and views that receive injections |

## Status and limits

- Version 0.1.1. See the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md).
- Main thread only. Opening, registering and queueing throw on another thread; a few stop-type calls are
  posted to the main thread. See [Threading](Documentation~/Threading.md).
- uGUI only, with a `Screen Space - Overlay` or `Screen Space - Camera` root. World-space UI and UI
  Toolkit are not supported. One root per application is the documented setup.
- Diagnostics have stable ids, `UIDIRECTOR101` to `UIDIRECTOR126`. Ids 101 to 120 and 126 are logged at
  run time in the editor and in development builds. Ids 121 to 124 come only from the catalog validator,
  and 125 from the validator and from the root when a catalog with a row whose id is empty or only whitespace is registered (that row is refused). Each
  has a section in [Troubleshooting](Documentation~/Troubleshooting.md).
- What the package deliberately leaves to the game is listed in
  [Limitations](Documentation~/Limitations.md#not-in-010).

<!-- file: Documentation~/index.md -->

# UIDirector documentation

UIDirector runs uGUI screens, popups and overlays from prefabs under one persistent root: typed keys, awaitable results, one back rule and an optional priority queue. Requirements, install steps and a five-minute start are in the [README](../README.md); every public type is listed in the [API reference](API-Reference.md).

## Start here

Read these in order the first time.

- [Concepts](Concepts.md): the root and its layers, views, rows and keys, a request from start to finish, outcomes as data, owners and scopes.
- [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md): creating the root, every Inspector field, `ViewRootSetup`, overlay and camera roots, the sorting band, adding a layer of your own.
- [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md): catalog rows, typed keys, giving catalogs to the root, adding and removing a catalog at run time, the validator.
- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md): writing a view on the base class or the interfaces, every hook, `Decline`, `Complete`, scopes and kept instances.
- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md): `Open` against `ShowAsync`, `OpenOptions`, the handle, reading a result, owners, closing many views.
- [FAQ](FAQ.md): short answers, each linking to the page that explains it.

## Guides

One task each.

- [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md): opening screens forward, returning to one, `CloseTo`, `Back()` and its order, `BackPolicy`, `BackInput`.
- [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md): awaiting a popup's answer, the shared backdrop, closing on a tap, the input shield, `RejectWhenBusy`.
- [System overlays](System-Overlays.md): a blocking overlay around a piece of work, back while it is up, waiting until it is gone.
- [Transitions](Transitions.md): the fade, scale and slide transitions, time, writing a custom transition and the contract it keeps.
- [Queue](Queue.md): presenting requests one at a time by priority, gates, holds, why the navigator's waiting cap is never reached and a feature that brings its own catalog.
- [Events and analytics](Events-and-Analytics.md): the observer interface, every event kind, the order at close, an analytics adapter.
- [Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md): the EventSystem, what the input shield blocks, double taps, `HoldInput`, time scale 0, the back button.
- [Migration](Migration.md): moving a project that has a UI manager of its own to UIDirector one view at a time.

## Integrations

Optional assemblies that compile only when the library is present.

- [DOTween](DOTween.md): turning the integration on, `TweenTransition`, and a custom transition that leaves no tween behind.
- [Assets and Addressables](Assets-and-Addressables.md): views loaded by address, preload leases, keep and trim, load failures, writing a provider.
- [Zenject](Zenject.md): `NavigatorInstaller`, injection into every view instance, the SceneContext and the EventSystem.

## Reference

- [API reference](API-Reference.md): every public type and member as declared, with its assembly and namespace.
- [Diagnostics](Diagnostics.md): console lines with stable ids, the `Window > UIDirector` window, the text read-out, the error handler, the catalog validator.
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md): one section per `UIDIRECTOR1xx` id with cause and fix, then problems that carry no id.
- [Performance](Performance.md): what the package guarantees about cost, which test holds each guarantee.
- [Threading](Threading.md): which calls throw off the main thread, which are posted to it and where an awaited result resumes.
- [Limitations](Limitations.md): what the package does not do and its provisional defaults.

## Design

Why the package is shaped the way it is.

- [Architecture](Design/Architecture.md): the root, requests and phases, the per-layer runner, the shield, back resolution, scopes, events, the queue, the provider seam.
- [ADR-001 Outcomes as data](Design/Decisions/ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md): `ShowAsync` always completes with a result and never throws for what happens to a view.
- [ADR-002 Strict serialization](Design/Decisions/ADR-002-Strict-Serialization.md): one operation at a time per layer and a started step is never interrupted.
- [ADR-003 Begin-only hooks and scopes](Design/Decisions/ADR-003-Begin-Only-Hooks-And-Scopes.md): hooks only begin things, and the package ends what a scope holds.
- [ADR-004 The queue sits above the navigator](Design/Decisions/ADR-004-Queue-Above-The-Navigator.md): `ViewQueue` talks to the navigator through `INavigator` only.
- [ADR-005 Token owners](Design/Decisions/ADR-005-Token-Owners.md): every request and registration takes a required `CancellationToken` as its owner.

For AI tools, [llms.txt](../llms.txt) holds a summary, the rules that bite and a description of every page, and [llms-full.txt](../llms-full.txt) is all of it in one file.

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Concepts.md -->

# Concepts

[Back to index](index.md)

This page is the model behind every other guide: what the root and its layers are, how a prefab
becomes a view through a catalog row and a key, what a request is and how it ends, why an ending is
data and never an exception, who owns an open, and what a scope is. Read it once; each guide then
goes deep on one task.

---

## The picture

```text
Canvas                         yours: render mode, scaler, sorting layer
  ViewRoot                     one per UI; owns the navigator (INavigator)
    screens   order 0          History, TakesBack, ShieldsInput
    popups    order 1          Modal, TakesBack, ShieldsInput, ClosedByNavigation
    system    order 2          Modal, ShieldsInput
    toasts    order 3          your own layer: no rules at all
    shield                     above every layer; counted; blocks all input while it is up

view      = a prefab with a ViewHost on its root and a component that implements IView<TArgs, TResult>
row       = one line of a ViewCatalog asset: id, prefab or asset key, layer, policies
key       = ViewKey<TArgs, TResult> in code: the id plus the two types
request   = one call to Open or ShowAsync; Waiting > Loading > Opening > Open > Closing > Ended
outcome   = a ViewResult: how it ended, why it was refused, and the value when there is one
owner     = a CancellationToken you pass with every open; when it ends, the view ends
scope     = what the package ends for you: bindings and tasks of one open, or of one visible span
```

---

## One root, layers with rules

A `ViewRoot` sits on a canvas that your project owns. It builds the layers under itself, creates the
navigator and exposes it as `ViewRoot.Navigator`. It is not a singleton: each root has its own
navigator, input shield and back rule.

A layer is an immutable `ViewLayer`: an id, an order and a set of `ViewLayerRules` flags. Every root
has three:

| Layer | Order | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| `ViewLayers.Screens` (`screens`) | 0 | `History`, `TakesBack`, `ShieldsInput` |
| `ViewLayers.Popups` (`popups`) | 1 | `Modal`, `TakesBack`, `ShieldsInput`, `ClosedByNavigation` |
| `ViewLayers.System` (`system`) | 2 | `Modal`, `ShieldsInput` |

What each flag does:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `History` | The layer is a stack and the back history. A view covers what is below it. Opening an id that is already in the stack returns to it instead of stacking a second copy; a key with arguments reopens it in place. The bottom view is the root of `Back()`. |
| `Modal` | One shared backdrop sits under the layer's top view, and everything below that view is non-interactive. |
| `TakesBack` | `Back()` may close the layer's top view. Without it a modal layer swallows back and a plain layer lets it pass. |
| `ShieldsInput` | Opens, closes and loads on this layer hold the input shield. |
| `ClosedByNavigation` | Views on this layer end when a view opens on a `History` layer. |

A project adds layers in code. The Basic Usage sample declares one above the system layer, with no
rules, so a toast never blocks a tap:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppLayers.cs -->
```csharp
// Above the system layer, no history, no back and no input shield: a toast never blocks a tap.
public static readonly ViewLayer Toasts = new ViewLayer("toasts", 3, ViewLayerRules.None);
```

The root takes it in `ViewRootSetup.ExtraLayers`; see [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md).

Two rules are easy to get wrong:

- `ClosedByNavigation` fires when a view **opens** on a history layer, never on a pop, `Back()` or
  `CloseTo`. It ends only the views and waiting requests that were **accepted earlier** than the view
  that opened. A popup that the new screen opens itself, or that is requested after the screen, stays.
  The views it ends are snapped to their hidden pose with `CloseReason.Navigated`; they get no hide
  transition.
- A tap on the backdrop closes the top view of a modal layer only when that view is fully open and its
  row sets `CloseOnBackdrop`. While the input shield is up, the tap does nothing.

The layers and their rules are the subject of [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md),
[Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md) and [System overlays](System-Overlays.md).

---

## Views, rows and keys

A view is a prefab. Its root carries a `ViewHost` (which also needs a `Canvas` and a
`GraphicRaycaster`) and one component that implements `IView<TArgs, TResult>`. The easy way to write
that component is to derive from `ViewBehaviour`, `ViewBehaviour<TArgs>` or
`ViewBehaviour<TArgs, TResult>`; see [View authoring](View-Authoring.md).

A **catalog row** describes the view: an id, the prefab (or an asset key), the layer id it opens on
and its policies. Rows live in `ViewCatalog` assets that you assign to the root.

A **key** is how code names a row. It is a typed value, `ViewKey<TArgs, TResult>`, made of the row's
id plus the argument and result types the view takes. Keep them in one static class marked
`[ViewKeys]`, so the editor can check them against the catalogs:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppViews.cs -->
```csharp
[ViewKeys]
public static class AppViews
{
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Home = ViewKey.Create("home");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Library = ViewKey.Create("library");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ItemArgs, NoResult> ItemDetail = ViewKey.Create<ItemArgs>("item-detail");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Settings = ViewKey.Create("settings");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ConfirmArgs, bool> Confirm = ViewKey.Create<ConfirmArgs, bool>("confirm");
    public static readonly ViewKey<RenameArgs, string> Rename = ViewKey.Create<RenameArgs, string>("rename");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Saving = ViewKey.Create("saving");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ToastArgs, NoResult> Toast = ViewKey.Create<ToastArgs>("toast");
}
```

`Confirm` takes a `ConfirmArgs` and answers with a `bool`. `Home` takes nothing and answers nothing,
which is what `NoArgs` and `NoResult` say. The compiler therefore checks what you pass in and what you
read out. Rows, keys and the validator are in [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md).

---

## A request, start to finish

Every `Open` or `ShowAsync` call is one **request**. The navigator decides at the call, synchronously,
whether to accept it. An accepted request has a request id and passes through six phases, each at most
once and never backwards:

| Phase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Waiting` | Accepted and in its layer's list; the layer's runner has not reached it. |
| `Loading` | The runner is getting the instance (a kept one, a direct prefab, or a provider load). |
| `Opening` | `OnOpen` returned and the show transition runs. |
| `Open` | Fully on screen. The view is interactive when nothing covers it. |
| `Closing` | The hide transition runs. |
| `Ended` | Finished. Its handle is inert and every awaiter has completed. |

Each layer runs one operation at a time, in the order requests were accepted, and a started step is
never interrupted. Two requests on one layer therefore never race; the second waits. A close asked
for while a view is still opening is remembered and runs when the open finishes. Only a terminate
cause (the owner ending, the view being destroyed or deactivated from outside, the root being
destroyed) or the transition timeout cut a transition short, and both snap the view. A load is also
cut short when its request is withdrawn (`Close()`, `Back()`, `CloseAll`, a screen change, or a
`CloseTo`, a return or a reopen in place that pops past it) or when the load timeout passes. See [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).

A request ends exactly once, with exactly one outcome. The first cause that ends it wins and later
causes are ignored.

---

## Outcomes are data

`ShowAsync` completes with a `ViewResult<TResult>` in every case. It does not throw for anything that
happens to the view: a refusal, a failed load, the owner ending or the root being destroyed all arrive
as values.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `WasShown` | The view reached the screen before it ended. |
| `Reason` | A `CloseReason`: `Completed`, `Dismissed`, `Back`, `Backdrop`, `Code`, `Navigated`, `OwnerEnded`, `Destroyed`, or `NotShown`. |
| `Rejected` | A `RejectReason` when it was never shown: `UnknownKey`, `Duplicate`, `Busy`, `Declined`, `OwnerEnded`, and others; `None` when it was shown. |
| `HasValue`, `Value` | The view's answer. `HasValue` is true only when the view was shown and closed itself with `Complete(value)`. |

A call site has one shape: await, then check `HasValue` or switch on `Reason`. The full tables and the
traps are in [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md); the reasoning is in
[ADR-001](Design/Decisions/ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md).

Exceptions are for usage errors only, raised at the call: a call off the main thread, a null argument,
an empty or whitespace-only view id, or a result factory given a combination that is not an outcome.
See [Threading](Threading.md).

---

## Every open has an owner

`Open` and `ShowAsync` take a `CancellationToken` as a required argument. That token is the **owner**
of the request. When it is cancelled, the request ends: a shown view is snapped away and reports
`CloseReason.OwnerEnded`, a waiting one is withdrawn and reports `NotShown` with `RejectReason.OwnerEnded`.
An owner that is already cancelled at the call ends the request at once, before anything is shown.

Pick the owner by asking what the view should not outlive:

| You want the view to end when | Pass |
|---|---|
| the UI as a whole goes away | `Navigator.RootToken`, cancelled when the root is destroyed |
| the screen that opened it ends | that screen's open-scope token, or a token it owns |
| a feature you control ends | a token source you cancel, linked to `RootToken` if you like |
| only someone closes it, or the root goes away | `CancellationToken.None` |

Do not pass the open-scope token of a screen to a view that replaces or pops that screen. A reopen in
place of the screen, or a pop that removes it, ends that scope, and the new request ends with it as
not shown. Pass `RootToken` there; the paragraph on reopening in
[Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#return-to-a-screen-that-is-already-open) has the details.

An owner decides the life of the **view**. It never cancels an awaiter: code that awaits
`ShowAsync` always resumes with a result, even when the owner ended first.

**A join is not bound to the token you pass.** A call that returns to a screen already on a history
layer (a key without arguments) joins that request and keeps its owner; the token you pass is
ignored. If your token ends, the request does not, and your `await` goes on until the request ends. To
stop waiting at a token of your own, wrap the call as shown in
[Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md#stopping-the-wait-at-your-own-token).

Registrations such as a
catalog, an observer or an input hold take an owner too and end with it; nothing needs a removal
line. A feature that brings its own catalog shows the pattern: a token source linked to the root's
token, handed to every registration the feature makes:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/NewsFeature.cs -->
```csharp
_owner = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(_navigator.RootToken);
_navigator.AddCatalog(_catalog, _owner.Token);
```

See [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md) for what ending that owner does and
[ADR-005](Design/Decisions/ADR-005-Token-Owners.md) for why the owner is a token.

---

## Scopes end what a view started

A view that subscribes to a button, starts a task or holds a disposable must undo that when it
closes. UIDirector gives the view no close hook for that. It hands the view a `ViewScope` and ends
the scope for you on every path.

| Scope | Created | Ends |
|---|---|---|
| Open scope | When the request is accepted; handed to `OnOpen` | When the request ends, however it ends: closed, withdrawn before it was shown, declined, owner ended, lost from outside, root destroyed |
| Visible scope | Each time the view comes on screen and is not covered; handed to `OnVisible` | When the view is covered, or when the request ends |

On a scope you `Bind` a `UnityEvent`, `Subscribe` to any other event, `Add` a disposable, register an
`OnEnd` action or `Run` a task. The package removes, disposes or cancels each one when the scope
ends, newest first. A scope that has already ended is inert: registering on it does the cleanup at
once and adds nothing. A scope reference kept after the view closed is therefore harmless, and
`ViewContext.Open` after the end returns that ended scope, never `null`.

[View authoring](View-Authoring.md) covers the hooks in full, and
[ADR-003](Design/Decisions/ADR-003-Begin-Only-Hooks-And-Scopes.md) explains why there are no close
hooks.

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Root-Canvas.md -->

# Root canvas

[Back to index](index.md)

This page is about the object everything else hangs on: the `ViewRoot` and the canvas under it. It
shows how to create a root, what every Inspector field does, how to initialize the root from code
with `ViewRootSetup`, how an overlay root differs from a camera root, how the sorting band is
numbered, how to add a layer of your own, what the Prefab Mode UI environment is for, and how to hide
the whole UI for a moment.

The examples come from the Basic Usage sample. Its root was made with the menu below, then
`Initialize On Awake` was turned off and the bootstrap initializes the root in code.

---

## Create a root

Choose `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root`. In the active scene it creates one outermost object,
`UIDirector Root`, on the UI layer, with:

- a `Canvas` in `Screen Space - Overlay` mode;
- a `CanvasScaler` set to `Scale With Screen Size`, reference resolution 1080 x 1920, match 0.5;
- a `ViewRoot`;
- a `BackInput`, which turns the Escape key into `Back()`. Android's back button is expected to arrive
  as Escape ([Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md#the-back-button)).

If the scene has no EventSystem, the menu also creates a separate outermost `EventSystem` object with
the input module that fits your project's input handling. It is not under the root, so Persist Across
Scenes does not keep it.

The root is built inactive and activated last, so its `Awake` sees the final render mode and camera.
The creation can be undone in one step. The canvas is yours: render mode, scaler, reference
resolution, sorting layer and shader channels are ordinary `Canvas` settings that you change as in any
uGUI project.

Then assign your catalogs in the `Catalogs` list ([Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md)). With
`Initialize On Awake` left on, the root initializes itself in its `Awake` with default settings, and
`ViewRoot.Navigator` is ready from then on. Turn it off when you want to initialize the root from code.

### The camera variant

Choose `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root (Camera)` when the UI must be drawn by its own camera. It
creates an outermost object `UIDirector` that holds two siblings:

```text
UIDirector                 outermost object, UI layer
  UIDirector Root          Canvas (Screen Space - Camera), CanvasScaler, ViewRoot, BackInput
  UI Camera                orthographic, clears depth only, draws the UI layer only
```

The camera clears depth only, so the scene stays visible under the UI. Its depth is set once, at
creation, to one above the highest camera depth in the loaded scenes. The new camera's own default of 0
counts, so the depth is at least 1 and the UI draws after the scene's cameras. The canvas takes the camera as its render camera, with a plane distance of 100.

The camera sits beside the root and not under it on purpose. A `Screen Space - Camera` canvas that is a
child of its own camera is placed at the camera's position and draws nothing.

---

## Initialize with ViewRootSetup

Numbers and references are Inspector fields. Code-only settings go through `ViewRootSetup`, passed to
`ViewRoot.Initialize` once, before anything reads `ViewRoot.Navigator`:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public void Initialize(ViewRootSetup setup);

public sealed class ViewRootSetup
{
    public Action<GameObject> Inject;
    public IViewProvider AssetProvider;
    public IReadOnlyList<ViewLayer> ExtraLayers;
    public ViewErrorHandler ErrorHandler;
}
```

The Basic Usage bootstrap keeps the root in a serialized field, turns `Initialize On Awake` off in the
Inspector, and initializes the root in its own `Awake`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// "Initialize On Awake" is off on this root; the bootstrap initialises it in Awake.
[SerializeField] private ViewRoot _viewRoot;
```

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
_viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup
{
    Inject = InjectServices,
    ErrorHandler = OnViewError,
    ExtraLayers = new[] { AppLayers.Toasts }
});
_navigator = _viewRoot.Navigator;
```

| Member | What it is | If left null |
|---|---|---|
| `Inject` | Runs on each new view instance while it is inactive, before its `Awake`. The seam for a container or for handing services to views. The sample's `InjectServices` gives its services to every component that asks. [Zenject](Zenject.md) shows a container as the injector | No injection |
| `AssetProvider` | Resolves catalog rows that carry an asset key ([Assets and Addressables](Assets-and-Addressables.md)) | An `IViewProvider` component on the root's object, if any; otherwise rows with an asset key fail with [UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120) |
| `ExtraLayers` | Layers declared in code, added to the three defaults. See [Add a layer of your own](#add-a-layer-of-your-own) | The three default layers |
| `ErrorHandler` | Receives exceptions from your code and from providers, with the view id, the request id and the failing step | The package logs them with `Debug.LogException` |

The Addressables sample passes an empty setup, so the provider component on the root's object is used:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/AddressablesBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// AssetProvider stays empty, so the AddressablesViewProvider on the root's GameObject is used.
_viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup());
```

What `Initialize` does and does not allow:

- **It runs once.** A second call throws `InvalidOperationException` ("The root is already
  initialised"). It also throws when the root was already initialized by `Initialize On Awake`, or by a
  read of `ViewRoot.Navigator`, and when the root was destroyed. A null setup throws
  `ArgumentNullException`.
- **Reading `ViewRoot.Navigator` on a root that is not initialized initializes it with default
  settings.** So code that needs a `ViewRootSetup` must call `Initialize` before any read. A
  destroyed root that was never initialized throws on that read.
- **Components that read the root early do not initialize it.** Before the root is initialized,
  `BackInput` ignores the back key, and a `ViewButton` with the Back or Open View action logs a warning
  and does nothing. Apart from `Initialize On Awake`, only your own read of `ViewRoot.Navigator` can initialize the root
  with defaults.
- **Both of the above are why `Initialize On Awake` must be off** when you call `Initialize`: with the
  setting on, the root initializes itself in `Awake`, and whether your call comes first depends on which
  `Awake` runs first.
- **Another script's `Awake` can initialize the root first.** With `Initialize On Awake` on, a script
  that reads `ViewRoot.Navigator` in its own `Awake` before the root's `Awake` has run initializes the
  root with default settings. The root's own `Awake` then sees an initialized root and skips its
  initialization without an error, and a later `Initialize(setup)` throws. Unity does not order the
  `Awake` methods of different objects, so do not rely on it. Initialize from one bootstrap with the flag
  off, as above, or read `Navigator` in `Start`: every `Awake` of the objects in a scene has run before
  the first `Start`, so with the flag on the root is already initialized by then.
- **It warns once when the scene has no EventSystem** ([UIDIRECTOR116](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector116)).
  Create the EventSystem before the call, as the sample does with `SampleEventSystem.EnsureExists()`.
- **A failure inside `Initialize` leaves nothing behind.** The layer list is validated before anything is
  built, and if a later step fails, the objects built so far are destroyed and the exception is
  rethrown.
- **A root can be initialized while it is inactive.** A dependency injection container may create the
  root inactive, call `Initialize` and activate it afterwards. Teardown happens in `OnDestroy`, which Unity
  sends only to an object that has been active; a root that is destroyed without ever becoming active
  never tears down ([Limitations](Limitations.md#lifetime-and-cleanup)).
- `ViewRoot.IsInitialized` is true once `Initialize` has completed, also after the root was destroyed.

---

## Every field of ViewRoot

`ViewRoot` requires a `Canvas` on the same object and allows one `ViewRoot` per object. Its
Inspector fields:

| Field | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Catalogs` | empty | `ViewCatalog` assets registered, in list order, when the root initializes. Add more later with `INavigator.AddCatalog`. Removing a catalog that was added that way leaves its open views open; they end only when their owner ends |
| `Base Sorting Order` | 0 | Sorting order where the package's band starts. Clamped to the 16-bit range in the Inspector. See [The sorting band](#the-sorting-band) |
| `Persist Across Scenes` | off | Keeps the root's outermost object across scene loads. See [Persist Across Scenes](#persist-across-scenes) |
| `Initialize On Awake` | on | Initializes the root with default settings in `Awake`. Turn it off to call `Initialize` with a `ViewRootSetup` |
| `Load Timeout Seconds` | 15 | Unscaled seconds a view may take to load. Then the open ends as not shown with `RejectReason.LoadTimedOut` ([UIDIRECTOR105](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector105)). Minimum 0.1 |
| `Transition Timeout Seconds` | 3 | Unscaled seconds a transition may run. Then it is snapped to its end pose ([UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106)). Minimum 0.1 |
| `Indicator Delay Seconds` | 0.4 | How long a load on a layer that shields input runs before the `Load Indicator` is shown. Minimum 0 |
| `Waiting Cap` | 4 | Requests one layer may hold waiting. The next is refused as `Busy` ([UIDIRECTOR112](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector112)). Minimum 1 |
| `Load Indicator` | none | An object the package activates while a load runs longer than the delay, and deactivates when no load is running |
| `Backdrop Color` | black, 60 percent opacity | Colour of the generated backdrop behind modal layers. Unused when a backdrop prefab is set |
| `Backdrop Prefab` | none | Instantiated behind each modal layer instead of the generated backdrop |

The Inspector keeps the minimums; a value below its minimum is raised when the field changes. The
timeouts and their clock are explained on
[Limitations](Limitations.md#timeouts-defaults-and-the-frame-clock).

**The sorting layer is not a field of `ViewRoot`.** It is the `Sorting Layer` of the root's `Canvas`, and
the package reads it every time it places a view, the shield, a backdrop or the load indicator. A
project that changes it at run time moves the whole band.

Details that the table cannot hold:

- **Load Indicator.** Start the object inactive. The package activates it when a load runs longer
  than the delay and deactivates it when no load is running. The indicator shows only for a
  load on a layer that shields input, which is the case for the three default layers. It gets its own
  canvas one order above the shield, and no raycaster, so it takes no input. A canvas that you put on
  it is reused: the package turns on its Override Sorting and sets its sorting layer and order as it
  would for a canvas it adds.
- **Backdrop Prefab.** The package instantiates it once for each modal layer under that layer, stretches
  it over the layer, and adds the `Canvas`, `GraphicRaycaster`, `CanvasGroup` and backdrop component it
  lacks. Give it a graphic with `Raycast Target` on, so a tap reaches it. A backdrop tap, its fade and
  the rule that a tap while the shield is up does nothing are on
  [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md).
- **Timeouts and the clock.** The root advances its clock in `Update` by the unscaled frame time, at
  most 0.1 s per frame, so a long hitch counts as one short step. Built-in transitions and the backdrop
  fade advance at most 1/30 s per frame, so below 30 fps they take longer than their duration, and a
  long one can be snapped by the transition timeout
  ([Limitations](Limitations.md#timeouts-defaults-and-the-frame-clock)).

---

## Overlay roots and camera roots

| | Overlay | Camera |
|---|---|---|
| Menu | `UIDirector Root` | `UIDirector Root (Camera)` |
| Canvas render mode | `Screen Space - Overlay` | `Screen Space - Camera`, render camera is the `UI Camera` |
| Outermost object | The root itself | The `UIDirector` holder with the root and the camera as siblings |
| Sorting layer | None: an overlay canvas has no sorting layer, and `Base Sorting Order` places the band | The `Sorting Layer` of the root canvas, plus `Base Sorting Order` |
| What the camera draws | No camera | The UI layer only |
| Content must be on | Any layer | The UI layer (layer 5): an object on another layer is culled |
| `Persist Across Scenes` | Keeps the root | Keeps the holder, so the camera survives with the root |
| If the camera is destroyed | Not applicable | Views may not render; logged as [UIDIRECTOR114](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector114) when the next view loads, once for each stretch of time the camera is missing |

Pick the overlay root unless the UI needs a camera of its own. Four rules for the camera root:

- **Keep the camera beside the root, never under it or under its canvas.**
- **Keep the camera alive as long as the root.** The holder layout does that; with `Persist Across
  Scenes` the camera persists with the root. A camera that lives elsewhere in the scene does not.
- **Put every object of a view on the UI layer,** including objects you create inside a view at run
  time. The camera's culling mask is the UI layer only. See [View authoring](View-Authoring.md).
- **Reassign `Canvas.worldCamera` if you replace the camera.** Unity reads a camera-mode canvas
  whose camera is gone as an overlay canvas; the package remembers the mode the root started with
  and warns with [UIDIRECTOR114](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector114) when the next view loads, once for
  each stretch of time the camera is missing.

World-space canvases are not supported ([Limitations](Limitations.md)).

---

## Persist Across Scenes

`Persist Across Scenes` calls `DontDestroyOnLoad` on the outermost object of the hierarchy the root
belongs to, in the root's `Awake`. It does not depend on `Initialize On Awake`. With the menu layouts
that is the root itself (overlay) or the `UIDirector` holder (camera), so the camera survives with the
root. If you parent the root under a larger object of your own, that whole object persists.

What it does not do:

- **It does not move an EventSystem.** The package keeps no EventSystem of its own. If the scene that
  loaded first owned the only one, the next scene has none and views stop receiving input. Keep exactly
  one EventSystem active at any time: put it under the persisted object, or create it from the code that
  starts the persisted root.
- **It does not load or unload scenes, and it closes nothing on a scene change.** A view lives as long
  as its owner token. Own long-lived views with `INavigator.RootToken`
  ([Limitations](Limitations.md)).
- **It does not stop a second root.** The root is not a singleton. Loading the scene that contains a
  persisted root again creates another root next to the first. Guard that in your own start-up code.

Without the setting a scene change destroys the root with its scene. Every view it holds ends, and the
awaiters complete: shown views with `CloseReason.Destroyed`, the others as not shown with
`RejectReason.RootGone`. A root that is destroyed this way logs nothing and `RootToken` is cancelled.

---

## The sorting band

Every view is a nested canvas with `Override Sorting` on. The root gives each one a sorting order
from a fixed formula, so the order depends only on the layer and on the view's slot:

```text
order = Base Sorting Order + layer order x 1000 + slot x 10
```

`slot` runs from 1 to 99 on each layer. A new view gets the highest live slot of its layer plus one,
and keeps it while it lives. The other objects sit relative to the layers:

| Object | Sorting order | With base 0 and the sample's `toasts` layer |
|---|---|---|
| A view on layer `L`, slot `s` | base + `L` order x 1000 + `s` x 10 | First popup: 1010. Second popup: 1020. First toast: 3010 |
| Reserved for canvases you nest in a view (you set them) | The view's order + 1 to + 4 | 1011 to 1014 for the first popup |
| The backdrop of a modal layer | The top on-screen view's order - 5 | 1005 under the first popup |
| The input shield | base + (highest layer order + 1) x 1000 | 4000. Without `toasts`: 3000 |
| The load indicator | The shield's order + 1, on its own canvas | 4001 |

Consequences:

- **Layers never interleave,** as long as every layer has its own order and keeps to its 99 slots. A
  popup is above every screen and a toast above every popup, however many views are open.
- **The shield and the indicator are above everything the package shows.** They sit above the highest
  layer, so a layer you add moves them up.
- **A view owns the four orders above its own.** Put particle systems or canvases that belong to a view
  on `ViewHost.SortingOrder + 1` to `+ 4`.
- **Your own canvases need a place in the band.** A HUD canvas that should always be under the views
  sorts below `Base Sorting Order`; one that should cover everything sorts above the shield. A value in
  between interleaves with views. A canvas that sorts itself above the shield, such as the open list of
  a TextMesh Pro dropdown, is not blocked by the shield
  ([Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md#the-input-shield)).
- **Two roots on one sorting layer need bases that keep their bands apart.** Nothing coordinates them.

### Canvas.sortingOrder is 16-bit and wraps silently

Unity stores `Canvas.sortingOrder` as a signed 16-bit value. A larger number does not throw: it wraps
to a negative one, and a view would draw under everything. The package therefore never assigns a number
outside the range. Before it accepts a request it checks that the view's order, with its four nested
orders, stays below 29999, that the backdrop's order stays in the 16-bit range, and that the shield
stays below 29999. A request that does not fit ends as not shown with `RejectReason.Busy` and logs
[UIDIRECTOR115](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector115), an error.

The causes are a `Base Sorting Order` near the top of the range, a layer of your own with a very high
order (each layer takes 1000 orders), or 99 live views on one layer. Slots come back only when the views
on top of a layer end. The Inspector clamps the base to the 16-bit range, which is not enough to stay
inside the band: keep the base low.

---

## Add a layer of your own

A layer is an immutable value: an id, an order and a set of rules. Declare it as a `static readonly`
field so that every place that needs it reads the same value. The Basic Usage sample declares a layer
for toasts above the system layer, with no rules, so a toast neither blocks a tap nor takes back:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppLayers.cs -->
```csharp
// Above the system layer, no history, no back and no input shield: a toast never blocks a tap.
public static readonly ViewLayer Toasts = new ViewLayer("toasts", 3, ViewLayerRules.None);
```

Hand it to the root in `ViewRootSetup.ExtraLayers` (the `Initialize` call above does), and name its id
in the `Layer Id` field of a catalog row. The root merges your layers with the three defaults and sorts
them by order; layers with the same order keep the order you gave them.

- **The order decides where it draws.** A layer with order 3 is drawn above `system` (2) and, through
  the formula above, gets the orders from 3000 up.
- **The rules decide how it behaves.** `ViewLayerRules.None` is a plain layer: it holds no shield,
  takes no back and covers nothing. Combine the flags of `ViewLayerRules` for more; they are explained
  on [Concepts](Concepts.md#one-root-layers-with-rules).
- **The validator finds it.** `Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs` reads every static `ViewLayer`
  field of the assemblies that reference the package, so a row naming `toasts` is accepted. A layer
  that is not in a static field is unknown to it, and its rows are reported as
  [UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109).
- **Give each layer an order of its own.** Two layers with the same order get the same sorting orders
  and their views interleave.
- **Ids are unique.** An extra layer whose id is already used, including `screens`, `popups` and
  `system`, or the same layer listed twice, makes `Initialize` throw `ArgumentException` with the id in
  its message. The check runs before anything is built, so nothing is left under the root. A `null` entry
  is skipped.
- **A row can name only layers the root has.** On a root without the layer the row is refused when its
  catalog is registered ([UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109)), and opening that id ends as
  not shown with `RejectReason.UnknownKey` ([UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101)).

The view on that layer is an ordinary view. The sample's toast closes itself after two seconds, on
unscaled time:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ToastView.cs -->
```csharp
private async UniTask CloseAfterDelay(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Unscaled time, so a paused game (timeScale 0) still dismisses the toast.
    await UniTask.Delay(ShowTime, DelayType.UnscaledDeltaTime, cancellationToken: ct);
    Close();
}
```

Because the layer has no `ShieldsInput`, opening a toast never raises the input shield, and the screen
under it stays usable. Because it has no `TakesBack`, a toast never swallows a back press. The full
rules of the other layers are on [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md) and
[System overlays](System-Overlays.md).

---

## The Prefab Mode UI environment

A view prefab has a `Canvas` on its root (`ViewHost` requires it), and no `CanvasScaler`: the scaler is
on the root canvas. Opened in Prefab Mode, the prefab then has no scaler above it and opens at the wrong
size. Unity lets a project set a UI environment scene for Prefab Mode, and the package can write one
that matches your root.

Choose `Tools > UIDirector > Create Prefab UI Environment`. With a root selected (or one of its
children), the environment copies that root's canvas settings (render mode, plane distance, sorting
layer and order, pixel perfect, shader channels) and its `CanvasScaler`. With nothing selected it writes
an overlay canvas with a default scaler. The menu then asks where to save the scene and whether to
assign it as the project's Prefab Mode UI environment.

- The first time you create a root in an editor session, the package offers to create the environment
  once, when no UI environment is assigned. It does not offer in batch mode and never saves your open
  scene.
- The scene must be saved under `Assets/` and end in `.unity`. It cannot be created in Play Mode, over
  an open scene, or while an untitled scene is open: save that scene first.
- A camera is not copied. The environment scene has none, so a camera-mode canvas renders as an
  overlay canvas there.

With the environment assigned, Prefab Mode places a nested-canvas view prefab under the environment's
canvas and lays it out in the scaler's reference units. With a 1080 x 1920 scaler the view fills the
scaled canvas at the Scene view's aspect; without an environment Unity's default canvas has no scaler and
the same view is laid out in Scene view pixels.

---

## Hide the whole UI for a moment

To hide every view for a cutscene or a screenshot without ending any of them, add a `CanvasGroup` to the
root's object, set it to alpha 0 and not interactable, and hold input while it is hidden. Undo all of it
afterwards. The `rootCanvas`, `navigator` and `owner` below are the root's `Canvas`, its navigator and the
token that owns the hold:

<!-- source: Tests/Runtime/Stage/HideUiRecipeTests.cs -->
```csharp
var group = rootCanvas.gameObject.AddComponent<CanvasGroup>();
group.alpha = 0f;
group.interactable = false;
var hold = navigator.HoldInput("cutscene", owner);
```

And later:

<!-- source: Tests/Runtime/Stage/HideUiRecipeTests.cs -->
```csharp
hold.Remove();
group.alpha = 1f;
group.interactable = true;
```

To restore exactly, remember what was there. If the root already had a `CanvasGroup`, read its `alpha`
and `interactable` before you change them and write the same values back, instead of 1 and true. If you
added the group yourself, either keep it and reset it to alpha 1 and interactable true, as the recipe
does, or `Destroy` it when the hide ends.

Each part has a job. Alpha 0 on the root group hides every uGUI graphic under the root: the views, the
backdrops, the input shield, and the load indicator when it is a child of the root (an indicator placed
elsewhere in the scene keeps drawing). The group reaches the view canvases because a nested
canvas that does not set `ignoreParentGroups` inherits the alpha of its parents. `interactable = false`
stops keyboard and gamepad navigation, because `Selectable.IsInteractable` walks the groups above a
selectable across nested canvases. The hold raises the input shield, which takes pointer input. Views that
are opened, closed or restored while the UI is hidden behave as usual and are drawn again when the group
is restored. Keep the group and reuse it; take a new hold for each hide.

What to avoid and what to expect:

- **Do not disable the root `Canvas` component.** Each view is a nested canvas with its own sorting, and a
  disabled parent canvas does not stop it from drawing, and it keeps its own
  raycaster. The same goes for `blocksRaycasts = false` on the root group, which
  does not reach the nested canvases. The shield from `HoldInput` is what blocks input.
- **Do not deactivate the root object or a layer object.** That ends every view under it with
  [UIDIRECTOR107](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector107).
- **A view `CanvasGroup` with `ignoreParentGroups` set ignores the root group.** That view stays visible.
  Clear the flag on views that should hide.
- **Back is swallowed while the hold is up, except that it still withdraws a request that is waiting or loading.**
  While the hold is up, `Back()` closes no shown view and returns true, so `BackInput.Unhandled` is not
  raised. It does end the newest request that is
  still waiting or loading on a layer that takes back, unless its row's `Back` is `Ignore`, as not shown
  with `RejectReason.Cancelled`.
  To ignore the back key altogether during the hide, set `BackInput.enabled = false` and enable it again
  afterwards. A disabled `BackInput` does not read the key at all (with the Input System package its
  action is disabled too). Disable the component, not the object it sits on: with the menu layout that
  object is the root.
- **`ViewButton` clicks are blocked while the hold is up.** A pointer press reaches the input shield
  before it reaches the button, so a `ViewButton` with any action does not fire. `interactable = false`
  on the root group covers keyboard and gamepad submit.
- **A hold older than 30 seconds logs [UIDIRECTOR110](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector110).** Remove it when
  the hide ends.
- **Hidden views still run.** `Update`, animators and transitions keep running under alpha 0, so the cost
  is not zero. Particle systems and other renderers that are not uGUI graphics ignore the group and keep
  drawing: stop or disable them for the hide. For a long hide, close the views instead.
- **The group is yours to restore.** When `owner` ends, the hold is removed but the group stays at alpha 0
  and not interactable, so the UI stays hidden. Restore the group in the same place that ends the owner,
  or use an owner that lives as long as the code that restores it.

---

## Traps

- **`Initialize On Awake` on while `Initialize` is called from code.** The second initialization
  throws. Turn the setting off.
- **A read of `ViewRoot.Navigator` before `Initialize`.** It initializes the root with defaults and the
  later `Initialize` throws.
- **A camera root whose objects are not on the UI layer.** The views exist but nothing is drawn.
- **A `UI Camera` placed under the root.** The canvas draws nothing.
- **A persisted root and no EventSystem in the next scene.** Views are drawn and do not react.
- **A very high `Base Sorting Order` or layer order.** Requests are refused with
  [UIDIRECTOR115](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector115); the sorting order would otherwise wrap.
- **A Load Indicator left active in the scene.** It shows from the start until a load that outlasts the
  delay ends, and is then switched off.
- **Deactivating the root object or a layer object.** It ends every view under it. Hide the whole UI with
  the group and hold in [Hide the whole UI for a moment](#hide-the-whole-ui-for-a-moment) instead.
- **Disabling the root `Canvas` to hide the UI.** Nested view canvases keep drawing.

## See also

- [Concepts](Concepts.md)
- [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md)
- [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md)
- [System overlays](System-Overlays.md)
- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md)
- [Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md)
- [Zenject](Zenject.md)
- [Assets and Addressables](Assets-and-Addressables.md)
- [Limitations](Limitations.md)
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md)
- [Architecture: the root and its layers](Design/Architecture.md#2-the-root-and-its-layers)
