<!-- file: Documentation~/Catalogs-and-Keys.md -->

# Catalogs and keys

[Back to index](index.md)

A view prefab becomes openable when a catalog row describes it and a key names that row. This page
covers the whole path: creating a `ViewCatalog` asset and its rows (every field of a row), writing
typed keys, giving the catalogs to the root, adding and removing a catalog at run time, keeping ids
unique, and checking everything with the validator before you press Play. The model behind it is in
[Concepts](Concepts.md).

---

## The shortest path

1. Create a catalog: `Assets > Create > UIDirector/View Catalog`.
2. Select it, add a row to the list and fill it: an `Id`, the `Prefab`, and the `Layer Id` it opens on
   (the default is `screens`). The prefab root needs a `ViewHost` and a component that implements
   `IView<TArgs, TResult>`; see [View authoring](View-Authoring.md).
3. Drag the catalog into the `Catalogs` list of the `ViewRoot` in your scene.
4. Write a key for the row, in a static class marked `[ViewKeys]`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppViews.cs -->
```csharp
[ViewKeys]
public static class AppViews
{
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Home = ViewKey.Create("home");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Library = ViewKey.Create("library");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ItemArgs, NoResult> ItemDetail = ViewKey.Create<ItemArgs>("item-detail");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Settings = ViewKey.Create("settings");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ConfirmArgs, bool> Confirm = ViewKey.Create<ConfirmArgs, bool>("confirm");
    public static readonly ViewKey<RenameArgs, string> Rename = ViewKey.Create<RenameArgs, string>("rename");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Saving = ViewKey.Create("saving");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ToastArgs, NoResult> Toast = ViewKey.Create<ToastArgs>("toast");
}
```

5. Run `Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs`. A clean run logs
   `UIDirector catalog validation PASSED: 0 error(s), 0 warning(s), 1 catalog(s).` (the last number is
   how many catalogs the project holds)

The key `Home` now opens the row whose `Id` is `home`; see [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).
Ids are plain strings and are compared exactly, so `Home` and `home` are two ids.

---

## Make a view and its row

Catalogs, rows, view prefabs and the root's `Catalogs` list are authored in the editor, in the
Inspector. Nothing here is built from code (see [Limitations](Limitations.md#setup)). The whole path for
one new view:

1. **Build the prefab.** Make a UI object (it has a `RectTransform`) and save it as a prefab. On its
   root add:
   - a `ViewHost`; Unity adds the `Canvas` and `GraphicRaycaster` it requires. Do not add a
     `CanvasScaler`.
   - your view component, on the same object: a class derived from `ViewBehaviour`,
     `ViewBehaviour<TArgs>` or `ViewBehaviour<TArgs, TResult>`, or one that implements
     `IView<TArgs, TResult>` ([View authoring](View-Authoring.md)). Assign its serialized fields (buttons,
     texts) in the prefab.
   - optionally a transition (`FadeTransition`, `ScaleTransition` or `SlideTransition`) dragged into the
     `Transition` field of the `ViewHost`. A view without one shows and hides instantly. See
     [Transitions](Transitions.md#put-a-built-in-transition-on-a-view).
2. **Create or pick a catalog.** `Assets > Create > UIDirector/View Catalog` makes a `ViewCatalog`
   asset. Select it and press `+` on its list to add a row.
3. **Fill the row.** `Id` (unique, matches the key), `Prefab` (drag the prefab) or `Asset Key` (when the
   prefab loads on demand), `Layer Id` (`screens`, `popups`, `system` or a layer you declared), then
   the policies you need: `Retention`, `Back`, `Close On Backdrop`, `Cover`, `When Covered`,
   `Allow Multiple`. The defaults suit a plain screen. Every field is described in
   [A catalog row](#a-catalog-row).
4. **Give the catalog to the root.** Select the `ViewRoot` in the scene (create one with
   `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root`), add an element to its `Catalogs` list and drag the catalog in.
   A catalog that is not in that list, and was not passed to `AddCatalog`, opens nothing.
5. **Write the key** in a `[ViewKeys]` class, with the same id and the argument and result types of the
   view component (see [Keys](#keys)).
6. **Validate.** `Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs`, or the `Validate` button under the rows of the
   catalog. A missing `ViewHost`, a view component that does not match the key and an unknown layer are
   reported before you press Play. For a row with an `Asset Key`, the prefab checks run only when
   Addressables is installed and the key resolves to an address.

---

## A catalog row

A `ViewCatalog` is a list of `ViewEntry` rows. The Inspector draws the list with the default
Inspector, followed by a validation block (see [Validate](#validate)). Rows are authored in the
Inspector; `ViewEntry` has no public constructor and a catalog's row list cannot be filled from code, so a catalog that opens anything is an asset.

| Field | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Id` | empty | The name code and remote data use for this view. Must be set and unique across every catalog on the root. An id that is empty or only whitespace is [UIDIRECTOR125](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector125): the validator reports it and the root refuses the row. An id with spaces around other characters is valid and is not trimmed. |
| `Prefab` | none | A direct reference to the view prefab. The prefab stays resident while its catalog is loaded; opening instantiates it at once, under an inactive parent so `Awake` has not run yet. Its root needs a `ViewHost` ([UIDIRECTOR103](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector103)). |
| `Asset Key` | empty | Used only when `Prefab` is empty. A string the root's view provider resolves, so nothing is resident until the view opens. With neither prefab nor key the row is [UIDIRECTOR121](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector121). With a key and no provider the open fails with `RejectReason.LoadFailed` ([UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120)). See [Assets and Addressables](Assets-and-Addressables.md). |
| `Layer Id` | `screens` | The id of the layer the view opens on: `screens`, `popups`, `system`, or a layer you declared. A row naming a layer the root does not have is refused at registration ([UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109)). |
| `Retention` | `ReleaseOnClose` | What happens to the instance when the view closes. `ReleaseOnClose` releases it. `KeepInstance` parks one idle instance per id, hidden and deactivated, and reuses it on the next open without injecting again. The view's `OnOpen` runs again on every open either way. |
| `Back` | `LayerDefault` | What `Back()` does when this view is the back target. `LayerDefault` follows the layer, `Close` closes the view with `CloseReason.Back`, `Ignore` swallows back and keeps the view open, `HandledByView` asks the view's `IViewBack.OnBack`; when it returns `false` the layer's rule applies, as with `LayerDefault`. `Close` on a layer without `TakesBack` is [UIDIRECTOR122](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector122). See [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md). |
| `Close On Backdrop` | off | On a modal layer, a tap on the backdrop closes this view with `CloseReason.Backdrop`, when the view is fully open. A tap while the input shield is up does nothing. See [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md). |
| `Cover` | `LayerDefault` | Whether the view hides what is below it once it is fully open. `LayerDefault` covers on a history layer and does not elsewhere; `Covers` always hides what is below; `Transparent` never does. |
| `When Covered` | `DisableCanvas` | How a covered view is hidden. `DisableCanvas` turns off every enabled canvas under the view and turns only those back on at reveal; the view keeps running. `Deactivate` deactivates the view object, which stops its `Update`, animators and particles, at the cost of a rebuild when it returns. |
| `Allow Multiple` | off | More than one instance of this id may exist at once. Without it a second open of an id that is already open or in flight is refused with `RejectReason.Duplicate` on a non-history layer, or returns to the existing screen on a history layer (and reopens it in place when the key has arguments). |

Some notes on the fields people ask about:

- **`Prefab` wins over `Asset Key`.** When both are set the direct reference is used and the key is
  ignored. Use the key alone when you want the asset to load on demand.
- **The id and the asset key are separate on purpose.** Code and remote data name the id; the key may
  change when an address is renamed, and only the row changes.
- **`KeepInstance` keeps one idle instance per id and nothing more.** There is no budget and no
  timer. `INavigator.Trim()` releases every idle kept instance, and the root calls it on
  `Application.lowMemory`. A deep stack of heavy screens stays resident, so keep stacks shallow with
  `CloseTo`.
- **`Cover` and `When Covered` are independent.** One says whether the view hides what is below it,
  the other says how a view that is hidden is switched off.

---

## Keys

A key is the compile-time half of a row: the id plus the type of the arguments the view takes and the
type of the value it answers with.

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public readonly struct ViewKey<TArgs, TResult>
{
    public ViewKey(string id);
    public string Id { get; }
}
```

You rarely call the constructor. `ViewKey.Create` has three forms:

| Call | Key type | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `ViewKey.Create("home")` | `ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult>` | A view with no arguments and no answer |
| `ViewKey.Create<ItemArgs>("item-detail")` | `ViewKey<ItemArgs, NoResult>` | A view that takes arguments and answers nothing |
| `ViewKey.Create<ConfirmArgs, bool>("confirm")` | `ViewKey<ConfirmArgs, bool>` | A view that takes arguments and answers with a value |

A null id throws `ArgumentNullException`, and an id that is empty or only whitespace throws
`ArgumentException`, at the point the key is created. An id with spaces around other characters is
accepted as written and compared exactly. In a static field the exception surfaces as a
`TypeInitializationException` when the class is first used, and the class's other keys fail with it.
The validator cannot read any key of such a class and skips them all, so fix a blank id first.

**What the types do.**

- The call site is checked by the compiler: `Navigator.ShowAsync(AppViews.Confirm, new ConfirmArgs(...), ...)`
  takes a `ConfirmArgs` and completes with a `ViewResult<bool>`.
- At open time the package looks for a component on the prefab root that implements
  `IView<TArgs, TResult>` for exactly the key's types. If there is none the request ends as not shown
  with `RejectReason.TypeMismatch` ([UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102)). The key and the
  view must agree on both types, including `NoArgs` and `NoResult`.
- Use `NoArgs` and `NoResult` for "nothing". They are empty structs defined by the package.
- Argument and result types can be any type. Small `readonly struct` types, as in the sample's
  `ViewArgs.cs`, make the arguments immutable and allocate nothing. Under IL2CPP each struct
  combination adds its own copy of the generic code, so keep the number of distinct struct types
  modest, or use classes where code size matters.
- On a history layer the type of the arguments matters to the stack: a key without arguments
  (`NoArgs`) returns to an existing screen of that id, and a key with arguments reopens that screen in
  place with the new arguments. See [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md).

**Shortcuts.** For a key without arguments, `INavigator` has extension methods that fill in the empty
arguments: `ShowAsync(key, owner)` and `Open(key, owner)`. `CloseTo(key)` and `IsOpen(key)` take any
key and read its id.

**Where keys live.** Put the keys of one area in one static class and mark it `[ViewKeys]`, as
`AppViews` does above. The mark costs nothing at run time. It tells the validator to read every
static `ViewKey` field of that class, public or not, and report any key with no row
([UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101)) or whose prefab has no matching view
([UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102)). A feature that ships its own catalog ships its
own keys class, apart from the app's:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/NewsViews.cs -->
```csharp
[ViewKeys]
public static class NewsViews
{
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoticeArgs, NoResult> News = ViewKey.Create<NoticeArgs>("news");
}
```

A key that is not in a `[ViewKeys]` class still works, but nothing checks it before you press Play.
Classes in test assemblies (assemblies that reference NUnit) are skipped, because test fixtures have
no catalog rows.

---

## Give the catalogs to the root

The `ViewRoot` Inspector has a `Catalogs` list. Every catalog in it is registered when the root
initialises, in list order. Catalogs are Inspector data, so they are not part of `ViewRootSetup`;
`ViewRootSetup` carries the code-only settings (`Inject`, `AssetProvider`, `ExtraLayers`,
`ErrorHandler`).

A row can only name a layer that exists on the root. The three built-in layers always exist. A layer
of your own is declared in code, as the Basic Usage sample does for its toast layer:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppLayers.cs -->
```csharp
// Above the system layer, no history, no back and no input shield: a toast never blocks a tap.
public static readonly ViewLayer Toasts = new ViewLayer("toasts", 3, ViewLayerRules.None);
```

and passed to the root in `ExtraLayers`, with the rest of the code-only setup. Turn off
`Initialize On Awake` on the `ViewRoot`, then call `Initialize` once, before anything reads
`ViewRoot.Navigator`. With the flag on, the root initialises itself with default settings and a second
`Initialize` throws `InvalidOperationException`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
_viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup
{
    Inject = InjectServices,
    ErrorHandler = OnViewError,
    ExtraLayers = new[] { AppLayers.Toasts }
});
```

Rows then set `Layer Id` to `toasts`. The root merges extra layers with the three defaults and sorts
them by order; layers with an equal order keep the order you gave. An extra layer whose id repeats
the id of another layer makes `Initialize` throw an `ArgumentException`.

Declare each extra layer as a `static` field of type `ViewLayer`, as above. The validator finds
layers by reading those fields; a layer built inline and never stored in a static field is unknown to
it, and every row that names it is reported as [UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109)
although it works at run time.

---

## Add and remove a catalog at run time

A feature that is not always present can bring its own catalog and register it while the app runs.
`INavigator.AddCatalog(catalog, owner)` registers every row of the catalog until `owner` ends or the
returned `ViewRegistration` is removed. The owner is the same kind of token as the owner of a view
(see [Concepts](Concepts.md#every-open-has-an-owner)), so the registration needs no removal line.

`NewsFeature` in the Queue Usage sample keeps one token source for everything the feature adds. It is
linked to the root's token, so the feature ends with the root, or earlier on `Remove`:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/NewsFeature.cs -->
```csharp
_owner = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(_navigator.RootToken);
_navigator.AddCatalog(_catalog, _owner.Token);
```

Taking the feature away is ending that owner:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/NewsFeature.cs -->
```csharp
_owner.Cancel();
_owner.Dispose();
_owner = null;
```

What each call does:

- **Registration.** Every acceptable row is registered. The checks run in this order, and a refused
  row claims no id: a row whose id is empty or only whitespace is refused with
  [UIDIRECTOR125](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector125), a row that names an unknown layer with
  [UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109), and a row whose id is already registered with
  [UIDIRECTOR108](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector108). All three are logged as errors, and the other
  rows of the same catalog still register.
- **Bad calls.** A null catalog throws `ArgumentNullException`. A call off the main thread throws
  `InvalidOperationException`. When the root is gone or the owner is already cancelled the call
  registers nothing and returns an inactive registration (`IsActive` is `false`).
- **Removal.** `registration.Remove()` and the owner ending do the same thing, and either is safe to
  repeat. The ids of the catalog become unknown to new opens (`RejectReason.UnknownKey`) and are free
  again, so the same rows can be registered later without [UIDIRECTOR108](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector108).
- **Views that are already open keep their row.** Removing a catalog does not close them; they
  finish normally. A kept instance of a removed row is released, and a view of a removed row that
  closes later is released instead of kept.
- **An open view ends with the catalog only when it shares the owner.** In the sample the news popup
  is opened with the same owner as the catalog, so ending the owner removes the catalog and also ends
  the popup: a shown popup closes with `CloseReason.OwnerEnded` and a waiting one is withdrawn.

---

## Ids are unique across all catalogs

All catalogs registered on one root share one id space. Ids are compared exactly, including case.

- If two rows share an id, the **first one wins**. At run time the second row is refused and logged as
  [UIDIRECTOR108](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector108); the first row opens normally. The order is the
  `Catalogs` list order, then the order of `AddCatalog` calls, then the order of rows in a catalog.
- Registering the same catalog twice refuses every row of the second registration.
- The validator treats every `ViewCatalog` in the project as one id space, so it reports a clash even
  between two catalogs that no root registers together. Give each feature its own id prefix or pick
  ids that cannot meet. The Basic Usage and Queue Usage samples use disjoint ids for this reason.
- A row refused for an unknown layer ([UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109)) or an empty
  id claims no id, in the root and in the validator. A later row with the same id on a known layer is
  the one that registers, and it is not reported as a duplicate.

---

## Validate

`Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs` checks every `ViewCatalog` in the project and every static class
marked `[ViewKeys]`. It logs one line per finding, with the id first and the Troubleshooting anchor
last, then a summary:

```text
UIDIRECTOR108: Row 3 ('item') in catalog 'Ui' repeats the id first used by Row 0 ('item') in catalog 'Core'; the second row is refused. (see Troubleshooting#uidirector108)
UIDirector catalog validation FAILED: 1 error(s), 0 warning(s), 2 catalog(s).
```

The same checks run in the catalog's Inspector. The block under the rows lists the findings of that
catalog; the `Validate` button runs it again and the `?` next to a finding opens its section of the
documentation. The Inspector validates every catalog in the project, so a clash with another catalog
shows up on the catalog that holds the second row.

| Id | Severity | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| [UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101) | Error | A key field of a `[ViewKeys]` class has no catalog row the root registers; when rows with that id exist but all name an unknown layer, the message names the first of them |
| [UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102) | Error | The prefab root has no component implementing `IView<TArgs, TResult>` for the key |
| [UIDIRECTOR103](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector103) | Error | The prefab root has no `ViewHost` |
| [UIDIRECTOR108](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector108) | Error | Two rows on known layers share an id; the first wins |
| [UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109) | Error | A row names a layer that does not exist |
| [UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120) | Warning | A row has an asset key and Addressables is not installed |
| [UIDIRECTOR121](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector121) | Error | A row has neither a prefab nor an asset key |
| [UIDIRECTOR122](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector122) | Warning | `Back` is `Close` on a layer that does not take back |
| [UIDIRECTOR123](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector123) | Warning | The prefab contains a dropdown |
| [UIDIRECTOR124](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector124) | Warning | The asset key matches no Addressables address, GUID or label |
| [UIDIRECTOR125](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector125) | Error | A row has an empty or whitespace-only id; the root reports it too when it refuses the row |

In a build pipeline run the validator in batch mode with
`-executeMethod Ecanakli.UIDirector.EditorTools.CatalogValidation.RunFromCommandLine`. It exits with
code 1 when any error exists and 0 otherwise; warnings never fail a run.

---

## Traps

- **A key is not checked until it is in a `[ViewKeys]` class.** A mistyped id in an unmarked class
  fails at the first open with `RejectReason.UnknownKey` ([UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101)).
- **The key's types must match the view's.** The compiler cannot see the prefab. A `ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult>`
  for a view that implements `IView<ItemArgs, NoResult>` fails at open time, not at compile time. The
  validator finds it before you press Play.
- **The view component sits on the prefab root,** next to the `ViewHost`. A component on a child
  object is not found.
- **A catalog that is not on the root opens nothing.** Check the `Catalogs` list, or call `AddCatalog`
  before the first open of its ids.
- **A refused row is silent in the game, loud in the log.**
  [UIDIRECTOR108](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector108),
  [UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109) and
  [UIDIRECTOR125](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector125) are logged in the editor and in development
  builds only; a release build refuses the row without a message. Run the validator before you ship.
- **The validator is not run for you.** Nothing checks catalogs at build time unless your pipeline
  calls the batch entry point.

---

- [API reference](API-Reference.md): `ViewCatalog`, `ViewEntry`, `ViewKey`, `ViewLayer`

<!-- file: Documentation~/View-Authoring.md -->

# View authoring

[Back to index](index.md)

This page covers the component on a view prefab: the two ways to write it, every hook the package calls and when, refusing an open, completing with a result, tying listeners and tasks to a scope so nothing has to be removed on close, kept instances, and what the prefab must look like. How a caller opens a view and reads its result is [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).

---

## Write a view on the base class

Derive from `ViewBehaviour`, implement `OnOpen`, and bind to the scope you are given:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ConfirmView.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class ConfirmView : ViewBehaviour<ConfirmArgs, bool>
{
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _title;
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _message;
    [SerializeField] private Button _accept;
    [SerializeField] private Button _decline;

    protected override void OnOpen(ConfirmArgs args, ViewScope open)
    {
        _title.text = args.Title;
        _message.text = args.Message;

        // The package removes both listeners when this open ends.
        open.Bind(_accept.onClick, Accept);
        open.Bind(_decline.onClick, Refuse);
    }

    private void Accept()
    {
        Complete(true);
    }

    private void Refuse()
    {
        Complete(false);
    }
}
```

The component sits on the prefab root, on the same object as the `ViewHost`. Pick the base class that matches the key the view is opened with:

| Base class | Key | `OnOpen` receives |
|---|---|---|
| `ViewBehaviour` | `ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult>` | `NoArgs args, ViewScope open` |
| `ViewBehaviour<TArgs>` | `ViewKey<TArgs, NoResult>` | `TArgs args, ViewScope open` |
| `ViewBehaviour<TArgs, TResult>` | `ViewKey<TArgs, TResult>` | `TArgs args, ViewScope open` |

The plain `ViewBehaviour` has no arguments and no result, so `OnOpen` takes `NoArgs` and ignores it (`HomeView` in the Basic Usage sample):

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/HomeView.cs -->
```csharp
protected override void OnOpen(NoArgs args, ViewScope open)
{
    open.Bind(_library.onClick, OpenLibrary);
    open.Bind(_settings.onClick, OpenSettings);
}
```

The key's argument and result types must equal the base class type arguments. A mismatch ends the open as not shown with [UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102). Keys are covered in [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md).

What the base class gives you:

| Member | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OnOpen(TArgs args, ViewScope open)` | Required. Runs once per open. |
| `OnVisible(ViewScope visible)` | Optional override. Runs each time the view comes on screen. |
| `OnBack()` | Optional override. Asked when Back targets the view and its row says `HandledByView`. Returns `false` by default. |
| `Complete(TResult value)` | Closes the view with a value. |
| `Close()` | Closes the view without a value. |
| `Decline(string reason = null)` | Inside `OnOpen` only: refuses the open. |
| `Navigator` | The `INavigator` of the root that opened the view. `null` before the first open. |
| `OpenScope` | The scope of the current open. `null` before the first open. |

## Write a view without the base class

A view that already derives from another class implements the interfaces. `IView<TArgs, TResult>` is required, `IViewVisible` and `IViewBack` are optional:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public interface IView<TArgs, TResult>
{
    void OnOpen(TArgs args, ViewContext<TResult> context);
}

public interface IViewVisible
{
    void OnVisible(ViewScope visible);
}

public interface IViewBack
{
    bool OnBack();
}
```

`ViewContext<TResult>` is what one open hands to the view: `Navigator`, `Handle`, `Open` (the open scope), `Complete(value)`, `Close()` and `Decline(reason)`. Keep the reference if the view completes later:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/RenameView.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class RenameView : MonoBehaviour, IView<RenameArgs, string>, IViewBack, IServiceReceiver
{
    [SerializeField] private TMP_InputField _input;
    [SerializeField] private Button _save;
    [SerializeField] private Button _cancel;
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _hint;

    private ViewContext<string> _context;
    private IItemLibrary _library;
    private bool _edited;
    private bool _discardHintShown;
```

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/RenameView.cs -->
```csharp
public void OnOpen(RenameArgs args, ViewContext<string> context)
{
    _context = context;

    // Decline is the right call inside OnOpen: nothing is shown and the caller sees Declined.
    if (!_library.CanRename(args.ItemId))
    {
        context.Decline("This item cannot be renamed.");
        return;
    }

    // A reused instance must not carry state from the previous open.
    _edited = false;
    _discardHintShown = false;
    _hint.text = string.Empty;
    _input.SetTextWithoutNotify(args.CurrentTitle);

    context.Open.Bind(_input.onValueChanged, MarkEdited);
    context.Open.Bind(_save.onClick, Save);
    context.Open.Bind(_cancel.onClick, Cancel);
}
```

The package finds the hooks by interface on the prefab root. `IViewVisible` and `IViewBack` must be implemented by the same component as `IView`, not by a second component. A view on a child object is not found ([UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102)).

`RenameView` also implements `IServiceReceiver`, a stand-in of the sample for however your project hands services to a view. It is not part of the package. Injection through the root is covered in [Zenject](Zenject.md).

---

## Lifecycle: what runs when

For a view whose row has the default retention (`ReleaseOnClose`), one open runs in this order:

1. **Created inactive.** The instance is created under the root's inactive staging object. The inject delegate of `ViewRootSetup` runs on it while it is inactive, so injection happens before `Awake`.
2. **Placed.** The package deactivates the instance, parents it to its layer and activates it. It does not switch any canvas or raycaster: `Awake` and `OnEnable` run now, without arguments, on an object whose canvases and raycasters are as you authored them, and a canvas or raycaster that they or `OnOpen` turn on or off stays that way. The transition's hidden state and the own canvas's sorting are applied after `OnOpen`. Do not read arguments or `Navigator` here.
3. **`OnOpen(args, context)`.** Once per open, before the first visible frame. This is where the view reads its arguments and binds.
4. **`OnVisible(visible)`.** The first visual state is applied and the visible scope begins. The show transition plays right after, so the hook runs at the start of the show, not at its end.
5. **Open.** The view is interactive when nothing covers it.
6. **Covered and revealed.** When another view covers it, its visible scope ends. When it is revealed, a new visible scope begins and `OnVisible` runs again. `OnOpen` does not.
7. **`OnBack()`.** Only when Back targets this view, the view is `Open`, and its catalog row sets `BackPolicy.HandledByView`.
8. **Closed.** The first close cause is latched. The views this one covered are revealed and get `OnVisible` at once, then the hide transition plays. At the end, in this order: the visible scope ends, the open scope ends, the instance is released or kept, the event is published and the awaiters complete. When a request ends without a hide (owner ended, closed by navigation, instance lost), the revealed views get `OnVisible` after the release and before the event.

| Hook | Interface | Runs | Arguments |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OnOpen` | `IView<TArgs, TResult>` | Once per open | The arguments of this open and the context |
| `OnVisible` | `IViewVisible` | Each time the view comes on screen and is not covered | The visible scope of that span |
| `OnBack` | `IViewBack` | When Back targets the view and the row says `HandledByView` | None. Returns `true` when handled |

There is no `OnClose`, `OnHide` or `OnCovered`, by design. Anything that has to end is registered on a scope and the package ends it; see [ADR-003](Design/Decisions/ADR-003-Begin-Only-Hooks-And-Scopes.md).

The Unity messages behave as follows. `Awake` runs once per instance. `OnEnable` and `OnDisable` run whenever the package activates or deactivates the instance: when it places it, when it parks it for reuse, and when a covered view uses `CoveredMode.Deactivate`. `OnDestroy` runs when the instance is released. Do not put cleanup of listeners in `OnDisable`; use the scope.

`OnVisible` is where per-span work starts, such as a spinner. It runs again on every reveal, which is why a screen can refresh itself there:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/LibraryView.cs -->
```csharp
// Runs on the first show and again each time this screen is revealed.
protected override void OnVisible(ViewScope visible) => _count.text = $"{_library.Count} items";
```

**Errors in hooks.** An exception in `OnOpen` ends the request as not shown with `RejectReason.Faulted` and reports [UIDIRECTOR117](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector117). An exception in `OnVisible` or `OnBack` goes to the root's error handler and the view stays open; a throwing `OnBack` counts as not handled.

**Never deactivate or destroy a view yourself.** Calling `Destroy` or `SetActive(false)` on a view, on one of its parents, or on its layer ends the request with `CloseReason.Destroyed` one frame later and reports [UIDIRECTOR107](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector107). This holds for a `KeepInstance` row too: the instance is released, not kept, and the next open creates a new one. Close a view through `Complete`, `Close`, `ViewHost.Close()`, the handle or Back.

---

## Refuse an open with Decline

When a view finds in `OnOpen` that it should not be shown, call `Decline`. Nothing is shown, no transition plays, the caller receives a result with `RejectReason.Declined` and your reason text, and the scope ends so anything bound before the call is removed:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/RenameView.cs -->
```csharp
// Decline is the right call inside OnOpen: nothing is shown and the caller sees Declined.
if (!_library.CanRename(args.ItemId))
{
    context.Decline("This item cannot be renamed.");
    return;
}
```

`Decline` only latches the refusal. It does not stop the method, so write the `return` yourself. Outside `OnOpen` the call is ignored. A decline needs no diagnostic; it is the expected way to say no.

Do not use `Complete` or `Close` for this. Inside `OnOpen` they are latched, the view opens and then closes at once, and the package reports [UIDIRECTOR118](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector118).

---

## Complete with a result

`Complete(value)` closes the view and hands the value to whoever awaits it:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ConfirmView.cs -->
```csharp
private void Accept()
{
    Complete(true);
}

private void Refuse()
{
    Complete(false);
}
```

The caller reads the outcome from the `ViewResult`. `ItemDetailView` opens the rename popup with its open scope's token as the owner, and applies the title only when the popup completed with one:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ItemDetailView.cs -->
```csharp
private void OnRenameClicked() => OpenScope.Run(RenameAsync);

private async UniTask RenameAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // The owner is this open's token: the popup cannot outlive this screen.
    var result = await Navigator.ShowAsync(
        AppViews.Rename,
        new RenameArgs(_itemId, _library.GetTitle(_itemId)),
        ct,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "item.rename" });

    // No value: the player went back, or the item cannot be renamed.
    if (!result.TryGetValue(out var title)) return;

    _library.Rename(_itemId, title);
}
```

| Call | `CloseReason` | `HasValue` |
|---|---|---|
| `Complete(value)` | `Completed` | `true` |
| `Close()` | `Dismissed` | `false` |

- **The first cause wins.** Complete, Close, Back, a backdrop tap, a handle close or the owner ending: the first one is latched and later ones are ignored. After `Complete` returns the view is still on screen, playing its hide transition, so do not touch it afterwards.
- **A close during the open is kept.** A `Complete` or `Close` that arrives while the view is still opening runs after the show finishes.
- **A value is a message, not a delivery.** It is held in memory and is lost if the process dies. Do not perform a one-time side effect, such as a purchase, from the awaiting code alone. See [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).

---

## Tie listeners and tasks to a scope

A scope owns bindings and tasks for one span of a view's life. You register the cleanup in the same call that starts the work, so there is no removal line to write and none to forget. The package ends the scope exactly once on every path: closed, withdrawn before it was shown, declined, owner ended, instance lost, root destroyed.

| Scope | Created | Ends | Reached through |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open scope | When the request is accepted | When the request ends | `ViewContext.Open`, the `open` parameter, `OpenScope` |
| Visible scope | Each time the view comes on screen and is not covered | When the view is covered, or when the request ends | The `visible` parameter of `OnVisible` |

Put long-lived listening on the open scope and per-span work on the visible scope. A view that a screen covers keeps its open scope and loses its visible scope. To decide where a piece of work goes: work that should stop while another view covers this one, such as a refresh timer, belongs to the visible scope and is started in `OnVisible`, so it starts again on every reveal; work that runs for as long as the view is open, such as a listener for a model change, belongs to the open scope. By default a popup over a screen does not cover it, so the screen's visible scope keeps running under a popup (a row's `Cover` policy can change that).

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public sealed class ViewScope
{
    public CancellationToken Token { get; }
    public bool IsEnded { get; }
    public void Bind(UnityEvent source, UnityAction handler);
    public void Bind<T>(UnityEvent<T> source, UnityAction<T> handler);
    public void Subscribe(Action<Action> add, Action<Action> remove, Action handler);
    public void Subscribe<T>(Action<Action<T>> add, Action<Action<T>> remove, Action<T> handler);
    public void Add(IDisposable disposable);
    public void OnEnd(Action action);
    public void OnEnd<TState>(TState state, Action<TState> action);
    public void Run(Func<CancellationToken, UniTask> work);
    public void Run<TState>(TState state, Func<TState, CancellationToken, UniTask> work);
}
```

**Buttons and other `UnityEvent`s.** `Bind` adds the listener now and removes it when the scope ends. `ConfirmView` above binds both buttons this way.

**Events that are not `UnityEvent`.** `Subscribe` takes an add delegate, a remove delegate and the handler. The package calls add now and remove at the end:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ItemDetailView.cs -->
```csharp
// The package removes the C# event handler when this open ends.
open.Subscribe<string>(handler => _library.Renamed += handler, handler => _library.Renamed -= handler, OnRenamed);

// A reused instance must not show the previous item for a frame.
open.OnEnd(() => _title.text = string.Empty);
```

For a plain `Action` event use the non-generic form, which takes the same three arguments without a type argument: `open.Subscribe(handler => _session.SignedOut += handler, handler => _session.SignedOut -= handler, OnSignedOut)`, where `OnSignedOut` is a `void` method with no parameters.

`OnEnd` runs an action at the end, here to clear the title of a reusable instance. `Add(IDisposable)` disposes an object at the end.

**Tasks.** `Run` starts an async method with the scope's token. When the scope ends the token is cancelled. Any `OperationCanceledException` the work throws is swallowed, whichever token it came from; any other exception goes to the root's error handler as a scope task error. The toast closes itself after two seconds, and the task disappears if the toast is closed or replaced first:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ToastView.cs -->
```csharp
protected override void OnOpen(ToastArgs args, ViewScope open)
{
    _message.text = args.Message;

    // The scope cancels this task if the toast is closed or replaced first.
    open.Run(CloseAfterDelay);
}

private async UniTask CloseAfterDelay(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Unscaled time, so a paused game (timeScale 0) still dismisses the toast.
    await UniTask.Delay(ShowTime, DelayType.UnscaledDeltaTime, cancellationToken: ct);
    Close();
}
```

Work that belongs to one span goes on the visible scope. The spinner of the saving overlay stops whenever the overlay is hidden or closed:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SavingOverlay.cs -->
```csharp
protected override void OnVisible(ViewScope visible)
{
    // Per-span work goes on the visible scope, so the spinner stops whenever the overlay is hidden or closed.
    visible.Run(SpinAsync);
}
```

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SavingOverlay.cs -->
```csharp
private async UniTask SpinAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // Unscaled time keeps the spinner turning while the game is paused.
        _spinner.Rotate(0f, 0f, -DegreesPerSecond * Time.unscaledDeltaTime);

        // A cancelled yield throws, and the scope swallows it as the normal end of the loop.
        await UniTask.Yield(ct);
    }
}
```

**The scope's token is an owner.** The rename call in `ItemDetailView` passes the token it received from `OpenScope.Run` as the owner of the popup, so the popup cannot outlive the screen that opened it. A request that should outlive the view uses `Navigator.RootToken` instead.

**Rules of a scope.**

- `Token` is created on first read, cancelled when the scope ends and never disposed, so a late holder stays valid. A token read after the end is already cancelled.
- The end routine cancels the token first, then runs the entries newest first. Each entry is isolated: a throw is reported and the rest still run.
- Registering on an ended scope cleans up at once: the listener is not added, the disposable is disposed, the action runs, the task does not start. A scope reference kept after the view closed is inert.
- Binding the same event and handler twice on one scope adds one listener.
- An `OnEnd` action runs inside the end routine. Calling the navigator from it is legal.
- Do not call `AddListener` yourself on an instance that is kept for reuse. The listener would be added again on every open.

---

## Kept instances

A catalog row decides what happens to the instance when its view closes (`ViewRetention`):

| Retention | On close | Next open of the same id |
|---|---|---|
| `ReleaseOnClose` (default) | The instance is released | A new instance is created: injection, `Awake`, `OnEnable` and `OnOpen` all run |
| `KeepInstance` | The instance is parked, deactivated, under the staging object | The same instance is placed again |

What runs again on a reopen of a kept instance: `OnEnable` (it was deactivated while parked), `OnOpen` with the new arguments and a fresh open scope, and `OnVisible` with a fresh visible scope. What does not run again: `Awake` and the root's inject delegate. The instance is not created again either, so its fields keep their values.

That is why `OnOpen` must reset the state a previous open left behind:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/RenameView.cs -->
```csharp
// A reused instance must not carry state from the previous open.
_edited = false;
_discardHintShown = false;
_hint.text = string.Empty;
_input.SetTextWithoutNotify(args.CurrentTitle);
```

Bindings made on the open scope were removed when the previous open ended, so they are added once per open and a click fires once.

When the package parks an instance it gives back only the canvases and raycasters it switched off itself, so a canvas or raycaster your prefab or your code keeps disabled stays disabled.

Limits of retention:

- One idle instance per id and no budget. A second concurrent instance of a row with `AllowMultiple` is released when it closes if the slot is taken.
- `INavigator.Trim()` releases every idle kept instance, and the root calls it on `Application.lowMemory`. A request in flight is never touched.
- An idle kept instance that is destroyed from outside is dropped from the cache.
- Removing a catalog releases the kept instances of its rows.

On a history layer, opening a screen that is already in the stack returns to it instead of creating it again. A key without arguments does not run `OnOpen` again. A key with arguments runs `OnOpen` again with the new arguments on a fresh open scope, without a transition. See [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md).

---

## Prefab structure

The steps from an empty prefab to an openable view, including the catalog row and the root's `Catalogs` list, are in [Make a view and its row](Catalogs-and-Keys.md#make-a-view-and-its-row). A view prefab follows these rules. `Tools > UIDirector > Validate Catalogs` checks rules 1, 2 and 8; rule 2 only for keys declared in a class marked `[ViewKeys]`.

1. **`ViewHost` on the root.** It requires a `Canvas` and a `GraphicRaycaster`, which Unity adds with it. Without it the open ends with [UIDIRECTOR103](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector103).
2. **The view component on the same object.** One component implements `IView<TArgs, TResult>` for the key and the optional hooks. Otherwise: [UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102).
3. **Do not set the root canvas's sorting.** The package sets `overrideSorting`, the sorting order and the sorting layer of the view's own canvas when it places the view. A view owns the four orders above its own, so a nested canvas that overrides sorting uses `ViewHost.SortingOrder` plus 1 to 4.
4. **No `CanvasScaler` on the view root.** The project's root canvas scales; the view is a nested canvas. In Prefab Mode a nested canvas has no scaler, so `Tools > UIDirector > Create Prefab UI Environment` writes a scene with a canvas and scaler to edit prefabs in.
5. **The canvases under a covered view are disabled.** While a view is covered, the package disables every enabled `Canvas` under it, including its own, nested ones and those of inactive children, and turns on again on reveal only the ones it disabled. A canvas that was already disabled is left alone, and one your code turns on while the view is covered stays on. The list is collected when the view is covered, so canvases created at run time are included. Disabling a canvas stops drawing and input but not scripts: `Update`, animators and particle systems keep running. A row with `CoveredMode.Deactivate` deactivates the view object instead, which stops them at the cost of a rebuild when the view returns.
6. **The raycasters of a non-interactive view are disabled.** A view that is not `Open`, is covered, is closing, or sits under a modal layer has every enabled `GraphicRaycaster` under it disabled, and the package turns on again only those when the view becomes interactive. A raycaster your code disables stays disabled. A `CanvasGroup` is not used to block input, so do not depend on its `interactable` or `blocksRaycasts` for this. If the selected object of the event system is inside the view when it loses input, the selection is cleared. Keyboard and gamepad navigation can still move the selection into such a view; see [Keyboard, gamepad and remote navigation](#keyboard-gamepad-and-remote-navigation).
7. **Content is on the UI layer when the root draws through a camera.** A root created with `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root (Camera)` has a UI camera whose culling mask is the UI layer only. A view whose objects are on another layer is culled and does not appear. Put every object of the prefab on the UI layer, and put objects that you create or instantiate inside the view at run time on it too. A root canvas in `Screen Space - Overlay` mode has no camera to cull. See [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md).
8. **No dropdowns that you cannot close.** An open dropdown draws above the package's sorting band and is not blocked by the input shield. The validator warns with [UIDIRECTOR123](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector123).

### Keyboard, gamepad and remote navigation

A non-interactive view (covered, opening, closing, or under a modal layer) takes no pointer input, but uGUI navigation does not use the raycaster. Navigation starts from the selected object and moves to a neighbouring `Selectable`. The package clears the selection when a view loses input, so a move starts from the view that has focus and can reach a `Selectable` of a view below it: with automatic navigation, uGUI searches every `Selectable` in the scene. The package does not set `CanvasGroup.interactable` or change `Selectable.navigation` for you, because both change state the project owns (a `CanvasGroup` change re-tints every `Selectable` under it).

On views used with a keyboard, a gamepad or a TV remote:

- Set the `Navigation` of the `Selectable`s in the view to `Explicit`, so a move never leaves the view.
- For a view that must be unreachable while another view covers it, set `When Covered` on its own row to `Deactivate`. A deactivated view unregisters its `Selectable`s. This does not apply to a screen under a modal popup: that screen is not covered, only non-interactive, so only `Explicit` navigation in the popup keeps a move inside it. See [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md#a-catalog-row).

---

## Traps

- **Reading arguments in `Awake` or `OnEnable`.** They run before `OnOpen`. Read arguments and `Navigator` in `OnOpen`.
- **A hook on a second component.** `IViewVisible` and `IViewBack` are found on the component that implements `IView`.
- **State that survives a kept instance.** Reset it in `OnOpen`, or register the reset with `OnEnd`.
- **`Complete` or `Close` inside `OnOpen`.** The view opens and closes. Use `Decline`.
- **A hook for `OnBack` without a row policy.** `OnBack` is asked only for a row with `BackPolicy.HandledByView`. With another policy it is never called. When it returns `false`, the layer's rule applies as it does for `LayerDefault`.
- **Expecting a view to be switched off at placement.** Awake, OnEnable and OnOpen see your canvases and raycasters as authored. Do not rely on them being disabled there.
- **Hand-written cleanup.** `AddListener` plus a matching `RemoveListener` in `OnDisable` is the pattern the scope replaces.

## See also

- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md): opening a view and reading its `ViewResult`
- [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md): `BackPolicy`, `OnBack` and returning to a screen
- [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md): rows, retention, cover and back policies
- [Transitions](Transitions.md): the transition referenced by `ViewHost`
- [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md): modal layers and the shared backdrop
- [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md): render mode, the UI camera and the sorting band
- [Zenject](Zenject.md): injection into views before `Awake`
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md): [UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102), [UIDIRECTOR103](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector103), [UIDIRECTOR107](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector107), [UIDIRECTOR117](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector117), [UIDIRECTOR118](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector118)
- [Architecture: scopes](Design/Architecture.md#9-scopes) and [ADR-003](Design/Decisions/ADR-003-Begin-Only-Hooks-And-Scopes.md): why hooks only begin things

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Opening-and-Results.md -->

# Opening and results

[Back to index](index.md)

This page is about the code that asks for a view and learns how it went: `Open` against `ShowAsync`,
the options of a call, the handle you get back, reading a result (the value, the close reason, the
reject reason), who owns an open and what happens when the owner ends, and closing many views at
once. The model is in [Concepts](Concepts.md); the keys you pass are in
[Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md).

---

## Open a view, or open it and wait

Every call takes a key, the arguments (not for a key without arguments), an **owner** token and
optional `OpenOptions`. There are two ways to call:

| You want | Call | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| To start a view and carry on | `Open(key, owner, options)` | A `ViewHandle`, at once |
| To start a view and wait for how it ended | `await ShowAsync(key, args, owner, options)` | A `ViewResult<TResult>` when the request ends |

`Open` suits a button that opens a screen. The Basic Usage sample's Home screen opens the library from
a button and does not care when it closes. The root owns the new screen, so it outlives the Home
screen that holds the button:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/HomeView.cs -->
```csharp
// The owner is the root: a screen opened from a button outlives the screen that holds the button.
private void OpenLibrary() =>
    Navigator.Open(AppViews.Library, Navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "home.library" });
```

`ShowAsync` suits a question: open a popup, wait, read the answer. The settings screen asks for a
confirmation, and the answer decides what happens next:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private async UniTask ConfirmResetAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // The owner is this screen's scope token: the popup cannot outlive the screen.
    var answer = await Navigator.ShowAsync(
        AppViews.Confirm,
        new ConfirmArgs("Reset settings", "All settings return to their defaults."),
        ct,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.reset", RejectWhenBusy = true });

    // Refused at once instead of waiting behind a view that is still opening.
    if (answer.Rejected == RejectReason.Busy)
    {
        _status.text = "Busy, try again.";
        return;
    }

    // Back, backdrop and a closed screen all end with no value, so this line also guards the screen.
    if (!answer.HasValue || !answer.Value)
        return;

    _settings.ResetToDefaults();
    _status.text = "Settings were reset.";

    // The toast outlives this screen, so the root owns it.
    Navigator.Open(
        AppViews.Toast,
        new ToastArgs("Settings were reset."),
        Navigator.RootToken,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.reset" });
}
```

Both forms accept the same keys. For a key without arguments (`NoArgs`) the extension methods
`Open(key, owner)` and `ShowAsync(key, owner)` fill in the empty arguments.

Both forms decide **at the call**, synchronously, whether the request is accepted. The call itself
never waits and never throws for anything that happens to the view. The only exceptions are usage
errors: a call off the main thread throws `InvalidOperationException`, and a null navigator in an
extension method throws `ArgumentNullException`. See [Threading](Threading.md).

---

## OpenOptions

`OpenOptions` is an optional struct. Leave it out and every field is its default.

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public struct OpenOptions
{
    public string Source;
    public bool RejectWhenBusy;
    public int RequestId;
}
```

| Field | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Source` | `null` | A free tag that travels with the request's events and diagnostics. Use one string per call site, such as `"home.library"`, so a log line or an analytics event names the code that asked. It has no effect on behavior. See [Events and analytics](Events-and-Analytics.md). |
| `RejectWhenBusy` | `false` | Refuse the call at once with `RejectReason.Busy` when the navigator is busy (an operation runs or pends on any layer, or an input hold exists) instead of queuing behind it. Use it in tap handlers. |
| `RequestId` | `0` | `0` allocates a fresh request id. A non-zero value must come from `INavigator.ReserveRequestId()`, so one id can follow a request from before it reaches the navigator. A queue does this for you; ordinary code leaves it at `0`. |

Every call also has two optional trailing parameters, `member` and `line`. The compiler fills them
with the calling method and line. The calling method names the request's shield hold in `Describe`
and the UIDirector window; the 30-second warning,
[UIDIRECTOR110](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector110), is for `HoldInput`. Do not pass them.

`RejectWhenBusy` is a per-call choice. Without it, a second open waits in its layer, in the order
requests were accepted, up to the waiting cap (4 per layer by default; the next request ends as
`Busy`, [UIDIRECTOR112](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector112)). A double tap on a button that opens a
popup therefore needs either `RejectWhenBusy`, or a layer that refuses the second request as a
duplicate, which a non-history layer does unless the row sets `Allow Multiple`.

---

## What happens at the call

The navigator runs these checks in order. The first one that fails ends the request as not shown:

1. The root was destroyed: `RootGone`.
2. The owner token is already cancelled: `OwnerEnded`.
3. No catalog row has the id: `UnknownKey` ([UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101)).
4. The row names a layer the root does not have: `UnknownKey` ([UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109)).
5. A [queue](Queue.md) presented the request and the row is on another layer than the queue's:
   `WrongLayer` ([UIDIRECTOR126](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector126)). Nothing is placed and the shield
   is not taken.
6. The id is already open or in flight on a layer that is not a history layer, and the row does not
   allow multiple instances: `Duplicate`.
7. The call set `RejectWhenBusy` and the navigator is busy: `Busy`.
8. The layer is a history layer, the id is already in its stack, the row does not set
   `Allow Multiple` and the key has no arguments: not refused and not new. You join the request that exists (see [Joining](#joining-an-open-view)).
9. The layer already holds the waiting cap of requests that have not started: `Busy`
   ([UIDIRECTOR112](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector112)).
10. The layer's sorting band has no free slot: `Busy` ([UIDIRECTOR115](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector115)).

"Already open" in checks 6 and 8 means a request whose end is not decided yet. A request whose close
or withdrawal is already latched does not count, and neither does a request that a newer reopen is
replacing. That includes the views a `CloseAll`, `CloseTo`, a return to an earlier screen or a reopen
in place is about to remove: a new open of their id is a new request that runs after the operation.

A request that passes is added to its layer in `Waiting`. If the layer shields input, the input
shield goes up in the same call. That is why a second tap in the same frame lands on the shield and
not on the button.

A refused request still has a request id and publishes a `NotShown` event at the call. `ShowAsync`
returns a result that says why. `Open` returns an **empty handle**, described below.

---

## The handle

`Open` returns a `ViewHandle`, a small read-only struct that refers to one request. It is cheap to
copy and keep. It is **not awaitable**.

| Member | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `RequestId` | The id of the request; `0` for an empty handle. |
| `ViewId` | The id of the requested view; `null` for an empty handle. |
| `Phase` | `Waiting`, `Loading`, `Opening`, `Open`, `Closing` or `Ended`. `Ended` for an empty handle. |
| `IsAlive` | `true` until the request has ended. |
| `Close()` | Closes the view, or withdraws the request if it has not started. Never throws. |
| `WaitForCloseAsync(CancellationToken waiter)` | Completes with a `ViewClosed` when the request ends. |
| `TryGetInstance(out GameObject)` | The live instance while the view is opening, open or closing. |

After the request ends the handle is **inert**: `Phase` stays `Ended`, `Close()` does nothing, and
`WaitForCloseAsync` returns the stored outcome at once. A handle is therefore safe to keep in a field;
check `IsAlive` before you rely on it.

`INavigator` also finds handles by id: `IsOpen(viewId)` is `true` while a request for the id is open
or in flight, `TryGetOpen(viewId, out handle)` gives its handle, and `TryGetTop(layer, out handle)`
gives the top request of a layer. They report a request until it has ended, including a view that a
`CloseTo` or `CloseAll` is closing, so a closing view still has a handle. They are not the duplicate
check: a new `Open` of that id already starts a new request, as
[What happens at the call](#what-happens-at-the-call) describes.

The sample's save button keeps a handle for a system overlay, does the work, and closes the overlay in
a `finally`, so no path leaves it up. Then it waits for the overlay's hide transition:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private async UniTask SaveAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // The root owns the overlay, so the finally below is what guarantees it never stays up.
    var overlay = Navigator.Open(AppViews.Saving, Navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.save" });

    try
    {
        await _settings.SaveAsync(ct);
    }
    finally
    {
        overlay.Close();
    }

    // Wait for the hide transition, so the status appears once the overlay is gone.
    var closed = await overlay.WaitForCloseAsync(ct);
    _status.text = closed.Reason == CloseReason.Code ? "Saved." : "Saved. The overlay ended early.";
}
```

**What `Close()` does depends on where the request is.** Before it started (`Waiting` or `Loading`)
the request is withdrawn at once and ends as not shown with `RejectReason.Cancelled`. From `Opening`
on, the view closes with `CloseReason.Code` and plays its hide transition; during `Opening` that
happens when the show transition has finished, because a started step is never interrupted. The first
cause that ends a request wins, so `Close()` after the view already closed itself changes nothing.

**`WaitForCloseAsync` has its own token.** Any number of callers can wait, and each call gets its own
completion. The call throws `OperationCanceledException` only when `waiter` is cancelled, and that
leaves the view alone. The owner of the request never cancels a waiter; see
[Owners](#owners-and-what-happens-when-one-ends).

**The empty handle.** A refused `Open` returns `default(ViewHandle)`. Its `Close()` does nothing and
its `WaitForCloseAsync` completes at once with `NotShown`, `RejectReason.Cancelled` and the detail
"The handle is empty." It does not say why the request was refused. When you need the reason, use
`ShowAsync`, or read the `NotShown` event ([Events and analytics](Events-and-Analytics.md)).

The view itself reaches its own request through `ViewContext.Handle`, and ends it with
`ViewContext.Complete(value)` or `ViewContext.Close()`; see [View authoring](View-Authoring.md).

---

## Reading a result

`ShowAsync` completes with a `ViewResult<TResult>`. It never throws for what happens to the view.

| Member | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `HasValue` | `true` only when the view was shown and closed itself with `Complete(value)`. |
| `Value` | The value; the default value when `HasValue` is `false`. |
| `TryGetValue(out TResult)` | Returns `HasValue` and writes the value. |
| `WasShown` | The view entered its show transition before the request ended. |
| `Reason` | A `CloseReason`: how a shown view ended, or `NotShown`. |
| `Rejected` | A `RejectReason`: why a request ended without being shown; `None` when it was shown. |
| `Detail` | Optional text with more about the outcome. |
| `RequestId` | The id of the request, the same id the events carry. |

**Read the answer with `TryGetValue`** when all you need is "did the user answer, and with what". The
rename popup's caller does exactly that:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ItemDetailView.cs -->
```csharp
// No value: the player went back, or the item cannot be renamed.
if (!result.TryGetValue(out var title)) return;
```

`HasValue` is `false` for every ending that is not `Complete(value)`: the popup was dismissed, the
back key closed it, the owner ended, it was refused. A close with `Complete(value)` after the view
was shown is the only way to get a value. For a view with no result (`NoResult`) `HasValue` is
`false` unless the view called `Complete`, so test `Reason` there.

### Close reasons

A view that was shown reports one of these in `Reason`. The first cause that ends a view is latched;
later causes are ignored.

| `CloseReason` | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Completed` | The view called `ViewContext.Complete(value)`. `HasValue` is `true`. |
| `Dismissed` | The view called `ViewContext.Close()`, or `ViewHost.Close()` ran from an Inspector event, such as a `ViewButton`. |
| `Back` | `Back()` closed it. |
| `Backdrop` | A tap on the backdrop of a row with `Close On Backdrop`. |
| `Code` | `ViewHandle.Close()`, `CloseTo` or `CloseAll`. |
| `Navigated` | A screen change ended it, or it was reopened in place. A request that was not shown yet reports `NotShown` and `Cancelled` instead. |
| `OwnerEnded` | The owner token ended while it was shown. |
| `Destroyed` | The instance was destroyed or deactivated outside the package, or the root was destroyed. |
| `NotShown` | The request never reached the screen; read `Rejected`. |

### Reject reasons

A request that never reached its show transition always reports `CloseReason.NotShown` and one of
these in `Rejected`:

| `RejectReason` | When |
|---|---|
| `UnknownKey` | No row has the id ([UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101)), or the row names an unknown layer ([UIDIRECTOR109](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector109)). |
| `TypeMismatch` | The prefab root has no component for the key's types ([UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102)) or no `ViewHost` ([UIDIRECTOR103](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector103)). |
| `Duplicate` | The id is already open or in flight on a layer that does not allow it. |
| `Busy` | `RejectWhenBusy` and the navigator was busy, the waiting cap was reached ([UIDIRECTOR112](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector112)), or the sorting band is full ([UIDIRECTOR115](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector115)). |
| `Denied` | A queue gate denied the request. See [Queue](Queue.md). |
| `LoadFailed` | The asset could not be loaded ([UIDIRECTOR104](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector104), [UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120)). |
| `LoadTimedOut` | The load took longer than the load timeout ([UIDIRECTOR105](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector105)). |
| `Cancelled` | The request was withdrawn before it was shown: `ViewHandle.Close()`, `Back()`, `CloseAll`, a screen opening on a history layer (`ClosedByNavigation`), a `CloseTo`, a return or a reopen in place that popped past it while it had not started, a newer reopen that took its place, or the instance was lost. |
| `Declined` | The view called `Decline` in `OnOpen`. `Detail` carries its reason text. |
| `Faulted` | `OnOpen` threw ([UIDIRECTOR117](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector117)). |
| `OwnerEnded` | The owner ended, or was already cancelled, before the view was shown. |
| `RootGone` | The root no longer exists. A [queue](Queue.md) ends its waiting items this way when its navigator's root is destroyed. |
| `WrongLayer` | A queue presented the request, but the row is on another layer than the queue's ([UIDIRECTOR126](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector126)). See [Queue](Queue.md). |

`WaitForCloseAsync` completes with a `ViewClosed` (`WasShown`, `Reason`, `Rejected`, `Detail`).
Observers get the same facts in a `ViewEvent` whose `Kind` is `Closed` or `NotShown`. No arguments and
no value travel with either.

### Joining an open view

On a history layer, opening an id that is already in the stack with a key **without arguments** does
not create a second view, unless the row sets `Allow Multiple`. `ShowAsync` joins the existing request: `OnOpen` does not run again, you
complete when that request ends, and any view above it is popped with `CloseReason.Navigated`. `Open`
returns the existing handle. A key **with arguments** reopens the screen in place with the new
arguments instead; see [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md).

A joined `ShowAsync` that was made with other argument or result types gets the same outcome but not
the value: `HasValue` is `false`, and a view that completed with a value reports `Reason` as
`Completed` to such a joiner.

**A join does not bind the owner you pass.** The request keeps the owner it was opened with. If your
token ends, nothing happens to the request or to your wait: the `await` keeps waiting until the
request ends, and it completes with that request's own outcome and request id.

### Stopping the wait at your own token

`ShowAsync` never throws and has no wait token. To make an `await` stop when a token of your own ends,
wrap the call with UniTask's `AttachExternalCancellation` and `SuppressCancellationThrow`:

<!-- source: Tests/Editor/Navigation/NavigationHistoryTests.cs -->
```csharp
private static async UniTask<(bool IsCanceled, ViewResult<NoResult> Result)> ShowUntilStopped(
    UniTask<ViewResult<NoResult>> show,
    CancellationToken stop)
{
    return await show.AttachExternalCancellation(stop).SuppressCancellationThrow();
}
```

Call it as `ShowUntilStopped(navigator.ShowAsync(key, owner), stop)`. When `stop` ends, `IsCanceled` is
`true`, your code carries on, and a request you joined goes on without you. Other joiners and the
view are not affected.

Two traps:

- `IsCanceled` is `true` whenever your token ended, and the result is then `default`, not an outcome. If the same
  token is also the owner of a call that started a new request, the view ended too, as
  `CloseReason.OwnerEnded` or `RejectReason.OwnerEnded`, and the wrapped `await` reports a stop and not
  that result.
- If you need the outcome as well as the stop, pass a separate token as `stop` and a different token
  as the owner.

### Faking a result in tests

`ViewResult.Completed(value)`, `ViewResult.Closed<TResult>(reason)` and
`ViewResult.NotShown<TResult>(reason, detail)` are public factories, so a game can fake an
`INavigator` and return any outcome without a test assembly from the package.

Two combinations are refused with an `ArgumentException`, because they do not describe an outcome:

- `Closed<TResult>(CloseReason.NotShown)`: a closed result was shown. Use `NotShown` for a request
  that was not shown.
- `NotShown<TResult>(RejectReason.None, ...)`: a request that was not shown always has a reject
  reason.

`Closed<TResult>(CloseReason.Completed)` is allowed. It is a view that completed without a value,
which is what a joiner with other argument or result types receives; use `Completed(value)` for a view
that completed with a value. `default(ViewResult<T>)` is not an outcome the navigator returns.

---

## Owners and what happens when one ends

Every open takes a `CancellationToken`, the **owner**. It decides how long the request lives. The
sample passes two kinds; the table adds the third. Each is a deliberate answer to "what should this
view not outlive?":

| Owner | Where in the sample | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Navigator.RootToken` | `HomeView`, the toast and the saving overlay | The view ends when the root is destroyed, and not before. |
| `ct`, the token of the screen's scope | The confirm popup in `SettingsView` | The popup ends with the screen that asked for it. |
| `CancellationToken.None` | Not used in the sample | Nothing ends it until someone closes it, the instance is lost, or the root is destroyed (in practice the same as `RootToken`). |

Two cases do not behave as the table suggests:

- **A call that joins an existing request ignores its owner.** A key without arguments that returns to
  a screen already on a history layer binds nothing: the request keeps its own owner. See
  [Joining](#joining-an-open-view).
- **A screen's own scope token is a poor owner for a view that replaces or pops that screen.** A
  reopen in place replaces the screen it reopens, and pops the screens above it. A token that ends
  with one of those screens ends the new request. Pass `Navigator.RootToken` there; see
  [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#return-to-a-screen-that-is-already-open).

When the owner is cancelled:

| State of the request | What happens | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Not shown yet (`Waiting`, `Loading`) | Withdrawn at once; a running load is cancelled | `NotShown`, `RejectReason.OwnerEnded` |
| Shown (`Opening`, `Open`, `Closing`) | The view is **snapped** to its hidden pose, with no hide transition, and finished | `CloseReason.OwnerEnded` |
| Already cancelled at the call | Refused before anything is touched | `NotShown`, `RejectReason.OwnerEnded` |
| An outcome was already latched | The latched outcome stands | The latched reason |

Ending by owner is a **terminate**: it cuts a running step short and does not play the hide
transition. The two other terminate causes behave the same way: the instance being destroyed or
deactivated from outside the package, and the root being destroyed. A transition that exceeds the
transition timeout is cut and snapped to its end pose too ([UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106)).
Every other close waits for the running step. `ViewHandle.Close()`, `Back()`, a backdrop tap,
`ViewContext.Close()` and `Complete` play the hide transition. `CloseTo` and `CloseAll` animate only
the topmost view and snap the rest. A screen change snaps the popups it ends
(`CloseReason.Navigated`).

**The owner never cancels an awaiter.** `ShowAsync` has no cancellation parameter, and when the owner
ends the awaiting code resumes with a result, not an exception: `CloseReason.OwnerEnded` for a shown
view, `RejectReason.OwnerEnded` for a request that was not shown yet. That
matters in `ConfirmResetAsync` above. Its owner is the screen's scope token; if the screen closes
first, the popup ends with `OwnerEnded`, the `await` returns, and `HasValue` is `false`. The line
`if (!answer.HasValue || !answer.Value) return;` is what stops the method from touching a screen that
is gone. After any `await` on a view that someone else can end, check the result before you use state
that the owner's end may have cleaned up.

**The await always completes, also after the owner is destroyed.** The method that awaits `ShowAsync`
resumes and the code after the `await` runs, even when the owner (for example the screen that opened
the popup) was destroyed first. A call that joined an existing request is the exception: its owner is
not bound, so it resumes only when that request ends, with that request's outcome (see
[Joining](#joining-an-open-view)). Otherwise, what it receives depends on the request's state when the
owner ended:

- The request was shown: `Reason` is `CloseReason.OwnerEnded`.
- The request was not shown yet, or the token was already cancelled at the call: `Rejected` is
  `RejectReason.OwnerEnded`.
- An outcome was latched before the owner ended (the user answered, the view was closed, the root was
  destroyed): that reason is reported instead, so `OwnerEnded` is not the only value to expect.

In every case code after the `await` runs on the main thread with no exception. Guard any access to a
destroyed object there: test the result first, as `ConfirmResetAsync` does, or check a Unity object
against `null` before you use it.

An owner token can be cancelled from any thread. The package handles it on the main thread and logs
[UIDIRECTOR113](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector113) when the cancellation arrived elsewhere. See
[Threading](Threading.md).

The same ending also happens to everything the view started. The view's scopes end with its request:
the bindings, tasks and cleanup actions it put on the open scope or the visible scope. The saving
overlay starts its spinner on the visible scope, so the spinner stops whenever the overlay is hidden,
closed or terminated, with no close line in the view:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SavingOverlay.cs -->
```csharp
protected override void OnVisible(ViewScope visible)
{
    // Per-span work goes on the visible scope, so the spinner stops whenever the overlay is hidden or closed.
    visible.Run(SpinAsync);
}

private async UniTask SpinAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // Unscaled time keeps the spinner turning while the game is paused.
        _spinner.Rotate(0f, 0f, -DegreesPerSecond * Time.unscaledDeltaTime);

        // A cancelled yield throws, and the scope swallows it as the normal end of the loop.
        await UniTask.Yield(ct);
    }
}
```

**`ViewContext.Open` stays readable after the request ended.** A view that kept its
`ViewContext` can still read `context.Open` later. It returns the scope that ended with the request,
never `null`, and registering on an ended scope does the cleanup at once and adds nothing. A late
`Complete`, `Close` or `Decline` on the context does nothing and does not throw; the first outcome
stays.

---

## Closing many views

Closing one view is `handle.Close()`, or the view closing itself. Two calls close several.

### CloseTo

`INavigator.CloseTo(viewId)` and the extension `CloseTo(key)` pop every view above a screen on a
history layer and keep the screen. The item detail screen of the sample uses it to return to the
library:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ItemDetailView.cs -->
```csharp
// Pops everything above the library.
private void GoToLibrary() => Navigator.CloseTo(AppViews.Library);
```

- It returns `true` when a request with that id, whose close is not already decided, is in a history
  layer, also when no view sits above it and nothing needs to close. It returns `false` when the id
  is not there, the root is gone, or the call is off the main thread.
- The views above the target close with `CloseReason.Code`. The top one plays its hide transition,
  the ones between it and the target are snapped.
- The views to close are latched at the call, so a new `Open` of their ids starts a new request that
  runs after the pop. Requests above the target that have not started (`Waiting` or `Loading`) are
  withdrawn at the call as not shown with `RejectReason.Cancelled`. If the target ends before the pop
  runs, the views above it are still closed.
- Returning to the screen by opening its key without arguments pops the same views with
  `CloseReason.Navigated` instead of `Code`. Neither touches the popups layer. `ClosedByNavigation`
  runs only when a new screen opens or a screen is reopened in place with arguments. See
  [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md).

### CloseAll

`INavigator.CloseAll(layer)` empties one layer: it closes every view on it and withdraws every
request that is still waiting.

- **It withdraws waiting requests at once.** Requests in `Waiting` or `Loading` end immediately as
  not shown with `RejectReason.Cancelled`, and a running load is cancelled. They do not wait for the
  views that are on screen.
- What is on screen closes as one operation with `CloseReason.Code`. The topmost view plays its hide
  transition; every other view is snapped away. On a layer with `ShieldsInput` the input shield stays up from the call until the last view has closed.
- The views on screen are latched at the call. A new `Open` of one of their ids is a new request, not
  a join and not a `Duplicate`.
- Requests accepted after the call are not part of it. They open as usual once `CloseAll` has run.
- The operation runs in order on the layer, so a view that is still opening finishes its open first.
- On the wrong thread the call is posted to the main thread instead of throwing. An unknown layer
  does nothing.

Use the layer constants (`ViewLayers.Popups`) or your own `ViewLayer` value; layers are matched by id.

---

## Traps

- **An empty handle is not an error.** A refused `Open` hands back `default`. Test `IsAlive`, not
  `null`; the handle is a struct.
- **Do not treat `Open` as "it opened".** The request is only accepted. It can still be withdrawn,
  fail to load or decline. Read the outcome through `ShowAsync`, `WaitForCloseAsync` or an observer.
- **`HasValue` false is normal.** A popup that closes with Back, a backdrop tap or a dismiss carries no
  value. Decide what "no answer" means before you write the line that reads `Value`.
- **A terminate does not animate.** An owner ending, a destroyed view or a destroyed root snaps the
  view away. If a hide animation matters, close with `handle.Close()` or the view's own `Complete`
  before the owner ends.
- **A close during `Opening` is delayed.** It runs after the show transition, so a fast
  `Close()` is not instant. This is deliberate: a started step is never interrupted.
- **`CloseAll` is not synchronous.** The call returns at once, the waiting requests end at once, and
  the views on screen close over the following frames.
- **`RejectWhenBusy` is not a debounce.** It refuses while any layer is busy, including a transition on
  another layer. Use it where a refused tap is acceptable, as the sample does for the reset button.
- **A request owned by a screen's token ends with the screen.** That is the intent for a popup; for a
  toast or an overlay that must outlive the screen, pass `RootToken`, as the sample does.
- **A join is not bound to your token.** Opening a screen that is already in a history stack, with a
  key without arguments, waits for the existing request however your token ends. Wrap the `await` as
  shown in [Stopping the wait at your own token](#stopping-the-wait-at-your-own-token) when the
  caller must be able to leave.

---
