<!-- file: Documentation~/Popups-and-Backdrop.md -->

# Popups and backdrop

[Back to index](index.md)

A popup is a view on the `popups` layer that opens over a screen and usually answers a question. This
page shows how to open one and await its answer, what the shared backdrop does, how a tap on it
closes a popup and what the awaiter sees, why a double click lands on the input shield, how
`RejectWhenBusy` refuses a request while anything is running, and how a confirm popup completes
with `true` or `false`.

The examples come from the Basic Usage sample: the settings screen opens a confirm popup before it
resets the settings.

---

## Open a popup and await its answer

A screen opens a popup with `ShowAsync` and reads the result. The click handler starts the work on
the screen's open scope, so the work ends with the screen:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private void OnResetClicked()
{
    OpenScope.Run(ConfirmResetAsync);
}
```

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private async UniTask ConfirmResetAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // The owner is this screen's scope token: the popup cannot outlive the screen.
    var answer = await Navigator.ShowAsync(
        AppViews.Confirm,
        new ConfirmArgs("Reset settings", "All settings return to their defaults."),
        ct,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.reset", RejectWhenBusy = true });

    // Refused at once instead of waiting behind a view that is still opening.
    if (answer.Rejected == RejectReason.Busy)
    {
        _status.text = "Busy, try again.";
        return;
    }

    // Back, backdrop and a closed screen all end with no value, so this line also guards the screen.
    if (!answer.HasValue || !answer.Value)
        return;
```

`ShowAsync` never throws for anything that happens to the view. It completes with a
`ViewResult<bool>` that says what became of the request:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `HasValue` | `true` only when the popup closed with `Complete(value)` |
| `Value` | The answer; `default` when `HasValue` is `false` |
| `WasShown` | `true` when the popup reached the open state before it ended |
| `Reason` | How it closed: `Completed`, `Dismissed`, `Back`, `Backdrop`, `Code`, `Navigated`, `OwnerEnded`, `Destroyed`; `NotShown` when it never appeared |
| `Rejected` | Why it never appeared, for example `Busy`, `Duplicate`, `Declined`; `None` when it was shown |

The owner token is the second-to-last argument. It decides the life of the popup, not of the
await. When the owner ends, the popup closes with `OwnerEnded`; the awaiter still completes, with a
result. Here the owner is the settings screen's scope token, so the popup closes if the screen does.
Pass `Navigator.RootToken` for a question no screen owns, such as the quit confirm in
[Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#backinput). The full contract of `ShowAsync`, `Open`,
owners and results is in [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).

### How a popup can end, and what the awaiter sees

| Cause | `Reason` | `HasValue` |
|---|---|---|
| The view calls `Complete(value)` | `Completed` | `true` |
| The view calls `Close()` | `Dismissed` | `false` |
| `Back()` | `Back` | `false` |
| A tap on the backdrop | `Backdrop` | `false` |
| `ViewHandle.Close()`, `CloseAll(ViewLayers.Popups)` | `Code` | `false` |
| A screen opened after the popup | `Navigated` | `false` |
| The owner token ended | `OwnerEnded` | `false` |
| The root was destroyed | `Destroyed` | `false` |

The line `if (!answer.HasValue || !answer.Value) return;` is the safe reading of every row except the
first: anything that is not an explicit `true` counts as "no". Code that must tell the causes apart
reads `answer.Reason`.

A popup that never appears has `WasShown == false`, `Reason == NotShown` and a `Rejected` value; the
values are listed in [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md#reject-reasons). `UnknownKey`,
`TypeMismatch`, `WrongLayer`, `LoadFailed` and `Faulted` are setup mistakes: fix the key, the row
(its layer), the prefab or asset provider, or the view's `OnOpen`. The others (for example `Busy`,
`Duplicate`, `Declined`, `OwnerEnded`, `Cancelled`) are events of normal running that the calling
code handles. The view itself can refuse inside `OnOpen`
with `Decline(reason)`; the caller then sees `Declined` and `Detail` carries the text. Calling `Complete` or `Close` inside `OnOpen` does not refuse the open: the
view opens and closes at once ([UIDIRECTOR118](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector118)).

---

## A confirm popup that completes with true or false

`ConfirmView` is a popup written on the base class, with typed arguments and a `bool` result:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ConfirmView.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class ConfirmView : ViewBehaviour<ConfirmArgs, bool>
{
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _title;
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _message;
    [SerializeField] private Button _accept;
    [SerializeField] private Button _decline;

    protected override void OnOpen(ConfirmArgs args, ViewScope open)
    {
        _title.text = args.Title;
        _message.text = args.Message;

        // The package removes both listeners when this open ends.
        open.Bind(_accept.onClick, Accept);
        open.Bind(_decline.onClick, Refuse);
    }

    private void Accept()
    {
        Complete(true);
    }

    private void Refuse()
    {
        Complete(false);
    }
}
```

The button handlers call `Complete`, which closes the popup with a value. The first close cause
wins: a second click, a press of back, or a tap on the backdrop after `Complete` changes nothing.
Both listeners are bound on the open scope, so there is no `OnDisable` and no unsubscribe line.

The key ties the types together, so the call site is checked by the compiler: `AppViews.Confirm` is a
`ViewKey<ConfirmArgs, bool>`, and `ShowAsync` returns `ViewResult<bool>`. See
[Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md).

Two things make a confirm popup safe to read with a single line:

- Pressing back closes it through the layer rule with `Back`, and a tap on the backdrop closes it with
  `Backdrop` when its row allows that. Neither has a value, so both read as "no".
- When the screen that owns it goes away, the popup ends with `OwnerEnded` and the same line returns
  before anything is changed.

---

## The backdrop

Every modal layer has one shared backdrop. `popups` and `system` are modal; a layer you add with
`ViewLayerRules.Modal` gets one too.

- It sits directly under the layer's top view that is on screen, and shows while that view is not
  hidden. With two popups stacked, there is still one backdrop; it jumps up under the newest.
- It fades in and out over 0.2 seconds of unscaled time, so it works while the game is paused. Below
  30 fps one frame advances at most 1/30 s, so the fade then takes longer ([Transitions](Transitions.md)).
  It stops taking pointer input at once when it hides, and its canvas is turned off when the fade ends. An idle
  backdrop costs nothing.
- Everything below the layer's top view is not interactive: the screens underneath cannot be clicked
  even where the backdrop is transparent. They stay visible, because a popup does not cover what is
  below it.
- Its look is the root's backdrop colour (black at 60 percent opacity by default) or a backdrop
  prefab you assign on the root. See [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md).

The `screens` layer is not modal and has no backdrop.

---

## Close on backdrop tap

A tap on the backdrop closes the top popup when that popup's catalog row has `Close On Backdrop`
set. The view ends with `CloseReason.Backdrop` and no value. In the Basic Usage catalog, the
`confirm` row has the flag and the `rename` row does not.

- The tap reads the row of the top view only. With `p1` (flag set) under `p2` (flag not set), a tap
  closes nothing.
- A tap closes only the top view of the layer, never one below it.
- Without the flag the tap is swallowed. It does not reach the screen below, and nothing closes.
- The tap is an ordinary pointer click on the backdrop, delivered by the scene's `EventSystem` and
  its input module, whichever input system the project uses
  ([Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md#give-the-ui-an-eventsystem)).
- The popup must be fully open. A tap while it is opening or closing does nothing, and a tap while the
  input shield is up does nothing.

A popup that closes by backdrop tap plays its hide transition like any other close.

---

## The input shield

The input shield is a counted, full-screen input blocker above every layer. A request takes a hold on
it when the request is accepted on a layer with `ShieldsInput` (`screens`, `popups` and `system` have
it), and gives it back when the open has finished. A close holds it again from the moment the close
is decided until the view is gone.

The hold is taken inside the `Open` or `ShowAsync` call, before the popup has loaded or drawn
anything. That is what protects a double click. The first click on "Reset" calls `ShowAsync`, which
raises the shield in the same call. The second click of the double click reaches the shield and not
the button. One popup opens, and the second click does nothing and logs nothing.

If a second request for the same popup id still gets through, for example from code, it is refused
as `RejectReason.Duplicate`: an id already open or in flight on a layer that is not a history layer is
not accepted again, unless the row sets `AllowMultiple`.

Things the shield does not cover:

- A control that was pressed before the shield was raised and released after it was lowered can still
  receive the release if the pointer is still over it.
- A canvas that sorts itself above the shield, such as the open list of a TextMesh Pro dropdown,
  is not blocked. The validator warns about dropdowns inside views
  ([UIDIRECTOR123](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector123)); see also
  [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md#a-dropdown-list-stays-above-everything).

Code can raise the shield on its own with `INavigator.HoldInput`; see
[Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md). A hold older than 30 seconds is reported once
([UIDIRECTOR110](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector110)).

---

## RejectWhenBusy

Each layer runs one operation at a time. Without the option, a request waits only behind operations
on its own layer; on an idle layer it starts at once. `OpenOptions.RejectWhenBusy` refuses the call
whenever `INavigator.IsBusy` is `true`, on any layer, even when the request would not have waited.
The request ends as not shown with `RejectReason.Busy` and `Detail` reads "The navigator is busy and
the call asked not to wait". `SettingsView` sets it in
the options of the confirm call shown at the top of this page (`RejectWhenBusy = true`) and reads the
refusal:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
// Refused at once instead of waiting behind a view that is still opening.
if (answer.Rejected == RejectReason.Busy)
{
    _status.text = "Busy, try again.";
    return;
}
```

`INavigator.IsBusy` is `true` while any operation runs or waits, on any layer, or while an input hold
exists. In the sample, a toast sliding in or out makes the navigator busy, so a click on "Reset" in
that short window is refused and the label reads "Busy, try again." Without the flag the popup would
open right away, because the toast runs on its own layer. While nothing is moving, the popup opens as
usual.

- **When to use it.** On handlers that a player can trigger repeatedly: buttons, shortcuts, gestures.
  A refused request costs nothing. Without the flag, a request behind work on its own layer waits,
  and its popup appears after the player has moved on.
- **What it does not do.** It does not refuse a request that would be a duplicate or an unknown id;
  those reasons are checked first and win.
- **Without it,** a request behind work on the same layer waits in `Waiting`, already holding the
  shield. A layer keeps at most four waiting requests by default; the next is refused as `Busy` and logged as
  [UIDIRECTOR112](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector112). A back press withdraws the newest waiting request
  first ([Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#resolution-order)).
- `Rejected == Busy` also comes from the waiting cap and from a full sorting band. Read `Detail` to
  tell them apart.

Notices that may wait their turn are better served by the queue, which orders them by priority; see
[Queue](Queue.md). A queue serves one layer: a queued key whose row is on another layer is refused as
`RejectReason.WrongLayer` and logged as [UIDIRECTOR126](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector126).

---

## Popups and screen changes

- **A screen that opens later closes the popup.** The `popups` layer has `ClosedByNavigation`: popups
  accepted earlier than the new screen are snapped away with `Navigated` and no hide transition. A
  popup that the new screen opens itself survives. See
  [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#closedbynavigation) and [Limitations](Limitations.md).
- **Back closes the popup first.** Back goes to the top popup before any screen and closes it with
  `CloseReason.Back`. A popup whose row says `HandledByView` is asked first, as `RenameView` does.
- **A system overlay is above the popup.** A popup opened while an overlay is up draws below it and
  cannot be clicked until the overlay is gone. See [System overlays](System-Overlays.md).
- **Hide transitions.** `Complete`, `Close`, back, a backdrop tap and a handle close all play the
  popup's hide transition. See [Transitions](Transitions.md).

## Traps

- **A popup whose id is already open is refused.** Opening the confirm twice gives `Duplicate`, not a
  second popup. For two instances at once, set `AllowMultiple` on the row.
- **Do not read `answer.Value` without `HasValue`.** It is `default` for every close that is not
  `Complete`. For `bool` that is `false`, which looks like an answer.
- **Do not own a popup with a token that outlives the question** unless that is intended. A popup
  owned by `RootToken` does not close when the screen below it closes or is popped; it can then sit
  over a different screen. Back, a backdrop tap, a handle close or a newly opened screen still close it.
- **Do not close inside `OnOpen`.** Use `Decline`.
- **Do not hold a `ViewHandle` as a lock.** It is inert once the request ended, and it is not
  awaitable; use `ShowAsync` or `WaitForCloseAsync`.

## See also

- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md)
- [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md)
- [System overlays](System-Overlays.md)
- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md)
- [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md)
- [Transitions](Transitions.md)
- [Queue](Queue.md)
- [Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md)
- [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md)
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md)
- [Architecture: projection and the input shield](Design/Architecture.md#7-the-input-shield)

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/System-Overlays.md -->

# System overlays

[Back to index](index.md)

The `system` layer is for blocking overlays: a "Saving..." screen, a "Connecting..." spinner, a
"please wait" while something that cannot be interrupted runs. This page shows how to open one around
a piece of work, what it blocks, how back behaves while it is up, how to close it through its handle,
and how to wait until it is gone with `WaitForCloseAsync`.

The examples come from the Basic Usage sample: the settings screen shows a saving overlay while a
fake save runs.

---

## Show an overlay around work

Open the overlay, do the work, close the overlay in a `finally`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private void OnSaveClicked()
{
    OpenScope.Run(SaveAsync);
}
```

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
private async UniTask SaveAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // The root owns the overlay, so the finally below is what guarantees it never stays up.
    var overlay = Navigator.Open(AppViews.Saving, Navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.save" });

    try
    {
        await _settings.SaveAsync(ct);
    }
    finally
    {
        overlay.Close();
    }

    // Wait for the hide transition, so the status appears once the overlay is gone.
    var closed = await overlay.WaitForCloseAsync(ct);
    _status.text = closed.Reason == CloseReason.Code ? "Saved." : "Saved. The overlay ended early.";
}
```

The overlay view is an ordinary view. `SavingOverlay` sets a label in `OnOpen` and spins an indicator
on the visible scope:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SavingOverlay.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class SavingOverlay : ViewBehaviour
{
    private const float DegreesPerSecond = 360f;

    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _label;
    [SerializeField] private RectTransform _spinner;

    protected override void OnOpen(NoArgs args, ViewScope open)
    {
        _label.text = "Saving...";
    }

    protected override void OnVisible(ViewScope visible)
    {
        // Per-span work goes on the visible scope, so the spinner stops whenever the overlay is hidden or closed.
        visible.Run(SpinAsync);
    }

    private async UniTask SpinAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            // Unscaled time keeps the spinner turning while the game is paused.
            _spinner.Rotate(0f, 0f, -DegreesPerSecond * Time.unscaledDeltaTime);

            // A cancelled yield throws, and the scope swallows it as the normal end of the loop.
            await UniTask.Yield(ct);
        }
    }
}
```

Its catalog row names the `system` layer and nothing else is special: no code in the view says that
it blocks. The layer does that.

---

## What the layer does

The `system` layer has two rules, `Modal` and `ShieldsInput`. It is the highest of the three default
layers, so it is drawn above screens and popups.

| It is | Which means |
|---|---|
| `ShieldsInput` | Opening and closing the overlay hold the input shield, so nothing under it can be clicked while it appears or leaves. |
| `Modal` | The layer has a backdrop under its top view, and every view below, popups and screens, is not interactive while the overlay is on screen. |
| Not `TakesBack` | `Back()` never closes a `system` view. It is swallowed. |
| Not `History` | There is no stack. Two overlays with different ids can be up together, and neither covers the other. |
| Not `ClosedByNavigation` | Opening a screen does not close it. |

What this gives you:

- **Input is blocked.** The player cannot click the screens or popups below. Code can still open and
  close views under the overlay; the overlay blocks the player and not the navigator.
- **A screen change leaves it alone.** A screen that opens under the overlay snaps the older popups
  away with `Navigated`, and the overlay stays.
- **A popup opened while the overlay is up draws below it.** The popup layer is under the system
  layer, and it is not interactive until the overlay is gone.
- **The overlay dims what is below** with the layer's backdrop. The backdrop colour is the root's
  setting ([Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md)). Leave `Close On Backdrop` off on an overlay row; the flag
  works on any modal layer, and a blocking overlay should not end because someone tapped the dim.
  With the flag off a tap on the dim is swallowed: it closes nothing and does not reach the views below.

A view that must not block input, such as a toast, does not belong on `system`. Declare a layer for
it with `ViewLayerRules.None` through `ViewRootSetup.ExtraLayers`, as the Basic Usage sample does for
its `toasts` layer ([Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#closedbynavigation)).

---

## Back while an overlay is up

`Back()` on a `system` overlay returns `true` and closes nothing, and `BackInput.Unhandled` is not
raised. That is what makes an overlay blocking: a press of Escape does not close the screens or the
popup under it and does not open a quit confirm. One exception is described below the table.

| Row policy of the overlay | What `Back()` does |
|---|---|
| `LayerDefault`, `Close`, `Ignore` | Swallowed. The view is not asked and not closed. |
| `HandledByView` | The view is asked through `IViewBack.OnBack()`. The press is swallowed whatever the answer; a `false` does not close the overlay, because the layer does not take back. |

Two more cases swallow back: the overlay is still opening or closing, and the input shield is up. In
both, `Back()` returns `true`.

Everything below the overlay, the popup and the screen under it, stays open and is not closed by back
until the overlay is gone.

One exception: a screen or popup that is still waiting or loading below the overlay is withdrawn by
back (`Rejected` is `Cancelled`), because withdrawing a pending request comes before everything else
(see [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#resolution-order)). This matters when an overlay
covers the load of the next screen. Set that row's `Back` to `Ignore` if it must not be cancelled while
the overlay is up.

Two traps:

- `BackPolicy.Close` on a `system` row has no effect. The catalog validator reports it as
  [UIDIRECTOR122](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector122).
- If the overlay must be dismissable by the player, it needs its own button that completes or closes
  the view, or it belongs on a layer that takes back, such as `popups`. See
  [Back does nothing while a system overlay is open](Troubleshooting.md#back-does-nothing-while-a-system-overlay-is-open).

---

## Close it through its handle

`Open` returns a `ViewHandle`. `handle.Close()` closes the overlay, or withdraws the request if the
overlay has not been shown yet. `SettingsView` calls it in a `finally`, so a thrown exception or a
cancelled save still takes the overlay down.

- **Reason.** A close through the handle ends with `CloseReason.Code`.
- **It never throws,** can be called any number of times, and does nothing after the request ended.
  The first close cause wins.
- **Closing right after opening still shows the overlay once.** A close that is decided while the
  overlay is opening is carried out after the show transition. A very short job therefore shows the
  overlay for its show and hide transitions. If the overlay is still loading or waiting when the job
  ends, the request is withdrawn and the overlay never appears, `WasShown` is `false` and `Rejected`
  is `Cancelled`.
- **A second `Open` of an id that is up is refused.** While the first overlay has no close cause, the
  id is open on a layer that is not a history layer, so the call gives `RejectReason.Duplicate` and
  returns an empty handle. `IsAlive` is `false` on it, `Close()` does nothing and `WaitForCloseAsync`
  completes at once. The first overlay stays up. Do not assume the handle you got is the one that
  owns the overlay.
- **After `Close()`, a new `Open` of the id is accepted,** even while the first overlay plays its hide
  transition. Two overlays with that id then exist for a moment, and the new handle is alive. This
  happens when one job closes the overlay and the next job opens it right away.

### Who owns the overlay

The sample passes `Navigator.RootToken` as owner. The overlay then ends only when something closes it
or the root is destroyed, which is why the `finally` is the guarantee. Two other choices exist:

- Pass a token that ends with the work, such as the open scope token of the view whose life matches
  the work. Or pass the token of your own `CancellationTokenSource` that the routine cancels in a
  `finally`; the package never cancels it for you, so that `finally` is a line you write. Either way
  the close reason is `OwnerEnded` and the overlay is snapped away with no hide transition.
- Pass the screen's scope token. The overlay then closes with `OwnerEnded` when the screen closes.

An overlay that stays up with nobody to close it blocks the whole interface. That is the main risk of
the layer; the `Window > UIDirector` view and `INavigator.Describe` list the open views and the
shield holders when you need to find the one that stayed.

---

## Wait for it to be gone

`WaitForCloseAsync` completes when the request ends:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public UniTask<ViewClosed> WaitForCloseAsync(CancellationToken waiter);
```

It is on `ViewHandle`, because an `Open` call has no await of its own. In `SaveAsync`, calling
`overlay.Close()` only starts the hide transition. Awaiting the handle holds the code until the
overlay is gone, so the status text appears after the overlay left and not under it:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
// Wait for the hide transition, so the status appears once the overlay is gone.
var closed = await overlay.WaitForCloseAsync(ct);
_status.text = closed.Reason == CloseReason.Code ? "Saved." : "Saved. The overlay ended early.";
```

`ViewClosed` carries the same facts as a `ViewResult` without a value: `WasShown`, `Reason`,
`Rejected` and `Detail`.

- Any number of callers can wait on one handle. A call after the request ended returns the stored
  outcome at once.
- It throws `OperationCanceledException` only when the token you pass is cancelled. The token you
  pass cancels your wait and never the overlay.
- The reason tells you who ended it. `Code` is a close by code of an overlay that was shown.
  `NotShown` with `Rejected` of `Cancelled` is your own close that withdrew the overlay before it
  appeared. `Destroyed` means the root or the instance went away. `OwnerEnded` is possible only for an
  overlay owned by a token other than `RootToken`. Anything but `Code` is what the sample's text
  "The overlay ended early." reports.

When the overlay itself produces an answer, for example a "connection lost, retry" overlay with a
button, open it with `ShowAsync` and read the `ViewResult`; back stays swallowed, so the view needs
its own button. See [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).

When no overlay is needed and input only has to be blocked for a while, `INavigator.HoldInput` does
that without a view; see [Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md).

## Traps

- **An overlay that nobody closes locks the interface.** Close it in a `finally`, or give it an
  owner that ends with the work.
- **Back does nothing while it is up.** That is the design; it is not a bug in `BackInput`.
- **A second overlay with the same id is refused** while the first has no close cause. Check
  `IsAlive` on the handle when two callers can ask for the same overlay.
- **Per-span work goes on the visible scope.** `SavingOverlay` starts its spinner there, so it stops
  when the overlay is hidden or closed and nothing needs an unsubscribe.
- **A popup opened while an overlay is up opens below it** and cannot be used until the overlay is
  gone. Open it after the overlay has closed, for example after `await overlay.WaitForCloseAsync(ct)`.

## See also

- [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md)
- [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md)
- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md)
- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md)
- [Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md)
- [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md)
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md)
- [Architecture: back resolution](Design/Architecture.md#8-back-resolution)

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Transitions.md -->

# Transitions

[Back to index](index.md)

A transition animates a view in and out. It is a component on the view prefab, referenced by the prefab's `ViewHost`. A view without one shows and hides instantly. This page covers the built-in transitions, putting one on a prefab, time, writing your own, and the contract a custom transition must keep. The DOTween based transition is on [DOTween](DOTween.md).

---

## Put a built-in transition on a view

1. Open the view prefab and select its root, the object that has the `ViewHost`.
2. Add `FadeTransition`, `ScaleTransition` or `SlideTransition` to it.
3. Drag that component into the `Transition` field of the `ViewHost`.
4. Set the duration and the eases.

Nothing else is needed: no code, no tween library. The same component plays both the show and the hide. A `ViewHost` references one transition, so a view has one.

| Transition | What it animates | Settings and defaults |
|---|---|---|
| `FadeTransition` | The alpha of a `CanvasGroup` on its own object: shown is 1, hidden is 0. It requires a `CanvasGroup`, which Unity adds with it. | `Duration` 0.25 s, `Show Ease` OutCubic, `Hide Ease` InCubic |
| `ScaleTransition` | The uniform scale of a target `RectTransform`: shown is 1, hidden is `Hidden Scale`. Optionally fades a `CanvasGroup` too, added when missing. | `Target` (empty means its own object), `Hidden Scale` 0.85, `Fade` off, `Duration` 0.25 s, `Show Ease` OutBack, `Hide Ease` InCubic |
| `SlideTransition` | The `anchoredPosition` of a target `RectTransform`: shown is the position authored in the prefab, hidden is that position moved one layer width or height past an edge. | `Target`, `Edge` (Left, Right, Top or Bottom; default Bottom), `Duration` 0.25 s, `Show Ease` OutCubic, `Hide Ease` InCubic |

The eases are `Linear`, `OutCubic`, `InCubic`, `InOutCubic` and `OutBack`; they are chosen in the Inspector and there is no easing API. `SlideTransition` measures the distance from the layer's rectangle in canvas units when it plays, not from the screen size, so it follows a resized layer. It reads the authored position the first time it is used.

To combine motions that the built-ins do not combine, such as a fade with a slide, write a custom transition or use `TweenTransition` from the [DOTween](DOTween.md) integration.

A built-in transition plays its motion in both directions: the same parts and the same duration run towards the shown pose on a show and towards the hidden pose on a hide. Only the eases (`Show Ease`, `Hide Ease`) differ. A view that needs a different show and hide, such as scaling in and fading out, needs a custom `ViewTransition`, because `PlayAsync(show, ct)` is where the two directions can differ.

## Time

Every built-in transition runs on unscaled time. A paused game (`Time.timeScale` 0) still shows and hides views. The backdrop of a modal layer fades on the same loop for 0.2 s; that fade is separate from the view's transition.

One frame advances a built-in transition or a backdrop fade by at most 1/30 s, while the clock of the timeouts advances by at most 0.1 s per frame. Below 30 fps a transition therefore takes longer than its duration: a duration of D seconds takes at least 30 x D frames, so the default 0.25 s fade takes 8 frames, about 0.4 s, at 20 fps. With the default 3 s transition timeout, a built-in transition longer than about fps / 10 seconds is snapped with [UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106) although it animates correctly (at 20 fps, a duration above 2 s). Below 10 fps the clock is capped as well, so any built-in transition of 1 s or longer is snapped. Raise `Transition Timeout Seconds` or shorten the transition. Custom transitions do not use this loop.

The timeout that bounds a transition counts on the root's clock, which also runs on unscaled time (see the contract below).

## When a transition does not play

The package snaps a view to its end pose, with no animation, when:

- the view is closed by navigation: popups that are older than a screen that opens are ended at once with `CloseReason.Navigated`, and a screen that is reopened in place with new arguments is shown again without a transition;
- the request is ended from outside: the owner token ended or the instance was deactivated (a destroyed instance, or an instance whose root was destroyed, is gone: the request just ends and nothing is snapped);
- a transition runs longer than the transition timeout, or throws.

A close that is requested while the show plays does not cut the show. When the view, its handle or a result call asks for the close during `Opening` (`Close`, `Complete`, a handle's `Close`), the show plays to its end and the hide plays after it. Only the cases above cut a show: a terminate cause (the owner ended, the instance deactivated, the view closed by navigation) snaps the view to the hidden pose; a timeout or a transition that throws snaps it to the end pose of the direction that was playing; a destroyed instance or root just ends the request.

A view without a transition is always snapped. See [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md) for what closes by navigation.

---

## Write a custom transition

Derive from `ViewTransition` and implement two members:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public abstract class ViewTransition : MonoBehaviour
{
    public abstract UniTask PlayAsync(bool show, CancellationToken ct);
    public abstract void Snap(bool shown);
}
```

`PlayAsync(show, ct)` animates to the shown pose when `show` is `true` and to the hidden pose when it is `false`. `Snap(shown)` writes the end pose at once. `PopTransition` fades and scales the view on unscaled time:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/PopTransition.cs -->
```csharp
[RequireComponent(typeof(CanvasGroup))]
public sealed class PopTransition : ViewTransition
{
    // One frame advances at most this much: a hitch cannot skip the animation, and below 30 fps it runs slower.
    private const float MaxStepSeconds = 1f / 30f;

    [SerializeField, Min(0f)] private float _duration = 0.2f;
    [SerializeField] private float _hiddenScale = 0.9f;

    private CanvasGroup _group;

    // Snap and a newer play bump this, which ends a play that is still running.
    private int _generation;

    public override async UniTask PlayAsync(bool show, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (ct.IsCancellationRequested || !TryGetGroup(out var group))
            return;

        var target = transform;
        var fromAlpha = group.alpha;
        var fromScale = target.localScale.x;
        var toAlpha = show ? 1f : 0f;
        var toScale = show ? 1f : _hiddenScale;
        var generation = ++_generation;
        var elapsed = 0f;

        while (elapsed < _duration)
        {
            await UniTask.NextFrame(PlayerLoopTiming.Update);

            // Stop on cancel, on Snap, and when the view was destroyed mid-play.
            if (ct.IsCancellationRequested || generation != _generation || group == null || target == null)
                return;

            // Unscaled, so a paused game still shows and hides views.
            elapsed += Mathf.Min(Time.unscaledDeltaTime, MaxStepSeconds);
            var t = Mathf.SmoothStep(0f, 1f, Mathf.Clamp01(elapsed / _duration));
            Apply(group, target, Mathf.Lerp(fromAlpha, toAlpha, t), Mathf.Lerp(fromScale, toScale, t));
        }

        // The last write is exact, whatever the frame steps added up to.
        Apply(group, target, toAlpha, toScale);
    }
```

What to read in it:

- The loop steps one frame at a time and adds `Time.unscaledDeltaTime`, capped, so it finishes while the game is paused.
- After every await it checks three things: the token, a generation counter and whether the view still exists. `Snap` and a newer play bump the counter, which ends an older play that has not yet seen the cancel. The older play returns on its next frame, never inside `Snap`.
- The last write is exact, so the pose never depends on how the frame steps added up.

`Snap` writes the end pose and ends a play that is still running:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/PopTransition.cs -->
```csharp
public override void Snap(bool shown)
{
    // Never throws: a destroyed view is skipped.
    if (!TryGetGroup(out var group))
        return;

    _generation++;
    Apply(group, transform, shown ? 1f : 0f, shown ? 1f : _hiddenScale);
}
```

The helpers treat a destroyed component or transform as missing instead of throwing:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/PopTransition.cs -->
```csharp
private static void Apply(CanvasGroup group, Transform target, float alpha, float scale)
{
    if (group == null || target == null)
        return;

    group.alpha = alpha;
    target.localScale = new Vector3(scale, scale, 1f);
}

private bool TryGetGroup(out CanvasGroup group)
{
    // A destroyed component cannot reach its transform, so it counts as missing.
    if (this == null)
    {
        group = null;
        return false;
    }

    if (_group == null)
        _group = GetComponent<CanvasGroup>();

    group = _group;
    return group != null;
}
```

Put the component on the prefab root, next to the `ViewHost`, and assign it to the `Transition` field, as for a built-in.

## The contract

The package gives a transition a fixed sequence. Before the first show it calls `Snap(false)`, turns the canvases on and calls `PlayAsync(true, ct)`. To hide, it calls `PlayAsync(false, ct)`. When a terminate cause cuts the request (owner ended, instance deactivated, closed by navigation), the package calls `Snap(false)` and then cancels `ct`. When the timeout fires or the play throws, it cancels `ct` and then calls `Snap` with the end pose of that direction. When the instance or the root is destroyed it only cancels `ct`.

In a cut, `Snap` runs before `ct` is cancelled. A play that `Snap` ends must therefore not report completion from inside `Snap`: the runner would continue as if the transition had finished normally while the request is still being cut.

A custom transition keeps these rules:

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| **Run on unscaled time.** | A transition on scaled time never finishes while `timeScale` is 0. The timeout then snaps it and reports [UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106). Use `Time.unscaledDeltaTime`, `UniTask.Delay(..., DelayType.UnscaledDeltaTime)` or DOTween with unscaled update. |
| **Start from the opposite end pose and finish on the pose `Snap` writes for the same direction.** | The runner never interrupts a transition with another one, so there is no "continue from the current pose" case. A play that ends on a different pose than `Snap` leaves the view in a state a later snap would change. The runner snaps to the hidden pose before every show, and a hide always starts from the shown pose, so starting from the current pose, as `PopTransition` does, is the same thing. |
| **Stop when `ct` is cancelled.** Return within a few frames, or throw `OperationCanceledException`, and write nothing after you have returned. | A terminate cause snaps and then cancels the token; the timeout cancels and then snaps. A play that goes on writing overwrites the snapped pose. On cancel, do not jump to the end pose; the runner snaps if it needs to. |
| **`Snap` is synchronous, idempotent and never throws, from any state.** | It can arrive before any play, during a play, after a play, twice in a row, or on a destroyed component. It writes the end pose and ends a running play. Guard every reference to Unity objects, because the component may already be destroyed. |
| **Never complete the returned task inside `Snap`, or inside a Unity destroy or disable message.** | If `Snap` ends the running play and that completes its task on the spot, the runner resumes inside `Snap`, before the package has cancelled `ct`, and carries on as if the play had finished normally. If your play ends because `OnDestroy` or `OnDisable` killed a tween or cancelled a source, the runner resumes inside that message, and its next steps activate, deactivate or reparent objects, which is an engine error inside `OnDisable`. A play that is ended by `Snap` finishes one player-loop step later, for example with `await UniTask.Yield()`, or polls as the DOTween sample does. |
| **Do not call the navigator.** | A transition is a presentation detail. Opening or closing views from inside one re-enters the runner that is waiting for it. |
| **Finish within the transition timeout.** | See below. |

An exception from `PlayAsync` or from `Snap` is reported to the root's error handler as a transition error (`ViewErrorSource.Transition`) with the view id, or logged with `Debug.LogException` when no handler is set. After a failed play the view is snapped. That is a fallback; do not rely on it.

### The timeout

A show or hide transition that does not finish within the transition timeout is cancelled, the view is snapped to its end pose, and the package logs [UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106), naming the view and whether it was the show or the hide. The runner then continues as if the transition had finished. The request is not lost.

- The timeout is the `Transition Timeout Seconds` field of `ViewRoot` (serialized as `_transitionTimeoutSeconds`). The default is 3 s, set by the constant `DefaultTransitionTimeoutSeconds`, and the minimum is 0.1 s.
- It counts on the root's clock. `ViewRoot.Update` advances that clock by `min(Time.unscaledDeltaTime, 0.1 s)` per frame, so it keeps running at `timeScale` 0, and a suspension or a breakpoint adds at most one step.
- If a transition really needs more than 3 s, raise the field.
- The runner stops waiting at the timeout even if the transition ignores its token, but a transition that ignores the token may keep running and write poses after the snap. Honour the token.

### Checking a custom transition

The package ships no checker for custom transitions, so check yours by hand: `Snap(true)` and `Snap(false)` write two different poses and each can be called twice; a play ends on the pose `Snap` writes; calling `Snap` in the middle of a play does not complete the play's task before `Snap` returns; cancelling a play stops it within a few frames and the pose stays put; a play finishes while `Time.timeScale` is 0; and destroying the view in the middle of a play throws nothing.

---

## Traps

- **Scaled time.** `Time.deltaTime`, `WaitForSeconds` and `UniTask.Delay` with the default delay type all stop at `timeScale` 0. The symptom is a 3 s stall and [UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106).
- **`Snap` that creates things.** Adding a component in `Snap` can fail on an object that is being destroyed. Resolve and cache references in advance, and guard them.
- **A tween library that completes from a kill callback.** The kill may run inside `OnDestroy`. See [DOTween](DOTween.md).
- **A transition on a child with the wrong target.** The built-ins act on their own object's `CanvasGroup` or on their `Target`. Put them on the prefab root unless you set a target on purpose.
- **Expecting a hide animation everywhere.** Navigation, a lost instance and the timeout snap without one.

## See also

- [DOTween](DOTween.md): `TweenTransition` and writing a transition on DOTween
- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md): the prefab structure a view needs
- [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md): the backdrop fade and the input shield during a transition
- [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md): what closes a view without a hide transition
- [Diagnostics](Diagnostics.md): how warnings and errors are reported
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106): UIDIRECTOR106, a transition that did not finish
- [Limitations](Limitations.md): transitions are not interruptible
- [Architecture: transitions](Design/Architecture.md#15-transitions): how the runner plays and cuts a transition

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Queue.md -->

# Queue

[Back to index](index.md)

A `ViewQueue` presents requests one at a time, the most important first, on one layer. Use it for
things that appear because of the app and not because the player asked: a maintenance notice, a
what-is-new card, a reward, a request for feedback. Several features can queue at the same moment
without knowing about each other, and the queue decides the order. It sits above the navigator and
talks to it through `INavigator` only; a project that needs no queue pays nothing for it
([ADR-004](Design/Decisions/ADR-004-Queue-Above-The-Navigator.md)).

This page covers creating a queue, queueing, priorities, gates, holds, the ways a request ends
without being shown, observing, and a feature that adds its own catalog. The examples are the
files of the Queue Usage sample.

---

## Present notices by priority

A queue needs the navigator, the layer it presents on, and a lifetime. The sample creates one for
the popups layer that lives as long as the UI, and adds a gate to it:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/StartupNotices.cs -->
```csharp
public StartupNotices(INavigator navigator, IOnboardingState onboarding)
{
    _lifetime = navigator.RootToken;
    _queue = new ViewQueue(navigator, ViewLayers.Popups, _lifetime, "startup");
    _queue.AddGate(new OnboardingGate(onboarding), _lifetime);
}
```

Two notices are then queued. The one queued second has the higher priority:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/StartupNotices.cs -->
```csharp
public void EnqueueAll()
{
    _queue.Enqueue(QueueViews.Notice, new NoticeArgs("What is new", "Two new guides were added."), _lifetime,
        new QueueOptions { Priority = 10, Source = "startup.news" });

    // Enqueued second but presented first: the higher priority wins.
    _queue.Enqueue(QueueViews.Notice, new NoticeArgs("Maintenance", "The service pauses at 02:00."), _lifetime,
        new QueueOptions { Priority = 100, Source = "startup.maintenance" });
}
```

In the sample, the bootstrap opens the lobby and queues the notices in the same moment:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/QueueBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
_navigator.Open(QueueViews.Lobby, _navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "boot" });

// The notices wait until the lobby is shown, then present by priority.
notices.EnqueueAll();
```

What you see when you press Play: the lobby opens. Once it is shown, the queue presents
"Maintenance" (priority 100) although it was queued second. You close it with "OK" and "What is
new" (priority 10) follows at once. Only one popup is on screen at a time. The Console shows
`[queue] Enqueued ...` lines for both notices, in queueing order, and then the navigator's
`Requested` lines in presentation order (see [Observing the queue](#observing-the-queue)).

The keys are ordinary keys; the queue takes the same `ViewKey` values as the navigator:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/QueueViews.cs -->
```csharp
[ViewKeys]
public static class QueueViews
{
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Lobby = ViewKey.Create("lobby");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoticeArgs, NoResult> Notice = ViewKey.Create<NoticeArgs>("notice");
    public static readonly ViewKey<AskArgs, bool> Ask = ViewKey.Create<AskArgs, bool>("ask");
    public static readonly ViewKey<TipArgs, NoResult> TutorialTip = ViewKey.Create<TipArgs>("tutorial-tip");
}
```

---

## Create a queue

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public ViewQueue(INavigator navigator, ViewLayer layer, CancellationToken lifetime, string name = null)
```

| Parameter | What it is |
|---|---|
| `navigator` | The navigator that presents the items. A queue built on the root's own navigator (`ViewRoot.Navigator`) is listed in the `Window > UIDirector` window and its events reach the window's event list. A queue built on any other `INavigator` works but is invisible to the window. |
| `layer` | The layer the queue watches and presents on, for example `ViewLayers.Popups`. The queue presents an item only while this layer is clear. On the root's own navigator the layer must exist there: a layer id that is neither one of `ViewLayers` nor in `ViewRootSetup.ExtraLayers` makes the constructor throw `ArgumentException` (parameter `layer`) before anything is registered. Another `INavigator` implementation is not checked. |
| `lifetime` | The queue lives until this token ends. Pass `INavigator.RootToken` for "as long as the UI exists". A token that is already cancelled gives an inert queue. |
| `name` | A label for the window and for `Describe`. Defaults to the layer id. |

There is no `Dispose`; ending the lifetime ends the queue. The queue also ends when the
navigator's root is destroyed, whatever lifetime you gave it, so a queue with an independent
lifetime does not outlive the UI. A queue built after the root is gone is inert from the start.
Create it on the main thread: the constructor registers an observer on the navigator
([Threading](Threading.md)). A project can have several queues, for different layers or different
features.

**When the queue presents.** After an enqueue, a removed hold, an added or removed gate, an ended item, or any navigator
request that ends or settles, the queue looks at its layer on the next `Update` tick. A gate that starts answering differently
does not wake the queue; the new answer is used the next time the queue looks. It presents the first waiting item only
when `INavigator.IsLayerClear(layer)` is true, which means all of these hold:

- the layer has no request at all, shown or waiting, including views opened by hand;
- no modal layer above it has a request (a system overlay stops a popups queue);
- the navigator is not busy: no operation is running on any layer and no input hold exists.

Two consequences follow from that rule. A queue waits while something else is open on its layer,
so a popup opened by hand keeps the queue waiting until it closes. And a queue on a history
layer such as `screens` is clear only while the layer is empty, because the bottom screen of the
stack stays; queues belong on layers whose views come and go, such as popups.

**Queue only keys whose rows are on the queue's layer.** The queue does not look at the rows when
you enqueue. It watches `layer` and asks the navigator to open the key; the navigator checks the
row at that moment. A row on another layer is turned away: the item ends as `NotShown` with
`RejectReason.WrongLayer`, nothing is placed, the input shield is not taken, and the navigator logs
[UIDIRECTOR126](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector126) naming both layers. The event carries the queue's
layer id, so every event of the item names one layer.

The usual cause is the row's layer. A row's `Layer Id` starts as `screens`, and the Inspector's +
copies the last row's layer, so a reward or news row that was added and never moved can still be on
`screens`. Queued on a `popups` queue it ends as `NotShown` with `WrongLayer` and UIDIRECTOR126, and
the view never appears. Set the row's `Layer Id` to the
queue's layer before you enqueue its key.

---

## Enqueue and EnqueueAsync

Both calls take the key, the arguments, an owner token and optional `QueueOptions`. They differ
in what they give back.

| Call | Returns | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `Enqueue(key, args, owner, options)` | `int`, the request id | You do not need the outcome. The id is the one every event of this item carries. |
| `EnqueueAsync(key, args, owner, options)` | `UniTask<ViewResult<TResult>>` | You need to know how it ended, or the view's answer. |

For a key without arguments pass `default(NoArgs)`; the queue has no shortcut overloads.

`EnqueueAsync` completes in every case, once. It completes when the view closes, and also when the
item ends inside the queue without being shown (denied, owner ended, cleared, queue ended). The
outcome is data, as with `ShowAsync` ([Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md)). The sample
asks a yes or no question and reads the answer only through `HasValue`:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/StartupNotices.cs -->
```csharp
public async UniTask<bool> AskForFeedbackAsync()
{
    // Completes also when the item never shows (denied, cleared), so the answer is read only through HasValue.
    var answer = await _queue.EnqueueAsync(QueueViews.Ask,
        new AskArgs("Would you like to tell us what to improve?"), _lifetime,
        new QueueOptions { Priority = 1, Source = "startup.feedback" });

    return answer.HasValue && answer.Value;
}
```

A turned-away item has `WasShown == false`, `Reason == CloseReason.NotShown`, a `Rejected` reason and
a `Detail`. In the sample, "Yes" completes with `true` and "No" with `false`. Escape, or an item that never
showed, carries no value (`HasValue` is `false`), so the method returns `false` for them too.

Neither call presents anything before the next tick, even when the layer is clear, so enqueues made
in one frame are ordered by priority and not by call order. Both throw `InvalidOperationException` off the main thread and `ArgumentNullException`
for a default key; a refused call reserves no request id and publishes nothing. A key whose id has
no catalog row is not noticed at enqueue; the navigator turns it away when the item is presented
(`RejectReason.UnknownKey`, [UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101)).

---

## QueueOptions

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public struct QueueOptions
{
    public int Priority;
    public string Source;
}
```

These are the only two options. Leave the struct out and both are default.

| Field | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Priority` | `0` | Higher is presented first. Negative values are allowed and go after the default. Equal priorities keep the order in which they were queued. The value is carried by the item's events and by `GateRequest.Priority`. |
| `Source` | `null` | A free tag, as `OpenOptions.Source`. It travels with the item's events and with the `GateRequest`. Use one constant string per call site, such as `"startup.news"`, so a log line or an analytics event names the code that queued. |

The priority only orders waiting items. It does not close or replace a view that is already on
screen ([Limitations](Limitations.md)); urgent content that must not wait opens immediately.

---

## Priority order

The queue keeps its waiting items sorted by priority, highest first, and equal priorities in the
order they were queued. A new item goes after every waiting item with the same or a higher priority.

- Items queued in one frame while the layer is clear are all waiting when the next tick comes, so the
  highest priority is presented first whatever the call order. The Queue Usage sample shows it
  with "Maintenance" (100) queued after "What is new" (10).
- An item queued while another is on screen, with a higher priority than the waiting ones, goes
  before them. It does not go before the item that is on screen.
- The item that is being presented is not in the waiting list, so `Count` does not include it.
- When the presented view closes, the code that awaited it resumes before the queue presents the
  next item, because the queue pumps on the next tick. If that code opens a follow-up popup
  immediately, the layer is busy again and the next queued item keeps waiting.

---

## Gates

A gate is a synchronous rule that sees a request and answers yes or no. Use one for a condition
that belongs to no single feature: do not show a promotion while a tutorial runs, or while the
player is in a purchase.

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public interface IViewGate
{
    GateDecision Evaluate(in GateRequest request);
}
```

The sample's gate turns away every queued request below priority 100 while the tutorial runs:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/OnboardingGate.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class OnboardingGate : IViewGate
{
    private const int UrgentPriority = 100;

    private readonly IOnboardingState _onboarding;

    public OnboardingGate(IOnboardingState onboarding) => _onboarding = onboarding;

    // Asked at enqueue and again right before presentation, so a notice queued earlier is caught too.
    public GateDecision Evaluate(in GateRequest request) =>
        _onboarding.IsRunning && request.Priority < UrgentPriority
            ? GateDecision.Deny("onboarding is running")
            : GateDecision.Allow;
}
```

A gate is added with an owner and an optional order, and it is asked until the owner ends or the
returned `ViewRegistration` is removed:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public ViewRegistration AddGate(IViewGate gate, CancellationToken owner, int order = 0)
```

**What the gate sees.** A `GateRequest` has these read-only fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `RequestId` | The id the item keeps from enqueue to close. |
| `ViewId` | The id of the requested view. |
| `Layer` | The layer the queue presents on. |
| `Priority` | The item's priority. |
| `Source` | The item's source tag; may be null. |
| `AtPresentation` | `false` at enqueue, `true` right before the item is presented. |

There are no arguments in it. A gate decides by view id, priority, source and your own state.

**When it is asked.** At enqueue, and again right before presentation, once the layer is clear and
the item is next. A gate that allowed an item at enqueue can deny it later. Gates run in ascending
`order`; equal orders keep the order they were added. The first deny wins and later gates are not
asked. While the queue is held or its layer is busy, no gate is asked at presentation.

**What a deny does.** The item ends as `NotShown` with `RejectReason.Denied`, and the reason string
you gave to `GateDecision.Deny(reason)` is its `Detail`. A deny at enqueue means the item never
entered the queue (see the next section). A deny at presentation ends that item and the queue goes
on to the next one in the same pump.

`default(GateDecision)` is `Allow`, so a `GateDecision` field or local that was never assigned lets
the request pass; only `GateDecision.Deny(reason)` denies.

**A gate that throws** counts as a deny. The exception goes to the root's error handler
(`ViewErrorSource.Gate`), the gate type's name is in the `Detail`, and the queue reports
[UIDIRECTOR119](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector119). Later gates are not asked for that item.

Keep a gate quick and free of side effects: it runs inside the enqueue call and inside the pump.
A gate is not the place to open a view or to hold the queue; a gate that does so at presentation
gets no `ShowAsync` for that item, which waits until the layer is clear again.

A gate answers yes or no. "Not now, later" is a hold.

**Postpone instead of refuse.** A deny at presentation ends the item for good: it is not kept for
later. To get "never during a fight, but do not lose it", do not deny in a gate and re-enqueue in a
loop. Hold the queue for as long as the condition lasts, so the items stay waiting. Call
`queue.Hold("fight", fightToken)` when the fight starts, with the fight's token as owner, and call
`Remove()` on the returned registration when the fight ends; ending the token removes the hold too.

A hold does not touch a popup the queue presented before the fight started; it stays until it closes
(a screen the fight opens closes it, see
[A screen closes a presented popup](#a-screen-closes-a-presented-popup)).

Use a gate to refuse an item, such as a promotion that must not appear while a tutorial runs.

---

## Holds

A flow that needs the screen for itself holds the queue: while any hold exists, the queue presents
nothing. The tutorial in the sample takes a hold, shows its own tips directly, and removes the hold
on every way out:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/TutorialFlow.cs -->
```csharp
IsRunning = true;
_onboarding.IsRunning = true;

// Queued items wait; the flow's own opens below are not affected by the hold.
var hold = _queue.Hold("tutorial", ct);
try
{
    for (var step = 1; step <= Tips.Length; step++)
    {
        var result = await _navigator.ShowAsync(QueueViews.TutorialTip,
            new TipArgs(Tips[step - 1], step, Tips.Length), ct,
            new OpenOptions { Source = "tutorial" });

        // Not shown, backed out, replaced or owner ended: the player left the tutorial.
        if (result.Reason != CloseReason.Dismissed && result.Reason != CloseReason.Completed)
            return;
    }
}
finally
{
    // Ending the hold lets the queue continue; while the tutorial ran, the gate denied notices below priority 100.
    hold.Remove();
    _onboarding.IsRunning = false;
    IsRunning = false;
}
```

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public ViewRegistration Hold(
    string reason,
    CancellationToken owner,
    [CallerMemberName] string member = null,
    [CallerLineNumber] int line = 0)
public bool IsHeld { get; }
```

The compiler fills in `member` and `line`; call `Hold(reason, owner)` and leave them out.

- **Holds are counted.** Two holds need two removals; the queue resumes when the last one ends.
  A hold ends when its `ViewRegistration.Remove()` is called or its owner token ends, whichever
  comes first. Ending it again does nothing.
- **A hold does not touch views.** It stops the queue from presenting the next item. A view that is
  already presented stays, and the flow's own `Open` and `ShowAsync` calls are not affected.
- **No automatic timeout.** An automatic release would let popups through in the middle of a flow.
  A hold that is older than 60 seconds logs [UIDIRECTOR111](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector111) once,
  naming the reason you gave and the member and line that called `Hold`. Give the hold the owner of
  the flow and remove it in a `finally`, as the sample does, so no way out leaves the queue held.
  On the root's own navigator the 60 seconds run on the navigator clock, which the root advances by
  at most 0.1 s per frame; below 10 frames per second the warning comes later in wall time, and the
  age in the message is measured in unscaled time. A queue on any other `INavigator` times the
  warning with a UniTask delay instead.
- **Hold and gate together.** In the sample, the hold keeps queued notices waiting until the
  tutorial ends, and the gate turns away the ones that should not wait. While the tutorial runs, a
  request below priority 100 is turned away at once and one at 100 or above waits for the hold.
  Escape on a tip leaves the tutorial early: the tip closes with `CloseReason.Back`, the remaining
  tips are not shown and the hold is removed in the same moment.
- A `Hold` with a null reason throws `ArgumentNullException`. On a queue that has ended, or with an
  owner that has ended, it takes no hold and returns an inactive registration.

---

## A screen closes a presented popup

The `popups` layer is closed by navigation. When code opens a screen, a queued popup the navigator
has already taken is ended, and the queue does not show it again. A popup that was on screen snaps
away with `CloseReason.Navigated`. One that was still loading or opening ends as `NotShown` /
`Cancelled`. A popup the new screen opens itself survives
([Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md#popups-and-screen-changes)).

If the item must be seen, read the result of `EnqueueAsync` and enqueue it again: when
`result.Reason == CloseReason.Navigated`, call `queue.Enqueue(...)` with the same key, arguments, owner
and options. An item that was still loading when the screen opened ends as `NotShown` / `Cancelled`
instead. `Cancelled` also comes from `Clear()` and from the queue's end, so do not enqueue again on it
blindly.

To keep waiting items from appearing between the steps of a screen flow, hold the queue while the
flow runs (see [Holds](#holds)). The hold does not protect the item that is already on screen.

---

## When a request is turned away

A request that fails a check in the call is never queued. It publishes a single `NotShown` event on
the queue's observers, with no `Enqueued` before it, and `EnqueueAsync` completes at once with the
same facts. The queue checks in this order:

| Check | `Rejected` | `Detail` |
|---|---|---|
| The queue has ended because its lifetime token was cancelled | `Cancelled` | The queue's lifetime ended. |
| The queue has ended because the root was destroyed (also a queue built after that) | `RootGone` | The root was destroyed. |
| The item's owner is already cancelled | `OwnerEnded` | The owner had already ended. |
| A gate denies it at enqueue, or throws | `Denied` | The gate's reason, or `gate <TypeName> threw` for a throw |

`Enqueue` still returns a request id in these cases, the one the `NotShown` event carries. After the
queue has ended it has no observers left, so that `NotShown` reaches only the `EnqueueAsync` result
(and the window's event list in the editor and in development builds).

An item that was accepted ends later, with `Enqueued` first and then one more event:

| Cause | Event after `Enqueued` | `Rejected` |
|---|---|---|
| The owner ends while the item waits | `NotShown` from the queue | `OwnerEnded` |
| A gate denies it at presentation | `NotShown` from the queue | `Denied` |
| `Clear()` is called | `NotShown` from the queue | `Cancelled` |
| The queue's lifetime ends | `NotShown` from the queue | `Cancelled` |
| The root is destroyed | `NotShown` from the queue | `RootGone`; an item owned by `RootToken` may end first as `OwnerEnded` |
| The navigator turns it away at its call (unknown key, a duplicate, a full sorting band, a row on another layer) | `NotShown` from the navigator, with no `Requested` | The navigator's reason; `WrongLayer` for a row on another layer |
| The navigator accepts it and the view then fails to load, declines or throws | `Requested`, then `NotShown`, both from the navigator | The navigator's reason |
| The call that presents the item throws, or the task it returned faults later | `NotShown` from the queue (for a task that faults later: unless the navigator already published an end for the item) | `Faulted` |

An item that the navigator ended without showing is not retried; the next item follows on the next
tick. If the navigator itself throws or faults while an item is presented, which the package's
navigator does not do for anything that happens to a view, the item ends as `NotShown` / `Faulted`
and the queue carries on. A task that faults after the call returned is handled the same way as a
throw at the call: the queue publishes its own `NotShown` on the main thread, so an observer sees
one end for the item (a navigator that is not the package's and publishes its own end before it throws
can cause a second), and then completes the `EnqueueAsync` result. The `Rejected` values
and what each means are listed in [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md#reject-reasons).

The Queue Usage sample is written for a denied request: when code queues a notice below priority 100
while the tutorial runs (a tip is a modal popup that covers the lobby, so its buttons cannot do it),
the Console shows no `Enqueued` line, only
`[queue] NotShown #n notice priority=10 source=startup.news rejected=Denied detail=onboarding is running`.
That is the only kind of turned-away request in the sample's Console that has no `Enqueued` before it.

---

## The waiting cap

A queue has no cap of its own. Its waiting list is not limited, so queueing many items is safe.

The waiting cap you may know from [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md) belongs to the
navigator: one layer keeps at most four requests waiting by default (`Waiting Cap` on the
`ViewRoot`), and the next one is refused as `Busy` with
[UIDIRECTOR112](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector112). A queue never reaches it: it presents an item
only when its layer has no request, so it hands the navigator one request at a time. That is the
reason a burst of notices belongs in a queue and not in a loop of `Open` calls.

---

## Owners end queued items

The owner token you pass to `Enqueue` decides how long the item may live.

- **While the item waits,** an owner that ends takes the item out of the queue: it ends as
  `NotShown` with `RejectReason.OwnerEnded`, and `EnqueueAsync` completes. The queue's
  `Count` drops and the next item can follow.
- **Once the item is presented,** the navigator owns the token. A shown view closes with
  `CloseReason.OwnerEnded`, and a view that is still loading is withdrawn as `NotShown` /
  `OwnerEnded`.
- **The queue's lifetime is different from an item's owner.** The queue ends when its lifetime
  token is cancelled and also when the navigator's root is destroyed. It then becomes inert:
  waiting items end as `NotShown`, every hold, gate and observer registration ends, and later calls
  do nothing harmful (`Enqueue` returns the reserved id and ends the item as `NotShown`, which only
  the `EnqueueAsync` result and the window's event list can see, as no observer is left; the
  registration calls return inactive registrations). The reason is `Cancelled` when the lifetime
  ended and `RootGone` when the root was destroyed. An item whose own owner also ends with the root
  (for example an owner of `RootToken`, as in the sample) can end as `OwnerEnded` first, and a queue
  observer whose owner is `RootToken` can already be gone when the queue ends; the package does not
  fix the order of callbacks on one token. Neither token keeps the ended queue alive: its end callbacks are released when it ends. A view that was already presented is left to
  its own owner and the navigator: that item ends once, through the navigator's result, which can
  arrive after the queue's waiting items have ended.
- `CancellationToken.None` as an owner means the item never ends by owner; only a close, the
  lifetime or `Clear()` ends it.
- An owner token cancelled on another thread is handled on the main thread and logs
  [UIDIRECTOR113](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector113); see [Threading](Threading.md).

`Clear()` ends every waiting item as `NotShown` / `Cancelled`, leaves the presented one alone, and
leaves the queue working. It is safe to call from any thread (it is posted to the main thread).

---

## Observing the queue

A queued request has two publishers. The queue publishes `Enqueued` when it accepts an item and its
own `NotShown` for an item that ends in the queue. Everything after the queue hands the item to the
navigator (`Requested`, `Shown`, `Closed`, and a `NotShown` from the navigator) is the navigator's.
The sample therefore registers one observer class twice, each time with the root's token as owner:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/QueueBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// Events of a queued request come from two publishers, so a log watches each.
_navigator.AddObserver(new QueueEventLog("[views]"), _navigator.RootToken);
notices.Queue.AddObserver(new QueueEventLog("[queue]"), _navigator.RootToken);
```

`ViewQueue.AddObserver(observer, owner)` delivers only the queue's own `Enqueued` and `NotShown`
events. The events, their fields and the observer rules are on
[Events and analytics](Events-and-Analytics.md). For one queued item the full story is:

```text
[queue] Enqueued #3 notice priority=100 source=startup.maintenance
[views] Requested #3 notice priority=100 source=startup.maintenance
[views] Shown #3 notice priority=100 source=startup.maintenance
[views] Closed #3 notice priority=100 source=startup.maintenance reason=Dismissed
```

Three ways to look at the queue itself:

- **In code.** `Count` is the number of waiting items (not the presented one) and `IsHeld` is true
  while at least one hold exists.
- **As text.** `Describe(StringBuilder)` writes the queue's state, its holds with their age, the
  number of gates, the presented item and the waiting items in order:

  ```text
  queue startup layer popups active held
    hold #1 'tutorial' age 12.4s at RunAsync (line 39)
  gates: 1
  presenting: none
  waiting: 1
    #4 notice priority 100 source startup.maintenance age 12.1s
  ```

  The request ids, ages and the call site are examples. This is the output to read when
  [UIDIRECTOR111](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector111) reports a long hold: the call site names the
  member and line that called `Hold`.
- **In the editor.** `Window > UIDirector` shows a `Queue <name>` section for every queue built on
  the root's navigator, with whether it is held, its gate count, its holds with the member and line
  that took each one, the presented item and the waiting items, and an event list that mixes the
  queue's events and the navigator's. A queue that has ended is no longer listed. The window shows
  something in Play Mode only.

---

## Add a catalog at run time from a feature

A feature that is not always present can bring its own keys and its own catalog, register the
catalog when it starts, and queue its views, all with one owner. When that owner ends, the catalog
leaves and the feature's queued items go with it. `NewsFeature` in the sample does this with one
token source linked to the root's token:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/NewsFeature.cs -->
```csharp
_owner = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(_navigator.RootToken);
_navigator.AddCatalog(_catalog, _owner.Token);

// The same owner: if the feature goes away while the notice waits, the notice ends with it.
_queue.Enqueue(
    NewsViews.News,
    new NoticeArgs("News", "A news feature was added at run time."),
    _owner.Token,
    new QueueOptions { Priority = 50, Source = "news.added" });
```

Taking the feature away is ending that owner:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/NewsFeature.cs -->
```csharp
// Ending the owner removes the catalog and releases its kept instances; the news popup ends too, because it was queued with this owner.
_owner.Cancel();
_owner.Dispose();
_owner = null;
```

In the running sample, "Add news feature" registers `NewsCatalog.asset` and the Console shows
`[queue] Enqueued ... news priority=50 source=news.added`; the popup appears at once. "Remove news
feature" ends the owner. If the popup were still waiting it would end as `NotShown` /
`OwnerEnded`, and if it were open it would close with `reason=OwnerEnded`. Pressing "Add news
feature" again registers a new catalog and queues a new popup.

What the catalog calls do, including what happens to views that are already open when a catalog
is removed (they stay open until their own owner ends), is on
[Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md#add-and-remove-a-catalog-at-run-time). The rule for the
queue is: register the catalog before the item is presented, and give the item the feature's owner.
An item whose catalog is gone when its turn comes is turned away by the navigator as `UnknownKey`.

---

## Traps

- **Reading the answer without `HasValue`.** `EnqueueAsync` completes for an item that never
  showed, and `Value` is then the default. Read the answer only when `HasValue` is true.
- **Treating `Enqueued` as shown.** `Enqueued` means the queue accepted the item. Wait for
  `Shown`, or await `EnqueueAsync`.
- **Expecting an `Enqueued` event for every `NotShown`.** An item turned away in the call has none.
- **A hold with no way out.** A flow that takes a hold and throws before it removes it holds the queue
  until its owner ends. Use a `finally` and an owner.
- **Gates that depend on state that may be gone.** A gate that throws is a deny and logs
  [UIDIRECTOR119](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector119).
- **A queue on a layer that never clears.** A queue on `screens` waits while a screen is open. Use
  the popups layer or a layer of your own.
- **A key whose row is on another layer.** The navigator turns the item away as `WrongLayer` and
  logs [UIDIRECTOR126](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector126). A row's `Layer Id` starts as `screens`
  (or is copied from the row above it), so a reward or news row for a `popups` queue must be checked first. Enqueue each key
  on the queue of its row's layer.
- **Denying in a gate to postpone.** A deny ends the item for good. Hold the queue for as long as
  the condition lasts instead ([Holds](#holds)).
- **Expecting a queued popup to survive a screen change.** A screen that opens ends a queued
  popup the navigator has taken, and the queue does not show it again
  ([A screen closes a presented popup](#a-screen-closes-a-presented-popup)).
- **A layer the root does not have.** `new ViewQueue(...)` throws `ArgumentException`. Pass one of
  `ViewLayers` or a layer you gave the root in `ViewRootSetup.ExtraLayers`.
- **Opening on the queue's layer by hand.** A popup opened directly keeps the queue waiting
  until it closes. That is the intended way to keep an item behind a flow, but it surprises code
  that expects the queue to be independent.
- **Waiting for the queue from a thread other than the main thread.** Queueing throws there;
  see [Threading](Threading.md).

---

- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md): `ShowAsync`, `OpenOptions` and the reject reasons the queue reuses
- [Events and analytics](Events-and-Analytics.md): the observer interface and every event field

- [Threading](Threading.md): which queue calls throw or are posted off the main thread
