<!-- file: Documentation~/Events-and-Analytics.md -->

# Events and analytics

[Back to index](index.md)

The navigator reports what happens to every request as events: accepted, shown, closed, not shown,
and the moment it settles. One observer interface receives all of them. Use it to log, to feed a
debug overlay, or to send screen views and funnels to an analytics service of your own. Events are
facts in the past tense; no command travels as an event, and they carry no view arguments, so
nothing is boxed and no argument data leaks into your analytics.

This page covers adding an observer, every event kind and when it is published, events caused inside
an observer, the fields of an event, the order at close, observing a queue as well, a generic analytics adapter, and what
dispatch costs.

---

## Watch every event

Add an observer with an owner token. The Basic Usage sample adds a log with the root's token as
owner, so it ends with the root:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// The observer ends with the root: RootToken is cancelled when the root is destroyed.
_navigator.AddObserver(new ViewEventLog(), _navigator.RootToken);
```

The observer prints one line per event:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ViewEventLog.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class ViewEventLog : IViewObserver
{
    public void OnViewEvent(in ViewEvent viewEvent)
    {
        // Settled has no request and no view.
        if (viewEvent.Kind == ViewEventKind.Settled)
        {
            Debug.Log("[views] Settled");
            return;
        }

        var line = $"[views] {viewEvent.Kind} #{viewEvent.RequestId} view={viewEvent.ViewId} layer={viewEvent.LayerId} source={viewEvent.Source}";

        switch (viewEvent.Kind)
        {
            case ViewEventKind.Shown:
                line += $" waited={viewEvent.SecondsWaiting:0.00}s";
                break;
            case ViewEventKind.Closed:
                line += $" reason={viewEvent.Reason} open={viewEvent.SecondsOpen:0.00}s";
                break;
            case ViewEventKind.NotShown:
                line += $" rejected={viewEvent.Rejected} detail={viewEvent.Detail}";
                break;
        }

        Debug.Log(line);
    }
}
```

Add the observer before the first `Open`. Events are published inside the navigator's own calls and
nothing is replayed, so an observer added later misses what already happened. Two safe places: right after
`Initialize`, as the sample does (it adds the observer in `Awake` and opens the first view in `Start`),
or, when the root initializes itself on `Awake`, from a component's `Start`, provided no other script
opens a view from its own `Awake` or `Start`. Unity orders neither `Awake` nor `Start` across objects, so
an open made in another script's `Awake` or `Start` can come before your observer. Make the first open
after the observer is added, from the same bootstrap or later.

Play the sample and the Console reads `[views] <Kind> #<request> view=<id> layer=<layer> source=<tag>`.
`Shown` adds `waited=`, `Closed` adds `reason=` and `open=`, `NotShown` adds `rejected=` and
`detail=`, and `Settled` has no request and no view. The `source` tags (`home.library`,
`settings.reset`, `back.root` and so on) say which line of code asked.

---

## The observer interface

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public interface IViewObserver
{
    void OnViewEvent(in ViewEvent viewEvent);
}
```

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
ViewRegistration AddObserver(
    IViewObserver observer,
    CancellationToken owner,
    [CallerMemberName] string member = null,
    [CallerLineNumber] int line = 0);
```

- **Owner.** The observer receives events until the owner token ends or the returned
  `ViewRegistration` is removed with `Remove()`, whichever comes first. Ending it again does nothing.
  Your code needs no removal line. An owner that is already cancelled adds nothing and returns an
  inactive registration.
- **Thread.** `AddObserver` throws `InvalidOperationException` off the main thread, and a null
  observer throws `ArgumentNullException`. Events are delivered on the main thread, from inside the
  navigator's own call. See [Threading](Threading.md).
- **Order.** Observers are called in the order they were added.
- **Isolation.** An observer that throws is routed to the root's error handler as
  `ViewErrorSource.Observer`, with the view id and request id of the event, and the observers after it
  still run. A throwing observer never changes what happens to the view.
- **Adding and removing during a dispatch.** An observer added while an event is being delivered
  receives events from the next one. A removal takes effect at once, so a removed observer is not
  called for the event in progress.
- **Navigator calls from an observer are legal.** An observer may call `Open`, `Close` or `Back`. They are
  accepted or refused as at any other call site; the outcome follows the usual rules. The events such a
  call causes are held back; see [Events caused inside an observer](#events-caused-inside-an-observer).
- **The event is passed by `in`.** It is a readonly struct on the dispatcher's stack. Copy the
  fields you need; do not keep a reference to it.

---

## Every event kind

| `ViewEventKind` | Published by | When |
|---|---|---|
| `Enqueued` | A queue | The queue accepted the item. The queue's observers only. |
| `Requested` | The navigator | The request was accepted. It is already in its layer, and the input shield is already up when the layer shields input. |
| `Shown` | The navigator | The show transition ended and the view is open. |
| `Closed` | The navigator | The view ended after being shown. Its instance was released, or parked for reuse when the row says `KeepInstance`. |
| `NotShown` | The navigator, or a queue for an item that never reached it | The request ended without being shown, or was refused at the call. |
| `Settled` | The navigator | The navigator went from busy to settled. The request id is 0. |

The sequence for one request id is one of these:

- `NotShown`: refused at the call (unknown key, duplicate, owner already ended, the waiting cap, or
  `WrongLayer` for a queued key whose row is on another layer).
- `Requested`, `NotShown`: accepted, then ended before it was shown (the load failed, the view
  declined, the owner ended, it was withdrawn).
- `Requested`, `Shown`, `Closed`: shown, then closed.

A request that came from a queue has `Enqueued` in front, published by the queue. An item that never
reaches the navigator ends with the queue's own `NotShown` and has no `Requested`. See
[Observing the queue too](#observing-the-queue-too).

`Settled` is published once for each change from busy to settled, after the events of the work that
ended it. The navigator is busy while an operation runs or pends on any layer or an input hold
exists. It is not published while the root is being torn down; at teardown every request that is
still alive receives its terminal event, and `Settled` does not follow. When the root is destroyed while the navigator is delivering a
notification, observers do not receive those terminal events either; see
[Events caused inside an observer](#events-caused-inside-an-observer).

An event describes state that is already in place when it arrives. At `Requested` the request is
in its layer and, on a layer that shields input, the shield is up. At `Shown` the view is open and the open's shield hold is
released. At `Closed` the request has left its layer, the shield holds are released and the
instance has been released, or parked when the row says `KeepInstance`. The one exception is an event
that was held back because it was caused inside an observer callback, described next.

An observer that frees per-instance resources must not do it on `Closed` for a `KeepInstance` row:
the parked instance is the object the next open reuses.

---

## Events caused inside an observer

An observer may call the navigator from `OnViewEvent`, and that call may cause events of its own: the
`Requested` or `NotShown` of a new request, a `Shown`, the `Closed` of a view it closed. While an
observer dispatch is running on the navigator, those events are held back. They are delivered, in the
order they were caused, after the event in progress has reached every observer. So each event reaches
every observer before any event that one of them caused. Outside an observer callback
nothing is held back and the timing is unchanged.

What this means for code:

- The call itself is not held back. The navigator accepts or refuses it and changes its state as it
  does anywhere else; only the notifications for it (the scopes ending, `Closed` or `NotShown`, the
  `ShowAsync` awaiters, `Settled`) wait until the dispatch is over.
- A held-back `Requested` or `Shown` can describe a state that has since moved on. If an observer
  opens view B from a callback and then closes it in the same callback, the observers see `Requested`
  for B after B has already been withdrawn; the `NotShown` for B follows it.
- Order is kept for every request: an observer never sees `Closed` before `Shown`, or a terminal event
  before `Requested`.
- An observer added with `ViewQueue.AddObserver` receives the queue's own events directly; its callbacks do not hold
  anything back by themselves.
- If the root is destroyed while the navigator is delivering a notification (inside an observer
  callback, a `ShowAsync` continuation or a view hook, for example with `DestroyImmediate`), the
  observers are removed before the pending terminal events are delivered, so no observer and no entry
  of the event list in the window sees them. The awaiters of those requests still complete, with the result that says the root was
  destroyed.

---

## The fields of an event

| Field | Type | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `Kind` | `ViewEventKind` | The kind of fact. |
| `RequestId` | `int` | The id of the request, the same on every event of one request. A queue reserves it at enqueue, so one id follows an item from `Enqueued` to `Closed`. 0 for `Settled`. |
| `ViewId` | `string` | The view id. `null` for `Settled`. |
| `LayerId` | `string` | The id of the layer the view is on. `null` for `Settled`, and `null` for a request refused before its row was looked up (the root is gone, the owner already ended, an unknown id or layer). A queued key refused as `WrongLayer` carries the queue's layer id. |
| `Source` | `string` | The free tag from `OpenOptions.Source` or `QueueOptions.Source`. `null` when none was given: a `ViewButton` with the Open View action passes no options, so its `Requested`, `Shown` and `Closed` carry `null`. |
| `Priority` | `int` | The queue priority of the item. 0 for a request that did not come from a queue. A queued item carries its priority on its navigator events as well. |
| `Reason` | `CloseReason` | How the view closed. Set on `Closed`, and `CloseReason.NotShown` on `NotShown`. |
| `Rejected` | `RejectReason` | Why the request was not shown. Set on `NotShown`; `None` on every other kind. |
| `Detail` | `string` | Optional text with more detail about the outcome, such as a gate's reason or a decline reason. |
| `SecondsWaiting` | `float` | Seconds from acceptance to `Shown`. Set on `Shown`; 0 on every other kind. |
| `SecondsOpen` | `float` | Seconds from `Shown` to `Closed`. Set on `Closed`; 0 on every other kind. |

How the values are measured:

- **`SecondsWaiting` includes the show transition**, because `Shown` is published when the transition
  ends. It starts when the navigator accepts the request. For a queued item that is when the queue
  presents it, so the time spent waiting in the queue is not in it. To measure that, note the clock
  when you see `Enqueued` for the request id and subtract when `Requested` arrives.
- **`SecondsOpen` starts at `Shown`**, not when the show transition starts.
- **Both run on the navigator clock**, which the root advances once per frame in unscaled time and by
  at most 0.1 s per frame. A long hitch or a suspension therefore adds one short step, not the time
  that really passed; the figures can be shorter than wall-clock time. See [Limitations](Limitations.md).

Traps in the fields:

- `Reason` has a value on every event, because an enum has a default. On `Enqueued`, `Requested`
  and `Shown` it reads `CloseReason.NotShown`, which is the enum's zero. Read `Reason` only on
  `Closed` and `NotShown`.
- A request that ended during its show transition counts as shown. It publishes `Closed` with the
  reason it ended with, not `NotShown`.

The `CloseReason` and `RejectReason` values are listed in
[Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md#close-reasons).

---

## The order at close

An observer never sees `Closed` without `Shown`. A request that ends after its show transition began
but before `Shown` went out publishes `Shown` immediately before `Closed`, in the same sequence.

For one view that ends, the package first applies the state with no user code: the request leaves its
layer, its hidden state is applied, its shield holds are released and the layers below are
recomputed. Then it runs the notifications one at a time, each isolated, in this order:

1. The visible scope ends.
2. The open scope ends.
3. The instance is released: handed to the provider, destroyed, or parked for `KeepInstance`.
4. Views that were revealed begin their visible scopes (`OnVisible`).
5. `Shown`, if it is owed.
6. `Closed` or `NotShown` is published.
7. The `ShowAsync` awaiters resume, in the order they joined, then the `WaitForCloseAsync` awaiters.
8. `Settled`, if the navigator is now settled.

A notification caused by another notification runs right after it. What this means for code:

- When an observer sees `Closed`, the view's scopes have already ended and its instance is released,
  or parked when the row says `KeepInstance`.
- The code that awaited `ShowAsync` resumes after `Closed` was published, so an observer sees the
  event first.
- A queue pumps on the next tick, so the continuation of an awaited popup runs before the queue
  presents the next item. A follow-up popup that the continuation opens makes the layer busy and the
  queued item waits for it. See [Queue](Queue.md).

---

## Observing the queue too

A queued request has two publishers. The queue publishes `Enqueued`, and its own `NotShown` for an
item that ends in the queue. The navigator publishes everything after the queue hands the item over.
A queue sends its events only to the observers added with `ViewQueue.AddObserver`, and a navigator
observer never sees `Enqueued` or a queue's own `NotShown`. To see the whole story of an item,
register an observer on both. The Queue Usage sample uses one class and a tag:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/QueueEventLog.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class QueueEventLog : IViewObserver
{
    private readonly string _tag;

    // A queue observer sees only Enqueued and the queue's own NotShown; everything after presentation is a navigator event.
    public QueueEventLog(string tag)
    {
        _tag = tag;
    }

    public void OnViewEvent(in ViewEvent viewEvent)
    {
        var line = $"{_tag} {viewEvent.Kind} #{viewEvent.RequestId} {viewEvent.ViewId} priority={viewEvent.Priority} source={viewEvent.Source}";

        if (viewEvent.Kind == ViewEventKind.NotShown)
            line += $" rejected={viewEvent.Rejected} detail={viewEvent.Detail}";
        else if (viewEvent.Kind == ViewEventKind.Closed)
            line += $" reason={viewEvent.Reason}";

        Debug.Log(line);
    }
}
```

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/QueueBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// Events of a queued request come from two publishers, so a log watches each.
_navigator.AddObserver(new QueueEventLog("[views]"), _navigator.RootToken);
notices.Queue.AddObserver(new QueueEventLog("[queue]"), _navigator.RootToken);
```

What each publisher sends for a queued item:

| Moment | Publisher | Event |
|---|---|---|
| The queue accepts the item | queue | `Enqueued` |
| A gate denies it at enqueue, the owner already ended, or the queue ended (lifetime `Cancelled`, root `RootGone`) | queue | `NotShown` only; no `Enqueued`. After the queue ended no observer is left, so only the `EnqueueAsync` result and the window's list see it |
| It ends while it waits (owner, gate at presentation, `Clear()`, lifetime, root destroyed; an observer or item owned by `RootToken` may end first) | queue | `NotShown` |
| The navigator accepts it | navigator | `Requested` |
| It is shown and then closed | navigator | `Shown`, `Closed` |
| The navigator refuses it at the call (including `WrongLayer`), or it ends before being shown | navigator | `NotShown` (the queue publishes nothing more) |
| The call that presents it throws, or the task it returned faults and the navigator published no end | queue | `NotShown` with `Rejected = Faulted`, published on the main thread |

A `NotShown` exists once per request when the package's navigator presents the item; for a task that
faults after the navigator already ended the request, the queue publishes nothing more. In
the sample, a request that a gate denies is the only kind that shows `NotShown` without a preceding
`Enqueued`; it appears only when code queues a notice while the tutorial runs, because the tutorial
tip covers the lobby buttons. The fields are the same; `SecondsWaiting` and `SecondsOpen` are 0 on the queue's events.

In the editor and in development builds the navigator keeps the last 100 events in a ring, queue
events included, and `Window > UIDirector` lists them. Release builds have no ring.

---

## Send the events to an analytics service

The package ships no analytics adapter and names no service. An adapter is a class that implements
`IViewObserver` and turns an event into a call to whatever your project uses. `ViewEventLog` above is
the pattern: a `switch` on `Kind`, with the fields that matter for each kind.

A reasonable mapping:

| Event | What to record | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `Shown` | A screen or popup was viewed | `ViewId`, `LayerId`, `Source`, `SecondsWaiting` |
| `Closed` | How long it was open and how it ended | `ViewId`, `Reason`, `SecondsOpen` |
| `NotShown` | A view that should have appeared did not | `ViewId`, `Rejected`, `Source` |
| `Enqueued` | An item entered a queue | `ViewId`, `Priority`, `Source` |
| `Requested` | The start of a funnel step | `RequestId`, `ViewId` |

`Settled` carries nothing worth sending.

`Shown` fires once per request. A screen revealed again by Back, `CloseTo` or by opening an id that is
already in the stack publishes no event. To count those views, record them from the covering view's
`Closed` or from `OnVisible` in the view.

Rules for an adapter:

- **Copy, do not keep.** The event arrives by `in`. Read the fields inside `OnViewEvent` and hand
  strings and numbers on. Do not store the struct or a reference to it.
- **Pair by `RequestId`.** The same id appears on `Requested`, `Shown` and `Closed` (and on
  `Enqueued` for a queued item), so a funnel or a duration is a lookup on the id. `Closed`
  already carries `SecondsOpen`, so a session timer is not needed for it.
- **Send enums as names, keep `Detail` out.** `Rejected` and `Reason` are stable enum values with a
  small set of names, which suits an analytics dimension. `Detail` is free text: gate reasons and
  decline reasons are written by your code, and a load failure carries an exception message. Keep it
  for logs.
- **Expect a `null` `Source`.** The package adds no tag of its own. A `ViewButton` opens with no tag,
  and `Back()` adds no tag of its own: it closes the top view, which publishes `Closed` with `Reason`
  `Back`, or it withdraws a request still waiting or loading, which publishes `NotShown` with `Rejected`
  `Cancelled`. Either event carries the `Source` of the call that opened that view. A view whose row says
  `HandledByView` decides in its own back hook, and any view that hook opens carries the tag the hook
  passes. A screen that Back reveals publishes no event. Map `null` to
  a fixed value such as `"untagged"` in the adapter.
- **Keep `Source` constant.** It is a free tag; use one constant string per call site so the number
  of distinct values stays small.
- **Do not wait.** Events are delivered on the main thread inside the navigator's call. Queue the
  record for your service and return. A slow observer delays the view that caused the event; an
  exception is isolated, but the delay is not.
- **Arguments are not in the event.** By design. If an analytics record needs a value, such as which
  item a detail screen showed, the code that opens the view knows it and can record it.

The adapter needs no removal line: give it `INavigator.RootToken`, or the token of the feature that
owns the analytics, as the owner.

---

## What dispatch costs

- **Dispatch allocates nothing once warm.** The event is a struct built on the stack and handed on by
  `in`; delivering it to any number of observers allocates nothing.
- **Your observer's work is the cost.** `ViewEventLog` builds a string for every event with string
  interpolation and writes it to the Console, so it allocates; it is a debug aid, not a production
  pattern. An adapter that copies a few fields into a preallocated buffer costs almost nothing.
- **Events are built whether or not anyone listens.** With no observer the dispatch is an empty loop.
- **The ring is development only.** The editor and development builds keep the last 100 events for the
  window; release builds have no ring and no recording cost.
- `INavigator.Describe(StringBuilder)` writes the current layers, requests and holds as text on any
  build, which helps when you need a snapshot instead of a stream.

Opening and closing a view is not a zero-allocation path; see [Performance](Performance.md).

---

## Traps

- **Expecting `Enqueued` to mean shown.** It means the queue accepted the item.
- **Reading `Reason` on `Shown`.** It reads `NotShown`, the default; the field is meaningful on
  `Closed` and `NotShown` only.
- **Observing only the navigator for a queued flow.** `Enqueued` and the queue's own `NotShown` never
  reach it.
- **Doing slow work in `OnViewEvent`.** It runs in the navigator's own call, on the main thread.
- **Expecting the answer to a navigator call at once, inside `OnViewEvent`.** The events and awaiters of
  a call made from a callback arrive after the dispatch; read the state through `INavigator` if you need it now.
- **Freeing per-instance data on `Closed` of a `KeepInstance` view.** The next open can reuse the
  same object.
- **Keeping the event after the call.** Copy fields; the event is not yours to keep.
- **Counting `Settled` as a request.** It has request id 0 and no view.

---

## See also

- [Queue](Queue.md): the queue's own observer and the order of events for an item
- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md): `OpenOptions.Source`, `CloseReason` and `RejectReason`
- [Threading](Threading.md): the main-thread rules for observers and their owners
- [Diagnostics](Diagnostics.md): the log messages the package writes beside the events
- [Performance](Performance.md): allocation and idle cost
- [Architecture](Design/Architecture.md#10-events-and-the-order-at-close): the stream and the order at close
- [API reference](API-Reference.md): `IViewObserver`, `ViewEvent`, `ViewEventKind`

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Input-and-Platform.md -->

# Input and platform

[Back to index](index.md)

This page covers what the UI needs from the platform and how the package treats input: the
EventSystem and the input module, what the input shield blocks and when it is up, double taps and
several fingers, blocking input from code with `HoldInput`, time scale 0, the Android back button,
scenes, and the Enter Play Mode options.

---

## Give the UI an EventSystem

uGUI delivers no click or touch without an `EventSystem` and an input module in the scene. The package
does not create one. When a root initializes and the scene has no `EventSystem`, it logs
[UIDIRECTOR116](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector116) once. Views are still shown, and they get no input.

Three ways to have one:

- **The create-root menu.** `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root` adds an `EventSystem` when the scene has
  none ([Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md#create-a-root)).
- **`GameObject > UI > Event System`,** if you built the root by hand.
- **Code,** when the scene is assembled at start-up. Create it before the root initializes, so the check
  finds it. The Basic Usage bootstrap does this in the first line of its `Awake`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// Before the root initialises, so the root finds an EventSystem.
SampleEventSystem.EnsureExists();
```

### Input System or the legacy input module

The input module has to match the project's Active Input Handling (`Project Settings > Player`). A
scene that bakes in one module breaks in a project with the other setting: the module is a missing
script, or it throws when it reads input. That is why the samples ship scenes without an EventSystem
and create it at start:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/Support/SampleEventSystem.cs -->
```csharp
        public static void EnsureExists()
        {
            if (Object.FindAnyObjectByType<EventSystem>() != null)
                return;

            var eventSystem = new GameObject("EventSystem", typeof(EventSystem));
#if UIDIRECTOR_SAMPLES_INPUT_SYSTEM && ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM
            eventSystem.AddComponent<InputSystemUIInputModule>();
#else
            eventSystem.AddComponent<StandaloneInputModule>();
#endif
        }
```

| Active Input Handling | Defines Unity sets | Module created |
|---|---|---|
| Input System Package (New) | `ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM` | `InputSystemUIInputModule` |
| Both | `ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM` and `ENABLE_LEGACY_INPUT_MANAGER` | `InputSystemUIInputModule` |
| Input Manager (Old), or no Input System package | `ENABLE_LEGACY_INPUT_MANAGER` | `StandaloneInputModule` |

`UIDIRECTOR_SAMPLES_INPUT_SYSTEM` is a define that the sample's assembly definition sets through
`versionDefines` when `com.unity.inputsystem` is installed. Your own assembly definition needs both: a
reference to `Unity.InputSystem` to use its types, and the same `versionDefines` entry so the guarded
code still compiles in a project without the package. The create-root menu makes the
same choice with the package's own define.

`FindAnyObjectByType<EventSystem>()` finds active objects only. An EventSystem that is deactivated does
not count as present.

---

## What the input shield blocks

The input shield is a counted, full-screen blocker above every layer. It is one graphic with an empty
mesh on its own canvas, always active, and only its `Raycast Target` switches. Because it never
activates or deactivates, it blocks in the same frame in which it is raised, inside the `Open` call.

What it blocks:

- **Pointer input to everything the package shows.** Mouse clicks and touches raycast to the shield
  first, so no button under it receives them. This is uGUI's own raycasting; it needs no code in your
  view.
- **The backdrop.** A tap on a backdrop while the shield is up does nothing, so a tap cannot close a
  popup in the middle of a transition ([Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md)).
- **Submit and Cancel on the selected control.** When the shield goes up, the package clears the
  EventSystem's selection unless it is selecting right now, because those keys go to the selection and
  would pass the shield.
- **The back key.** `Back()` is swallowed while the shield is up
  ([Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#resolution-order)).

What it does not block:

- **Code.** Calling `Open`, `ShowAsync` or `ViewHandle.Close()` still works; the shield is not a lock
  on the navigator. `Back()` is the exception, see above.
- **A canvas that sorts itself above the shield,** such as the open list of a TextMesh Pro dropdown, or
  interface the package does not own with a higher sorting order
  ([Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md#the-sorting-band)).
- **A press that began before the shield was raised and ends after it was lowered,** which is delivered
  if the same control is still under the pointer.

### When it is up

The shield holds a list of reasons, and it is up while the list is not empty. Each reason ends on every
path, including a failed request and a destroyed root.

| Reason | Taken | Released |
|---|---|---|
| An open, a load or another operation on a layer with `ShieldsInput` | In the `Open` or `ShowAsync` call that is accepted | When the open has finished, unless a close is pending |
| A close | When the close is decided | When the view is gone |
| A pop-to or close-all | When it is accepted | When it ends |
| `HoldInput` | In the call | When its owner ends, or on `Remove()` |

The three default layers have `ShieldsInput`. A layer without it, such as the sample's `toasts` layer,
never takes the shield. `INavigator.IsBusy` is true while an operation runs or waits, or an input hold
exists.

Operations are bounded: a load by the load timeout (15 s by default) and a transition by the transition
timeout (3 s by default), so a view that never finishes does not keep the UI blocked for good. A hold
from `HoldInput` has no such bound; it is reported after 30 seconds ([below](#block-input-yourself-with-holdinput)).

The Basic Usage sample shows the shield in a number of places. Open `Window > UIDirector` in Play Mode
and look at `Shield holders` during a transition: each holder is listed with its kind, its request, its
age and the call site.

---

## Double taps and several fingers

**A double tap on a button that opens a view opens it once.** The first tap calls `Open` or `ShowAsync`,
which raises the shield in the same call. The second tap raycasts to the shield and not to the button.
One popup opens and nothing is logged. `SettingsView` in the Basic Usage sample is the example; the
walk-through with the code is on [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md#the-input-shield).

Two more guards stand behind the shield:

- An id that is already open or in flight on a layer that is not a history layer is refused as
  `RejectReason.Duplicate`, unless the row sets `Allow Multiple`. On a history layer the second open
  returns to the screen that exists.
- A handler that can fire many times can ask not to wait: `OpenOptions.RejectWhenBusy` refuses the call
  while `IsBusy` is true ([Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md#rejectwhenbusy)).

**A layer without `ShieldsInput` has no shield guard.** Taps on a button that opens a toast reach the
button every time, and only the duplicate rule limits them.

**Several fingers.** The shield is a raycast target, so it blocks a second finger exactly as it blocks
the first: each pointer is raycast on its own and lands on the shield once it is up. The case that
matters is two fingers released in the same frame, where the first one's click raises the shield. The
second pointer is then blocked and its control gets no click.

The package does not serialize presses. Two fingers that press two different buttons of one view while
nothing raises the shield between them are two ordinary clicks.

---

## Block input yourself with HoldInput

`INavigator.HoldInput` raises the shield without a view, for as long as you need it:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
ViewRegistration HoldInput(
    string reason,
    CancellationToken owner,
    [CallerMemberName] string member = null,
    [CallerLineNumber] int line = 0);
```

Use it when work must not be interrupted by a tap and no overlay is wanted, for example while code
finishes a short animation of your own. `reason` is a short text for the Console and the editor window.
`member` and `line` are filled in by the compiler; do not pass them.

- **The owner ends the hold.** The shield goes down when `owner` is cancelled or when you call `Remove()`
  on the returned `ViewRegistration`. `Remove()` is safe to call twice. Pass a token that ends with the
  work, so the hold needs no line on the way out.
- **It counts.** The shield stays up until every reason, from views and from holds, has ended.
- **It makes `Back()` return `true` without closing a shown view,** and `IsBusy` true. A request still
  waiting or loading on a layer that takes back is withdrawn first
  ([Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#resolution-order)).
- **A hold older than 30 seconds is reported once** with its reason and call site
  ([UIDIRECTOR110](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector110)). The hold keeps blocking until it ends.
- **A token that is already cancelled, or a destroyed root, returns an inactive registration** and
  raises nothing. A null reason throws `ArgumentNullException`. Off the main thread it throws
  `InvalidOperationException` ([Threading](Threading.md)).

For an overlay that tells the player something is happening, open a view on the `system` layer
instead ([System overlays](System-Overlays.md)).

---

## Time scale 0

The UI keeps working while `Time.timeScale` is 0, for example under a pause menu. Everything the
package times runs on unscaled time:

- The root advances its clock in `Update` with `Time.unscaledDeltaTime`, at most 0.1 s per frame. The
  load timeout, the transition timeout, the load indicator delay and the 30-second hold warning count
  on that clock.
- The built-in transitions (fade, scale and slide) and the backdrop fade run on unscaled time, advancing
  by at most a thirtieth of a second per frame, so below 30 frames per second they run longer than
  their duration.
- The queue's delays are unscaled.

Your own code has to follow. A transition of your own must animate on unscaled time, or it never
finishes at time scale 0 and the transition timeout snaps it
([UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106)); see [Transitions](Transitions.md). The same holds
for a DOTween transition ([DOTween](DOTween.md)). A delay inside a view uses the unscaled delay type, as
the sample's toast does:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ToastView.cs -->
```csharp
// Unscaled time, so a paused game (timeScale 0) still dismisses the toast.
await UniTask.Delay(ShowTime, DelayType.UnscaledDeltaTime, cancellationToken: ct);
```

A default `UniTask.Delay` runs on scaled time and never returns while the game is paused. Animators,
particle systems and tweens inside a view follow Unity's rules: they stand still at time scale 0 unless
they are set to unscaled time.

---

## The back button

`BackInput` polls the Escape key once per frame and calls `Back()` on its root's navigator. Where
Unity reports Android's back button as the Escape key, one component serves both (see
[On a device](#on-a-device)). The
create-root menu adds it to the root. What it does with the answer is on [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#backinput):
when `Back()` returns `false`, it raises `Unhandled` and the game decides.

It reads the key from the Input System when that package is installed and active, and from the legacy
input manager otherwise. When neither is enabled it does nothing.

- **With the Input System,** `BackInput` owns an `InputAction` bound to `<Keyboard>/escape` and checks
  it with `WasPressedThisFrame` in `Update`. The action is created when the component is enabled and
  disposed when it is destroyed. It binds every keyboard, including one that appears later, and a press
  whose down and up arrive in the same input update still counts once. A key already held when the
  component is enabled does not fire. When the Input System has no keyboard device, it does nothing.
- **With the legacy input manager,** it checks `Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Escape)` in `Update`.
- **Before the root is initialised,** a press does nothing: reading the navigator then would initialise
  the root with default settings. A `ViewButton` set to `Back` or `OpenView` under a root that is not
  initialised does nothing either, and logs a warning.

The Basic Usage bootstrap listens to `Unhandled` to ask whether to quit:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// No removal needed: the bootstrap and the root live and die together.
_backInput.Unhandled.AddListener(OnBackUnhandled);
```

A project that needs a different key, or that must ask another UI first, replaces `BackInput`. The sample
ships `HardwareBackRouter` for that. It reads the key the same way as `BackInput`: with the Input System
through an `InputAction` it owns, otherwise through the legacy input manager.

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/HardwareBackRouter.cs -->
```csharp
#if UIDIRECTOR_SAMPLES_INPUT_SYSTEM && ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM
        private void OnEnable()
        {
            // An owned action binds every keyboard and keeps a press whose down and up land in one input update.
            if (_backAction == null)
                _backAction = new InputAction("Sample Back", InputActionType.Button, "<Keyboard>/escape");

            _backAction.Enable();
        }

        private void OnDisable()
        {
            if (_backAction != null)
                _backAction.Disable();
        }

        private void OnDestroy()
        {
            if (_backAction != null)
            {
                _backAction.Dispose();
                _backAction = null;
            }
        }
#endif

        private void Update()
        {
#if UIDIRECTOR_SAMPLES_INPUT_SYSTEM && ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM
            if (_backAction != null && _backAction.WasPressedThisFrame())
                HandleBack();
#elif ENABLE_LEGACY_INPUT_MANAGER
            if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Escape))
                HandleBack();
#endif
        }
```

Put it on the root instead of `BackInput`, never both: with both, one press is handled twice. The
router's `HandleBack`, and why the older UI is asked first, are on
[Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#a-project-that-still-has-an-older-ui).

### On a device

The package polls Escape and nothing else. It does not manage `Input.backButtonLeavesApp`, it offers no
predictive back animation, and it has no code for Android's predictive back gesture or its setting.

Whether the back button arrives as the Escape key depends on the device and on Unity's input
handling; the package only sees the key. In the editor, back is the Escape key, and the Game view needs
focus to receive it.

---

## Scenes and Persist Across Scenes

The package never loads a scene and closes nothing when a scene changes. What happens to the UI follows
from the root:

- **A root without `Persist Across Scenes` is destroyed with its scene.** Every view under it ends
  silently and `RootToken` is cancelled.
- **A root with it survives the load.** Its outermost object is kept, and with the camera variant the
  UI camera is kept too. Views stay open until their owners end them.
- **The EventSystem is not kept for you.** A persisted root needs exactly one EventSystem at all times:
  put it under the persisted object, or create it from the start-up code. See
  [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md#persist-across-scenes).
- **Own a view with `RootToken`** when it must outlive the scene that opened it, and with a token of the
  scene when it must not ([Concepts](Concepts.md)).

---

## Enter Play Mode options

Unity can enter Play Mode without a domain reload, which keeps static fields between runs. The runtime
code of the package keeps no mutable static state that a new session could trip over: the three default
layers and every key are immutable values, the one static collection is a cache of text suffixes for
log messages, and the one static flag, which records that the application is quitting, is reset by a
hook that runs when Play Mode starts. Entering Play Mode with domain reload disabled needs no reset
call from you.

Check your own code instead. A `static` field that holds a
service, an event handler or a cancellation source survives into the next Play Mode session.

---

## Traps

- **No EventSystem, or the wrong module for the input handling.** Views draw and do not react
  ([UIDIRECTOR116](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector116)).
- **A scene that bakes in an input module.** It breaks in a project with the other input handling. Create
  the EventSystem in code, as the samples do.
- **Both `BackInput` and your own router on the root.** One press is handled twice.
- **A hold that nothing ends.** The UI stays blocked and, after 30 seconds, logs
  [UIDIRECTOR110](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector110).
- **Scaled time inside a view or a transition at time scale 0.** The code never continues; a transition
  is snapped after the timeout.
- **A persisted root with no EventSystem in the next scene.** Views react to nothing.

## See also

- [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md)

<!-- file: Documentation~/Migration.md -->

# Migration

[Back to index](index.md)

This page is for a project that already has a UI manager of its own and wants to move to UIDirector
without a rewrite weekend. It shows what each old habit becomes, then moves one view at a time while
the old manager keeps running next to the new root. At the end of every step the project still
builds and plays.

The "before" code on this page is generic and short; it stands for whatever your manager looks like.
Every "after" block is copied verbatim from the Basic Usage and Zenject Usage samples, so it compiles
as shown.

---

## The old UI in one picture

A hand-written manager usually has the same five parts. This one is typical:

<!-- illustrative: before -->
```csharp
public class UIManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    public static UIManager Instance;

    [SerializeField] private GameObject[] _screens;
    private readonly List<GameObject> _stack = new List<GameObject>();

    private void Awake() => Instance = this;

    public void Push(int index)
    {
        if (_stack.Count > 0) _stack[^1].SetActive(false);
        _screens[index].SetActive(true);
        _stack.Add(_screens[index]);
    }

    public void Pop()
    {
        _stack[^1].SetActive(false);
        _stack.RemoveAt(_stack.Count - 1);
        _stack[^1].SetActive(true);
    }

    public void ShowPopup(string name, Action<bool> onAnswer)
    {
        var popup = Instantiate(Resources.Load<PopupView>("Popups/" + name), transform);
        popup.Init(onAnswer);
    }
}
```

and a screen that uses it:

<!-- illustrative: before -->
```csharp
public class SettingsScreen : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private Button _reset;

    private void OnEnable() => _reset.onClick.AddListener(OnReset);
    private void OnDisable() => _reset.onClick.RemoveListener(OnReset);

    private void OnReset() =>
        UIManager.Instance.ShowPopup("Confirm", yes => { if (yes) ResetSettings(); });
}
```

Screens are switched with `SetActive`, a list is the stack, a popup is found by name, the manager is
reached through a static field, and the answer comes back in a callback. The sections below replace
each of these.

---

## What replaces what

| Old habit | In UIDirector | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Screens switched with `SetActive` | Each screen is a prefab view on the `screens` layer. The package creates it, hides what it covers and releases it | [Concepts](Concepts.md) |
| A list used as the stack, a `Pop` method | The `screens` layer is the stack and the back history. Opening an id that is already in it returns to it | [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md) |
| One `Back` button handler per screen, or one `Update` that reads the key | One `Back()` rule on the navigator, and `BackInput` to call it | [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#back) |
| A popup instantiated from `Resources` by name | A catalog row with an id, and a typed key `ViewKey<TArgs, TResult>` in code | [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md) |
| An `Action<bool>` callback for the answer | `await ShowAsync(...)` returns a `ViewResult` with the value, or the reason there is none | [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md) |
| `Init(args)` on the popup | The key's argument type, read in `OnOpen` | [View authoring](View-Authoring.md) |
| `AddListener` in `OnEnable`, `RemoveListener` in `OnDisable` | `open.Bind(...)` on the scope; the package removes it | [View authoring](View-Authoring.md#tie-listeners-and-tasks-to-a-scope) |
| `UIManager.Instance` reached from everywhere | `INavigator` is an interface: views get it as `Navigator`, other classes receive it | [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md) |
| A `bool _busy` or a transparent panel that eats taps | The input shield, raised inside the `Open` call, and `RejectWhenBusy` | [Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md#the-input-shield) |
| A loading panel switched on and off by hand | A view on the `system` layer closed in a `finally`, or the root's `Load Indicator` | [System overlays](System-Overlays.md) |
| `canvas.sortingOrder = 100` on each popup | One sorting band per root, computed from the layer and the slot | [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md#the-sorting-band) |
| Fade coroutines on `Time.deltaTime` | A `ViewTransition` on unscaled time | [Transitions](Transitions.md) |
| A static event or a log line for analytics | An observer with an owner token | [Events and analytics](Events-and-Analytics.md) |
| A "show these in turn" list for notices | The priority queue | [Queue](Queue.md) |
| A popup that must not outlive its screen, closed by hand | The owner token of the open | [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md#owners-and-what-happens-when-one-ends) |

---

## Before you start

- The package needs UniTask and `com.unity.ugui`. Install steps are in the README.
- List what the old UI does: every screen, every popup with the data it takes and the answer it gives,
  the places that read the back key, and every canvas with its sorting order. The list is your
  migration order; the steps below move from the edges (a popup that only asks a question) toward
  the screens that other code calls.
- Calls into the package run on the main thread. Old code that opens UI from a worker thread or
  from a thread-pool continuation must hop to the main thread first; see [Threading](Threading.md).

---

## Step 1: put a root beside the old canvas

Choose `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root`. It adds a new outermost object with its own canvas, and it
adds an `EventSystem` only when the scene has none. A project that already has a working UI has one,
so nothing changes there: keep exactly one active `EventSystem`
([Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md#give-the-ui-an-eventsystem)).

The old canvas is not touched. Its manager keeps working, and nothing the package shows is a child
of it.

To pass code-only settings, turn `Initialize On Awake` off on the root and initialize it from code,
before anything reads `ViewRoot.Navigator`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
_viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup
{
    Inject = InjectServices,
    ErrorHandler = OnViewError,
    ExtraLayers = new[] { AppLayers.Toasts }
});
_navigator = _viewRoot.Navigator;
```

You can leave `Initialize On Awake` on and use the defaults until you need a setting. Every field of
the root is on [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md). If your old UI is drawn by its own camera, the
camera variant `UIDirector Root (Camera)` creates a camera of its own beside the root; see the
render-mode table on the same page before you choose.

The menu also adds a `BackInput` to the root, and it reads the back key every frame. It does nothing
until the root is initialized. As soon as the first package view is open (step 3), one press closes it
and is also handled by the old manager's own back code. If the old UI reads the back key, set up the router of
[step 7](#step-7-route-the-back-key-through-one-place) now, before step 3. It does not depend on
steps 3 to 6.

Press Play. Nothing visible changed, and the old UI still works.

---

## Step 2: give the two UIs separate sorting bands

Both UIs draw on the screen at once, so decide who is above whom now, before the first view moves.
The package puts every view on a nested canvas with a sorting order computed from the root's
`Base Sorting Order`:

```text
order = Base Sorting Order + layer order x 1000 + slot x 10
```

The first popup is at base + 1010, the input shield at base + 3000 with the three default layers.
An older canvas should sit outside that band:

| The old canvas | Give it | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Should stay under the package's views (a HUD, a background) | A sorting order below `Base Sorting Order` | Every package view covers it |
| Should cover everything (an old full-screen popup system you keep for now) | A sorting order above the shield | It draws above the views and above the shield, so it is not blocked by it |
| Somewhere in between | Do not | It interleaves with the package's screens and popups |

Orders compare only between overlay canvases, or between canvases drawn by the same camera on one
sorting layer. An overlay canvas always draws above camera canvases, and canvases on different cameras
follow camera depth first. Give the old canvas the same render mode as the root, and for a camera root
draw it with the root's UI Camera, before you set orders. A camera root takes the sorting layer of its
own canvas, so put the old canvas on that sorting layer when you compare their orders. How an overlay
root and a camera root differ is on [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md#overlay-roots-and-camera-roots).

If the old UI contains a popup system you will keep until the end, sorting it above the shield is the
simplest arrangement: a migrated screen never ends up over it. The trade-off is that the shield does
not block it, so a tap on an old button still works while a package transition runs. Decide per case
whether that matters.

---

## Step 3: turn one popup into a view

Start with a popup that asks a question and has no children of its own. Three things are needed.

**The prefab.** The root of the prefab gets a `ViewHost` (Unity adds the `Canvas` and
`GraphicRaycaster` it requires) and one component that implements the view contract. Remove any
`CanvasScaler` from the popup's root: the project's root canvas scales, and the view is a nested
canvas. The rest of the layout is yours. The rules are on
[View authoring](View-Authoring.md#prefab-structure).

**The view class.** `Init(args)` becomes `OnOpen(args, open)`, and the listeners move onto the scope,
so the `OnEnable` and `OnDisable` pair disappears:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ConfirmView.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class ConfirmView : ViewBehaviour<ConfirmArgs, bool>
{
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _title;
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _message;
    [SerializeField] private Button _accept;
    [SerializeField] private Button _decline;

    protected override void OnOpen(ConfirmArgs args, ViewScope open)
    {
        _title.text = args.Title;
        _message.text = args.Message;

        // The package removes both listeners when this open ends.
        open.Bind(_accept.onClick, Accept);
        open.Bind(_decline.onClick, Refuse);
    }

    private void Accept()
    {
        Complete(true);
    }

    private void Refuse()
    {
        Complete(false);
    }
}
```

The two type arguments, `ConfirmArgs` and `bool`, replace the `Init` parameter and the
`Action<bool>`. `Complete(value)` is the callback call.

**The row and the key.** Create a catalog with `Assets > Create > UIDirector/View Catalog`, add a row
with an `Id`, the prefab, and `Layer Id` set to `popups` (a new row defaults to `screens`), and
assign the catalog to the root's `Catalogs` list. In code, the id gets a typed name:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppViews.cs -->
```csharp
[ViewKeys]
public static class AppViews
{
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Home = ViewKey.Create("home");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Library = ViewKey.Create("library");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ItemArgs, NoResult> ItemDetail = ViewKey.Create<ItemArgs>("item-detail");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Settings = ViewKey.Create("settings");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ConfirmArgs, bool> Confirm = ViewKey.Create<ConfirmArgs, bool>("confirm");
    public static readonly ViewKey<RenameArgs, string> Rename = ViewKey.Create<RenameArgs, string>("rename");
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Saving = ViewKey.Create("saving");
    public static readonly ViewKey<ToastArgs, NoResult> Toast = ViewKey.Create<ToastArgs>("toast");
}
```

Run `Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs`. It reports a key with no row, a prefab with no matching
view component and a prefab without a `ViewHost` before you press Play
([Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md#validate)).

A popup the old code found by name with `Resources.Load` is now a direct prefab reference in a row.
A row with a `Prefab` keeps the prefab resident while its catalog is loaded, which `Resources.Load`
did not. For a large number of popups, use an `Asset Key` with a view provider so nothing is resident
until it opens ([Assets and Addressables](Assets-and-Addressables.md)), or split the rows into
catalogs that you add at run time ([Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md#add-and-remove-a-catalog-at-run-time)).

---

## Step 4: open it and read the answer

The call site changes from a callback to an `await`. The old line

<!-- illustrative: before -->
```csharp
UIManager.Instance.ShowPopup("Confirm", yes => { if (yes) ResetSettings(); });
```

becomes the call below. Its third argument is the owner, here the token of the screen that asks, so
the popup cannot outlive that screen. The old manager had no such rule and left the cleanup to each
callback:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
var answer = await Navigator.ShowAsync(
    AppViews.Confirm,
    new ConfirmArgs("Reset settings", "All settings return to their defaults."),
    ct,
    new OpenOptions { Source = "settings.reset", RejectWhenBusy = true });
```

Then read the outcome. A callback only ran when the popup answered. An `await` also resumes when the
popup closes some other way: Back, a backdrop tap, a closed screen, an owner that ended. That is
why the value has a flag:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/SettingsView.cs -->
```csharp
// Back, backdrop and a closed screen all end with no value, so this line also guards the screen.
if (!answer.HasValue || !answer.Value)
    return;
```

Where the old callback ran only on "yes", this line returns on every ending that is not an explicit
"yes". Code that must tell the causes apart reads `answer.Reason` and `answer.Rejected`. The full
list is on [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md#reading-a-result).

`RejectWhenBusy` is the replacement for a hand-made `_busy` flag: it refuses the call while the
navigator is busy. Leave it out where waiting is fine.

A double tap needs no code of yours. The first tap raises the input shield inside the call, so the
second tap lands on the shield and not on the button
([Popups and backdrop](Popups-and-Backdrop.md#the-input-shield)).

---

## Step 5: move the screens

A screen moves the same way: a prefab, a view class, a row on the `screens` layer, a key. What changes
is how it is reached. The stack and `Push` become `Open`:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/LibraryView.cs -->
```csharp
private void OpenItem(string itemId) =>
    Navigator.Open(AppViews.ItemDetail, new ItemArgs(itemId), Navigator.RootToken,
        new OpenOptions { Source = "library.item" });
```

`Open` returns at once and does not wait; use `ShowAsync` when the caller needs the outcome. The
`Source` string names the call site in events and diagnostics. The owner is the root because a screen
opened from a button should outlive the screen that holds the button.

The list-as-stack code becomes the layer. The screen below is covered and kept loaded, not destroyed,
and `Pop` becomes `Back()` or a jump to a known screen:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/ItemDetailView.cs -->
```csharp
// Home is already in the stack: this returns to it, and Home's OnOpen does not run again.
private void GoHome() =>
    Navigator.Open(AppViews.Home, Navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "item.home" });

// Pops everything above the library.
private void GoToLibrary() => Navigator.CloseTo(AppViews.Library);
```

Two differences from a hand-written stack are worth knowing before you port code that depended on
them:

- **`OnOpen` runs once per open, not once per visit.** A screen that was covered and is revealed again
  gets `OnVisible`, not `OnOpen`. Code that refreshed a screen in `OnEnable` goes in `OnVisible`:

  <!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/LibraryView.cs -->
  ```csharp
  // Runs on the first show and again each time this screen is revealed.
  protected override void OnVisible(ViewScope visible) => _count.text = $"{_library.Count} items";
  ```

- **Opening an id that is already in the stack returns to it** instead of pushing a copy. A flow that
  deliberately stacks two instances of one screen sets `Allow Multiple` on its row.

The details, with a table of what runs and what does not, are on
[Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#return-to-a-screen-that-is-already-open).

A screen that takes its data from a static field of the old manager now takes it from its key's
argument type (`ViewKey<ItemArgs, NoResult>` above). That is the end of `Init(args)` for screens too.

Popups that are open when a screen opens are closed by the screen change; this is the
`ClosedByNavigation` rule of the `popups` layer, and it does not touch old popups that are not views of
the package. See [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#closedbynavigation).

---

## Step 6: stop reaching for a singleton

`UIManager.Instance` was a global. `INavigator` is an interface with one instance per root, and it is
handed to whoever needs it.

- **A view** gets it as the `Navigator` property of `ViewBehaviour`. The snippets above use it.
- **A plain class** receives it where it is built. The Zenject sample's start class is an ordinary C#
  class; any other way of passing a constructor argument works the same:

  <!-- source: Samples~/ZenjectUsage/AppStart.cs -->
  ```csharp
  private readonly INavigator _navigator;

  public AppStart(INavigator navigator)
  {
      _navigator = navigator;
  }

  public void Initialize()
  {
      // Owned by the root, so the scoreboard ends only when the root does.
      _navigator.Open(ZenjectViews.Scoreboard, _navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "boot" });
  }
  ```

- **Services a view needs** (settings, a store) used to come from other singletons. The root's
  `Inject` delegate runs on every new view instance while it is still inactive, before its `Awake`.
  It is the one seam for handing services in, whether you use a container or not:

  <!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
  ```csharp
  // Runs on every new view instance while it is still inactive.
  private void InjectServices(GameObject instance)
  {
      instance.GetComponentsInChildren(true, _receivers);
      foreach (var receiver in _receivers)
          receiver.Receive(_services);

      _receivers.Clear();
  }
  ```

  A container integration is on [Zenject](Zenject.md).

- **Anything that logged or sent analytics from inside the old manager** becomes an observer. It sees
  every request, shown view, close and refusal in one place, and ends with its owner token:

  <!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/AppBootstrap.cs -->
  ```csharp
  // The observer ends with the root: RootToken is cancelled when the root is destroyed.
  _navigator.AddObserver(new ViewEventLog(), _navigator.RootToken);
  ```

While old and new code coexist, the simplest bridge is to keep the old manager's public methods and
make them forward. `Show("Settings")` calls `Open` for an id that has moved and does what it always
did for one that has not. A method that took an `Action<bool>` awaits `ShowAsync` and calls the
callback when `HasValue` is true. Callers do not change until you are ready to change them, and
the forwarders are the list of what is left.

---

## Step 7: route the back key through one place

The old UI and the package each have their own idea of what back means. While both are on screen, one
object must decide the order, or one key press is handled twice.

`BackInput` does not ask other UI first. A project with an older popup system replaces it on the root
with a small router that asks the older UI, and calls `Back()` only when the older UI did not use the
press. The Basic Usage sample ships that router, `HardwareBackRouter`, and its handler is:

<!-- source: Samples~/BasicUsage/HardwareBackRouter.cs -->
```csharp
public void HandleBack()
{
    // The older UI sits above the package's layers, so it answers first.
    if (_legacyPopup.TryClose())
        return;

    if (!_root.Navigator.Back())
        _unhandled.Invoke();
}
```

In your project `TryClose()` is a call into the old manager that returns `true` when it closed
something. The rules, and the complete recipe, are on
[Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#a-project-that-still-has-an-older-ui):

- Never keep both `BackInput` and the router on the root.
- Order follows the stacking. If the older UI is drawn below the package's layers, call `Back()`
  first and ask the older UI when `Back()` returns `false`.
- The quit logic stays in the router's `Unhandled` event, the way `BackInput.Unhandled` serves it.

When the last old popup is gone, delete the router and put `BackInput` back on the root.

If a flow of the old UI is on screen and the package has queued notices (a daily reward, a news
popup), the queue does not know about it. Take a hold for as long as the old flow runs, with the flow's
owner token, so queued items wait:

<!-- source: Samples~/QueueUsage/TutorialFlow.cs -->
```csharp
// Queued items wait; the flow's own opens below are not affected by the hold.
var hold = _queue.Hold("tutorial", ct);
try
{
    for (var step = 1; step <= Tips.Length; step++)
    {
        var result = await _navigator.ShowAsync(QueueViews.TutorialTip,
            new TipArgs(Tips[step - 1], step, Tips.Length), ct,
            new OpenOptions { Source = "tutorial" });

        // Not shown, backed out, replaced or owner ended: the player left the tutorial.
        if (result.Reason != CloseReason.Dismissed && result.Reason != CloseReason.Completed)
            return;
    }
}
finally
{
    // Ending the hold lets the queue continue; while the tutorial ran, the gate denied notices below priority 100.
    hold.Remove();
    _onboarding.IsRunning = false;
    IsRunning = false;
}
```

The hold is removed in a `finally`, so no way out leaves the queue held. [Queue](Queue.md#holds) has
the rules.

---

## Step 8: retire the old manager

A view is migrated when no code calls the old manager for it. When the last screen and popup have
moved:

1. Search for the manager's type name and its static field. Every remaining hit is a forwarder or a
   caller you have not changed.
2. Delete the router and put `BackInput` back on the root.
3. Delete the old canvas, or keep it for content that is not a screen (a HUD) with a sorting order
   below the band.
4. Run `Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs` and open `Window > UIDirector` in Play Mode to see the
   layers, requests and shield holders live ([Diagnostics](Diagnostics.md)).

---

## Running both side by side: what to expect

| Area | Behaviour while both exist |
|---|---|
| Drawing | The package draws only its own views, on the root's canvas, and covers only its own views. Old content stays visible until the old manager hides it |
| Input | The input shield blocks the package's views and old canvases that sort below it. A canvas sorted above the shield is not blocked |
| Back | `Back()` knows only package views. The router in step 7 is what joins the two |
| `ClosedByNavigation` | Applies to package popups only |
| The queue | Presents package views only. Hold it while an old flow runs |
| `Time.timeScale` 0 | Transitions, timeouts and the backdrop run on unscaled time. An old tween on scaled time still stops, as it did before |
| Scene changes | The root has no scene-change rule of its own. A root without `Persist Across Scenes` is destroyed with its scene and ends every view on it; turn it on when the old manager survives scene loads. An old manager that tears down on a scene change keeps doing so; give package views an owner that ends where you want them to end ([Limitations](Limitations.md#navigation)) |
| Two canvases, one `EventSystem` | One `EventSystem` serves both |

---

## Traps

- **A second `EventSystem`.** The menu adds one only when the scene has none. If the old UI creates its
  own at run time, the project can end up with two.
- **An old canvas sorted inside the band.** It interleaves with screens and popups. Put it below
  `Base Sorting Order` or above the shield.
- **A popup row left on `screens`.** `screens` is the default `Layer Id`. A popup left there is a
  screen: it joins the history and a later screen draws over it. Set `popups`.
- **Treating `Open` as "it is open".** `Open` accepts the request and returns. A request can still be
  refused, fail to load or decline. When a later line depends on the outcome, use `ShowAsync`.
- **Reading `Value` without `HasValue`.** For a `bool` the default is `false`, which looks like an
  answer of "no".
- **Opening UI from a worker thread.** The call throws. Hop to the main thread first
  ([Threading](Threading.md)).
- **Both `BackInput` and a router on the root.** One press is handled twice.
- **Calling `SetActive(false)` or `Destroy` on a package view.** One frame later the request
  ends with `CloseReason.Destroyed` (or `NotShown` with `Rejected` of `Cancelled` if the view had not been
  shown yet) and logs [UIDIRECTOR107](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector107).
  The package releases the instance instead of keeping it, so a `KeepInstance` row builds a new one on
  its next open. Close through `Complete`, `Close`, the handle or Back.
- **Keeping a view's own `OnDisable` cleanup.** Listeners bound on the scope are removed by the
  package. A hand-written `RemoveListener` is harmless and not needed.

## See also

- [Concepts](Concepts.md): the model behind the steps
- [Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md): the history stack, `Back()` and the older-UI recipe
- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md): `Open`, `ShowAsync`, owners and results

- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md): hooks, scopes and prefab structure
