<!-- file: Documentation~/DOTween.md -->

# DOTween

[Back to index](index.md)

UIDirector ships an optional integration for DOTween: a ready-made `TweenTransition` that you configure in the Inspector, and the pieces you need to write your own transition on DOTween without leaving a tween behind. This page covers turning the integration on, `TweenTransition` and its settings, writing a kill-safe custom transition, and the trap that `DOTween.KillAll()` ends a transition that is playing. The contract that every transition keeps is on [Transitions](Transitions.md); this page assumes it.

The core of the package needs no tween library. Without DOTween the integration is not compiled, the types on this page do not exist, and the rest of the package works unchanged.

---

## Turn the integration on

The integration is a separate assembly, `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DOTween`, in the namespace `Ecanakli.UIDirector`. Unity compiles it when one of two scripting defines exists:

- `DOTWEEN`. DOTween from the Asset Store adds it itself when it is imported; Setup DOTween in its Utility Panel (`Tools > Demigiant > DOTween Utility Panel`) keeps it.
- `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN`. The assembly sets it for itself, through a version define, when a package named `com.demigiant.dotween` is installed. DOTween publishes no UPM package of its own; this is for a project that wraps DOTween in a package under that name.

If neither define is set but the DOTween assembly is in the project, turn the integration on with the menu item `Tools > UIDirector > DOTween Integration`. It adds `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN` to every build target and removes it when you choose it again. It shows a check mark while the integration is on: when `DOTWEEN` is defined, when a package named `com.demigiant.dotween` is installed, or when `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN` is set. When `DOTWEEN` is already defined, or that package is installed, choosing the item only tells you that the integration is already on and that there is nothing to toggle; it writes no define. When no assembly named `DOTween` is loaded it asks you to import DOTween first.

The core `DOTween.dll` is enough. The integration references that precompiled library only. It does not need DOTween's module scripts (the extension methods for UI, physics and so on) and never calls them. A transition of your own can live in `Assembly-CSharp` (see below), or in an assembly definition that references `Ecanakli.UIDirector` and `UniTask` (every `PlayAsync` returns a `UniTask`) and, if it uses `TweenTransition`, `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DOTween`. Such an assembly definition turns on Override References, adds `DOTween.dll` to its precompiled references and copies the define constraint `DOTWEEN || ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN`, as the DOTween Usage sample's assembly definition does. The constraint keeps the assembly out of the build when DOTween or the integration is absent.

If DOTween is deleted from the project while a define that turns the integration on is still set, the integration assembly can no longer resolve `DOTween.dll`. Remove `DOTWEEN` from every build target, or, if you turned the integration on with the menu, choose `Tools > UIDirector > DOTween Integration` again to remove `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN`.

Game code in the default `Assembly-CSharp` can use `TweenTransition` and DOTween directly, with no assembly definition of its own: `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DOTween` and `DOTween.dll` are auto-referenced, so a loose script compiles against both whenever the integration is on. The version define `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN` is set inside the package's own assembly only, so game code does not test it with `#if`. When the menu item adds the same symbol as a scripting define it is project-wide, but game code still should not depend on it. A script that names these types fails to compile when the integration is off. If a project needs to build with and without DOTween, keep such scripts in an assembly definition with the define constraint shown above.

The DOTween Usage sample shows both transitions. Its bootstrap has no integration code at all, only the ordinary root setup:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/DOTweenBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class DOTweenBootstrap : MonoBehaviour
{
    // "Initialize On Awake" is off on this root; the bootstrap initialises it in Awake.
    [SerializeField] private ViewRoot _viewRoot;

    private void Awake()
    {
        // Before the root initialises, so the root finds an EventSystem.
        SampleEventSystem.EnsureExists();
        _viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup());
    }

    private void Start()
    {
        // Owned by the root, so the welcome screen ends only when the root does.
        var navigator = _viewRoot.Navigator;
        navigator.Open(TweenViews.Welcome, navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "boot" });
    }
}
```

---

## TweenTransition

`TweenTransition` fades, scales and offsets a view with DOTween on unscaled time. You use it exactly like a built-in transition ([Transitions](Transitions.md)): add it to the prefab root and assign it to the `Transition` field of the `ViewHost`. No code is needed. In the sample, the `Hint` prefab has it and its view class is a plain popup:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/HintView.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class HintView : ViewBehaviour<HintArgs>
{
    [SerializeField] private TMP_Text _text;
    [SerializeField] private Button _ok;

    protected override void OnOpen(HintArgs args, ViewScope open)
    {
        _text.text = args.Text;
        open.Bind(_ok.onClick, Close);
    }
}
```

The `Card` prefab uses the same class with a different transition; only the transition on the prefab differs.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Fade` | on | Fades a `CanvasGroup` on its own object, added when missing. Shown is alpha 1, hidden is 0. |
| `Scale` | on | Scales its own `RectTransform`. Shown is 1. |
| `Hidden Scale` | 0.85 | The uniform scale of the hidden pose. |
| `Offset` | off | Moves its own `anchoredPosition`. Shown is the authored position. |
| `Hidden Offset` | (0, -1) | The hidden position as a fraction of the layer rectangle's size. (0, -1) is one layer height below. |
| `Duration` | 0.25 s | Seconds of unscaled time per play. A duration of 0 jumps to the end pose. |
| `Show Ease` | OutCubic | The DOTween `Ease` when showing. |
| `Hide Ease` | InCubic | The DOTween `Ease` when hiding. |

Each part can be turned off. With every part off, a play returns at once.

The enabled parts apply to both directions: a show animates them towards the shown pose and a hide towards the hidden pose, with the same duration. Only the two eases differ. A view that scales in and fades out, or otherwise shows and hides with different motions, needs a custom `ViewTransition`, such as the one below.

What it does at run time:

- It builds one `Sequence` of `DOTween.To` tweens per play, from the opposite end pose to the target pose.
- It sets the ease, auto-kill and unscaled update on the sequence itself. Project-wide DOTween defaults, such as a changed default ease or auto-kill turned off, cannot compound the ease or stop the kill callback from firing.
- It awaits the end of the sequence through the sequence's own kill callback. A completed auto-kill sequence kills itself, which ends the await.
- A cancelled token kills the sequence with `Kill(false)` and ends the await at once, even when DOTween defers the kill inside its own update. The view stays in the pose the tween had reached; the runner snaps if it needs the end pose.
- `Snap` kills a running sequence and then writes the pose of the enabled parts.
- A kill that the component makes itself (`Snap`, a new play that replaces a running one, `OnDestroy`) resumes the awaiting caller on the next player-loop step, never inside that call. The task of a play that `Snap` ends therefore does not complete inside `Snap`, which is the rule for every custom transition ([Transitions](Transitions.md#the-contract)), and a kill from `OnDestroy` does not resume the caller inside Unity's destroy message.
- A kill that comes from outside, such as `DOTween.KillAll()` or `Kill()` on the sequence, ends the await at once.
- It drops its reference to the sequence inside the kill callback, so a tween that DOTween recycles is never touched.

---

## Write a kill-safe custom transition on DOTween

A transition on DOTween is kill-safe when nothing that kills its tween can leave the returned task pending, and no reference to a recycled tween is ever used. `PunchTransition` fades the view in with a scale punch and fades it out while shrinking. It starts with a few constants and the handles it needs:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/PunchTransition.cs -->
```csharp
[RequireComponent(typeof(CanvasGroup))]
public sealed class PunchTransition : ViewTransition
{
    private const float HiddenScale = 0.9f;
    private const float PunchStrength = 0.12f;
    private const int PunchVibrato = 4;
    private const float PunchElasticity = 0.5f;

    [SerializeField, Min(0f)] private float _duration = 0.35f;

    private CanvasGroup _group;
    private DOGetter<float> _getAlpha;
    private DOSetter<float> _setAlpha;

    // The only handle to the running sequence; no SetLink, so a kill happens only here.
    private Sequence _running;
```

The play builds the sequence, makes its settings explicit and returns a wait:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/PunchTransition.cs -->
```csharp
public override UniTask PlayAsync(bool show, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (ct.IsCancellationRequested || !Prepare())
        return UniTask.CompletedTask;

    KillRunning();
    if (_duration <= 0f)
    {
        Snap(show);
        return UniTask.CompletedTask;
    }

    // A punch returns to the scale it starts from, so a show starts at the shown scale.
    Write(show ? 0f : 1f, 1f);

    var sequence = DOTween.Sequence();
    if (show)
    {
        sequence.Join(DOTween.To(_getAlpha, _setAlpha, 1f, _duration).SetEase(Ease.OutQuad));
        sequence.Join(transform.DOPunchScale(new Vector3(PunchStrength, PunchStrength, 0f), _duration, PunchVibrato, PunchElasticity).SetEase(Ease.OutQuad));
    }
    else
    {
        sequence.Join(DOTween.To(_getAlpha, _setAlpha, 0f, _duration).SetEase(Ease.InQuad));
        sequence.Join(transform.DOScale(HiddenScale, _duration).SetEase(Ease.InQuad));
    }

    // Explicit, so project-wide DOTween defaults cannot change the ease or the lifetime of this tween.
    // Unscaled time, so a paused game still shows and hides the view.
    sequence.SetEase(Ease.Linear).SetAutoKill(true).SetUpdate(true).SetRecyclable(false).Play();
    _running = sequence;
    return WaitAsync(sequence, ct);
}
```

Four decisions make it safe.

**One handle, kept only while the tween lives.** `_running` is the only reference to the sequence, and the sequence is created with `SetRecyclable(false)`. DOTween can recycle a finished tween into a pool and hand the same object to another owner, so a stale reference would stop or move someone else's tween. The kill path takes the reference out before it kills:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/PunchTransition.cs -->
```csharp
private void KillRunning()
{
    // Dropped before the kill; the sequence is not recyclable, so a stale reference is inert.
    var running = _running;
    _running = null;
    if (running.IsActive())
        running.Kill();
}
```

The sample sets no `SetLink`, so the only kill is the one made here. A link adds a second, hidden kill path.

**Explicit settings.** The sequence sets its own ease, auto-kill, unscaled update and recyclability. Do not inherit them from project-wide DOTween defaults, which another team can change.

**A wait that does not depend on a callback.** The play does not resume from `OnKill` or `OnComplete`. It polls on the player loop while the sequence is active and playing:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/PunchTransition.cs -->
```csharp
// Polls on the player loop instead of resuming from OnKill or OnComplete: a kill from OnDestroy
// would then resume the runner inside Unity's destroy message.
private static async UniTask WaitAsync(Sequence sequence, CancellationToken ct)
{
    while (sequence.IsActive() && sequence.IsPlaying())
    {
        var cancelled = await UniTask.Yield(ct).SuppressCancellationThrow();
        if (!cancelled)
            continue;

        if (sequence.IsActive())
            sequence.Kill();

        return;
    }

    // Paused from outside, the sequence would never end; finish it at its end pose.
    if (sequence.IsActive())
        sequence.Kill(true);
}
```

Whatever kills the sequence, the loop sees `IsActive()` turn false on its next frame and returns. A kill from `OnDestroy` cannot resume the runner inside Unity's destroy message, because the loop only ever resumes on the player loop. When the token is cancelled, the loop kills the sequence and returns. When the sequence was paused from outside, it would never end, so the loop finishes it at its end pose.

**A `Snap` that cannot throw.** `Snap` kills the running sequence first and then writes the pose, and `OnDestroy` kills it too:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/PunchTransition.cs -->
```csharp
public override void Snap(bool shown)
{
    KillRunning();

    // Never throws: a destroyed view is skipped.
    if (Prepare())
        Write(shown ? 1f : 0f, shown ? 1f : HiddenScale);
}
```

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/PunchTransition.cs -->
```csharp
private void OnDestroy()
{
    KillRunning();
}
```

`Prepare` returns `false` for a destroyed component, so `Snap` skips it. It also creates the getter and setter once per component, so a play allocates no closure:

<!-- source: Samples~/DOTweenUsage/PunchTransition.cs -->
```csharp
// False on a destroyed component, which cannot reach its group.
private bool Prepare()
{
    if (this == null)
        return false;

    if (_group == null)
        _group = GetComponent<CanvasGroup>();

    // Created once per component, so a play allocates no getter or setter.
    _getAlpha ??= GetAlpha;
    _setAlpha ??= SetAlpha;
    return _group != null;
}
```

Other points in this sample:

- It uses `DOTween.To` with a getter and a setter for the alpha, and the `Transform` shortcuts `DOPunchScale` and `DOScale`. All of them are in the core `DOTween.dll`. The shortcut for fading a `CanvasGroup` (`DOFade`) lives in a DOTween module assembly, which the package does not reference, so the sample tweens the alpha through `DOTween.To`.
- `SetUpdate(true)` makes the tween independent of `Time.timeScale`. A DOTween transition on scaled time stalls at `timeScale` 0 and ends in [UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106).
- A punch returns to the scale it starts from, so a show starts at the shown scale, and the sample writes that pose before it builds the sequence.

---

## The trap: DOTween.KillAll() ends a playing transition

`DOTween.KillAll()` kills every tween in the project, including the tween of a transition that is playing. It runs the tween's `OnKill` callback but not its `OnComplete`. After `DOTween.KillAll()`, `TweenTransition` ends its play at once and `PunchTransition` on its next frame, and the view stays in the pose the tween had reached: the runner treats the play as finished, does not snap and logs nothing, so a popup can stay half-faded while it is open. `DOTween.Clear()` removes every tween too, but do not rely on it running `OnKill`. `TweenTransition` waits for `OnKill`, so after `Clear()` it ends only if `Clear()` runs `OnKill`; otherwise the transition timeout ends it, like the `OnComplete` case below. `PunchTransition` polls and ends on its next frame either way. A transition that completes from `OnComplete` is left waiting until the transition timeout (3 s by default, the `Transition Timeout Seconds` field of `ViewRoot`) cancels it, snaps the view and logs [UIDIRECTOR106](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106). The view is not lost, but it stalls for the timeout and on a layer that shields input the shield stays up for that time.

Two things follow:

- A custom transition should not hang its completion on `OnComplete`, which a kill never runs. Poll `IsActive()` on the player loop, as `PunchTransition` does.
- Game code should not call `DOTween.KillAll()` or `DOTween.Clear()` while a view is opening or closing. To stop a tween of your own, kill that tween.

`TweenTransition` ends its await when the sequence is killed from outside by `KillAll` or by killing the sequence, and its later plays and snaps stay clean. The view stays in whatever pose the tween had reached until a later snap writes the end pose.

## Traps

- **Holding a tween reference after the tween ended.** With recycling on, the object may belong to another tween. Drop the reference when you kill, or create the tween with `SetRecyclable(false)`.
- **Relying on project-wide defaults.** Set the ease, auto-kill and update mode on the tween you create.
- **Scaled time.** `SetUpdate(true)` is required.
- **Allocating getters and setters per play.** Create them once per component.
- **Using a module extension.** `DOFade` on a `CanvasGroup` and similar methods are not in the core library. Use `DOTween.To` unless your own assembly references the modules.
- **Integration defined but DOTween removed.** Remove `DOTWEEN` from the scripting define symbols, or choose `Tools > UIDirector > DOTween Integration` again to remove `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN`.

## See also

- [Transitions](Transitions.md): the built-ins and the contract every transition keeps
- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md): the view prefab, its `ViewHost` and the hooks
- [Diagnostics](Diagnostics.md): how warnings and errors are reported
- [Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector106): UIDIRECTOR106, a transition that did not finish
- [Limitations](Limitations.md): what the package does not do
- [Architecture: transitions](Design/Architecture.md#15-transitions): the `TweenTransition` design

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Assets-and-Addressables.md -->

# Assets and Addressables

[Back to index](index.md)

A catalog row names its view in one of two ways: a prefab reference that is resident while the
catalog is loaded, or an asset key that a provider resolves when the view opens. This page is
about the second way: loading views by address with the Addressables integration, loading them
ahead of time, releasing them, what happens when a load fails, and what a provider of your own
has to do. The examples are the files of the Addressables Usage sample.

---

## Open a view by address

Four steps. The core carries no Addressables type; the key is a plain string.

1. Install `com.unity.addressables`. The integration compiles itself (see
   [The integration turns on by itself](#the-integration-turns-on-by-itself)).
2. Add an `AddressablesViewProvider` component to the same GameObject as the `ViewRoot`.
3. In the catalog, leave a row's `Prefab` empty and write the prefab's Addressables address in
   `Asset Key`.
4. Mark that prefab addressable with exactly that address.

Open the view as you open any other. The keys of the sample are plain keys; nothing in them says the
rows have no prefab:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/RemoteViews.cs -->
```csharp
[ViewKeys]
public static class RemoteViews
{
    public static readonly ViewKey<NoArgs, NoResult> Gallery = ViewKey.Create("gallery");
    public static readonly ViewKey<PhotoArgs, NoResult> Photo = ViewKey.Create<PhotoArgs>("photo");
}
```

The root is initialised with an empty setup. Its `AssetProvider` stays empty, so the root finds the
`AddressablesViewProvider` component on its own GameObject:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/AddressablesBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
// AssetProvider stays empty, so the AddressablesViewProvider on the root's GameObject is used.
_viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup());
```

In the sample, the `gallery` row has the address `uidirector-samples/gallery` and is a screen that
keeps its instance, and the `photo` row has `uidirector-samples/photo` and is a popup that closes on a
tap on the backdrop. Pressing Play opens the gallery on its own (`source=boot`).

In the editor the default Addressables play mode script, "Use Asset Database", loads the prefabs
directly, so no content build is needed to try it. A player build needs the Addressables content
built first.

---

## Rows with a prefab and rows with an asset key

A project can mix both in one catalog.

| | Row with a `Prefab` | Row with an `Asset Key` |
|---|---|---|
| Resident | The prefab, while its catalog is loaded | Nothing until the view opens |
| Opening | `Object.Instantiate` in the call that opens it, under the inactive staging object, so `Awake` has not run | The root's `IViewProvider` loads and instantiates it, asynchronously |
| Needs a provider | No | Yes. Without one the open ends as `RejectReason.LoadFailed` with [UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120) |
| Load wait | None | Yes: the request is in `Loading` until the provider returns |
| Closing | The instance is destroyed, or parked for `KeepInstance` | The instance is handed back to the provider's `Release`, or parked for `KeepInstance` (the provider's handle then stays alive) |
| Preload | `PreloadAsync` returns `true` at once and loads nothing | `PreloadAsync` asks the provider to keep the asset loaded |

When a row has both a prefab and an asset key, the prefab wins and the key is ignored. The row's
`Id` and its `Asset Key` are separate on purpose: code and remote data keep naming the id, and
renaming an address changes one catalog row, which the validator reports. See
[Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md#a-catalog-row) for every field of a row.

---

## The provider seam

The root resolves asset keys through one `IViewProvider`:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public interface IViewProvider
{
    UniTask<GameObject> AcquireAsync(string assetKey, Transform inactiveParent, CancellationToken ct);
    void Release(GameObject instance);
    UniTask<IDisposable> PreloadAsync(string assetKey, CancellationToken ct);
}
```

The root takes its provider when it initialises, in this order:

1. `ViewRootSetup.AssetProvider`, when it is set.
2. An `IViewProvider` component on the same GameObject as the `ViewRoot`.
3. None. A row with an asset key then ends as `LoadFailed` with
   [UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120), and `PreloadAsync` returns `false`.

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public IViewProvider AssetProvider;
```

Because the provider is read once in `Initialize`, a component that is added to the root's
GameObject after the root has initialised is not seen. With `Initialize On Awake` on, the root
initialises in `Awake`, so the component must already be on the object, as a prefab or scene
setup has it. With `Initialize On Awake` off, set `AssetProvider` yourself or add the component
before you call `Initialize` ([Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md#give-the-catalogs-to-the-root)).
A second `Initialize` throws.

To add the provider from code, turn `Initialize On Awake` off on the root, create the component, and pass
it in the setup before anything reads `Navigator` (its first access initialises the root with default
settings, which has no provider unless one sits on the root's GameObject):
`_viewRoot.Initialize(new ViewRootSetup { AssetProvider = _viewRoot.gameObject.AddComponent<AddressablesViewProvider>() });`.
The component may sit on any GameObject that lives as long as the root; it does not have to be on the
root's. The root never destroys it. A root that initialised in `Awake` has already read its provider, so
adding the component afterwards and calling `Initialize` throws.

A direct-prefab row never touches the provider.

---

## The integration turns on by itself

The Addressables integration is a separate assembly, `Ecanakli.UIDirector.Addressables`. It
declares a version define for `com.unity.addressables` and requires it, so it compiles when the
Addressables package is installed and is absent when it is not. There is no menu to run and no
scripting define to set. The package does not list Addressables as a dependency; a project that
does not use it never compiles any Addressables type. The editor validator reads the same define,
so its Addressables checks run only when the package is installed.

The core has no reference to the integration. If you remove Addressables, the rows that carry an
asset key stay in your catalogs and fail until a provider is available; the validator warns
([UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120)).

---

## The AddressablesViewProvider component

`AddressablesViewProvider` is a `MonoBehaviour` that implements `IViewProvider`. Put it beside the
`ViewRoot`; it needs no settings.

- **Acquire.** It loads the prefab asset with `Addressables.LoadAssetAsync` and instantiates it itself
  with `Object.Instantiate` under the inactive parent, then returns the instance still inactive. It
  instantiates only when the call is still wanted, the provider is alive and the parent still exists;
  otherwise it releases the asset and no view code runs. It keeps the asset handle in a table keyed by
  the instance id and is the only code that releases it. View code never sees a handle. The instance is
  an ordinary object, not an Addressables-tracked instance, so `Addressables.ReleaseInstance` on it
  returns `false`; the asset stays loaded, and Addressables tracks its handle, while the instance lives.
- **Release.** It destroys the instance with `Object.Destroy` (the destroy happens at the end of the
  frame, and the provider is meant for Play Mode) and releases the asset handle that the instance came from. Every release is guarded by
  `IsValid()`, because a scene unload can invalidate a handle by itself. A failure while releasing is
  logged, never thrown. Releasing by instance id means an instance that was destroyed from outside
  still releases its handle.
- **Cancel and late results.** When the token is cancelled before the load completes, the call
  ends at once with `OperationCanceledException`, and the load's single completion callback releases
  the asset that arrives later without instantiating it. The load timeout takes the same path.
- **Failed loads.** A load that fails or produces nothing releases its handle and throws
  `InvalidOperationException` with a message that names the key; the inner exception is the one
  Addressables reported. The request then ends as `LoadFailed`.
- **A destroyed parent.** If the inactive parent is destroyed before the load completes, the asset is
  released, nothing is instantiated, and the task faults with `InvalidOperationException` that names the
  key. A parent that is already destroyed when the call is made fails the same way, and nothing is loaded.
- **Preload.** It loads the prefab asset with `LoadAssetAsync` without instantiating it, and returns
  a lease. The first `Dispose` of the lease releases the asset; later calls do nothing. A lease and
  the instances made from the same key are independent reference counts, so the order in which
  they are released does not matter.
- **Destroy.** When the component is destroyed it destroys every instance and releases its asset handle, then releases every lease.
  Later calls throw `ObjectDisposedException` or do nothing, and a load still in flight releases its
  late result.
- **Usage errors** throw at the call: a null or empty key throws `ArgumentException`, a null
  `inactiveParent` throws `ArgumentNullException`, a destroyed provider throws
  `ObjectDisposedException`, and a load that Addressables cannot start throws `InvalidOperationException`
  naming the key. A token that is already cancelled returns a cancelled task instead.

Call it from the main thread only; the root does.

---

## Mark the prefab addressable

The address is the row's `Asset Key`. The validator accepts an address, an Addressables GUID or a
label as a key, and the provider passes the key to Addressables unchanged; use the address so the
row reads clearly. Mark the prefab either way:

- **By hand.** Open `Window > Asset Management > Addressables > Groups`, create the settings if
  asked, drag the prefab into a group, and set its address to the row's `Asset Key`.
- **From an editor script.** The sample ships a menu helper,
  `Tools/UIDirector/Samples/Make Addressables Usage Prefabs Addressable`. It runs only when you click
  it, never on import. The lines that matter are:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/Editor/MarkSampleAddressables.cs -->
```csharp
var entry = settings.CreateOrMoveEntry(guid, settings.DefaultGroup);
entry.SetAddress(address);
settings.SetDirty(AddressableAssetSettings.ModificationEvent.EntryMoved, entry, true);
```

The addresses it uses are constants of that file:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/Editor/MarkSampleAddressables.cs -->
```csharp
private const string GalleryAddress = "uidirector-samples/gallery";
private const string PhotoAddress = "uidirector-samples/photo";
```

The prefab itself is an ordinary view prefab: a `ViewHost` on the root and a view component
([View authoring](View-Authoring.md#prefab-structure)). A view script that is referenced only from a
prefab inside an Addressables bundle can be removed by managed code stripping in a build; see
[Limitations](Limitations.md).

---

## Preload with a lease

A view that loads on demand makes the first open wait for the asset. `INavigator.PreloadAsync` loads
the asset ahead of time and keeps it loaded for as long as an owner lives:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
UniTask<bool> PreloadAsync(string viewId, CancellationToken owner, [CallerMemberName] string member = null, [CallerLineNumber] int line = 0);
```

The sample's gallery preloads the photo popup while it is visible, with the visible scope as owner,
so the lease ends when the gallery is covered by another screen or closed:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/GalleryView.cs -->
```csharp
// The lease lives on the visible scope: it is released when this screen is covered or closed.
protected override void OnVisible(ViewScope visible)
{
    visible.Run(PreloadAsync);
}

private async UniTask PreloadAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    // With the photo asset held, the first photo below opens without a load wait.
    var loaded = await Navigator.PreloadAsync(RemoteViews.Photo.Id, ct);
    _status.text = loaded ? "Photo popup preloaded." : "Photo popup could not be preloaded, see the console.";
}
```

What it does:

- **It loads the asset, not an instance.** It never creates a view instance. A later open still
  instantiates, but it does not wait for a download or a bundle load, because the asset is held.
- **It returns `true` once the asset is loaded and held.** It returns `false` when the id is
  unknown ([UIDIRECTOR101](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector101)), the row has an asset key and the
  root has no provider ([UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120)), the owner ended
  before or during the load, the root is gone, or the load failed. For a direct-prefab row it
  returns `true` at once.
- **The owner ends the lease, and only the owner.** A lease lives until its owner token ends, also after
  `PreloadAsync` has returned `true`. Neither `Trim()` nor a low-memory event releases it; only destroying the root or the provider component ends it earlier.
  When the owner token ends, the lease is disposed and the asset is released. A photo popup does not cover the gallery, so in the sample the lease stays while popups open
  and close. Ending the root releases every lease.
- **Preloads are not bounded by the load timeout.** The timeout applies to opening a view. A
  preload ends with its owner, or when the provider finishes or fails.
- **A failed preload** routes the provider's exception to the root's error handler and returns
  `false`; the id [UIDIRECTOR104](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector104) belongs to opening a view.
  In the sample, a photo address that is missing while the gallery address is right leaves the
  gallery open with the status "Photo popup could not be preloaded, see the console.", and a photo
  button then sets the status to `Photo '<title>' did not open: LoadFailed.`

Preloading is a main-thread call and throws off the main thread ([Threading](Threading.md)).
Several preloads of one id are independent leases.

---

## Keep and trim

A row's `Retention` decides what a close does to the instance of an asset-key row.

- `ReleaseOnClose` (the default) releases the instance to the provider at close. The next open loads
  and instantiates again.
- `KeepInstance` parks one idle instance per id, hidden and deactivated, and reuses it on the next
  open without injecting again. The instance and its asset handle stay alive while it is parked, so
  the asset stays loaded. There is no budget and no timer. See
  [View authoring](View-Authoring.md#kept-instances).

`INavigator.Trim()` releases every idle kept instance. It never touches a request in flight or a
preload lease: a lease lives until its owner token ends, also after `PreloadAsync` has returned. The root
calls `Trim()` on `Application.lowMemory`, so a low-memory event frees kept instances and leaves preloaded
assets loaded. The sample's gallery has a button that calls it:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/GalleryView.cs -->
```csharp
// Frees kept instances that are not on screen; this screen is open, so it stays.
private void TrimKept()
{
    Navigator.Trim();
    _status.text = "Trimmed: hidden kept instances were released.";
}
```

The gallery is open, so it stays. Nothing else in the sample is kept, so you see only the status line
change; the call matters in a project with several kept screens. `Trim` called off the main thread is
posted to it.

To release preloads on low memory, end their owner from your own `Application.lowMemory` handler. Pass the
token of a `CancellationTokenSource` you hold as the owner of those `PreloadAsync` calls, cancel the source
in the handler, and create a new source for later preloads. Cancelling the source disposes its leases and
releases their assets.

---

## What is released when

| Moment | What is released |
|---|---|
| A view with a `ReleaseOnClose` asset-key row closes | Its instance, through the provider's `Release`, before `Closed` is published |
| A view with a `KeepInstance` row closes | Nothing; the instance is parked |
| `Trim()` or `Application.lowMemory` | Every idle kept instance |
| A catalog is removed | The kept instances of its rows. A view of a removed row that closes later is released, not kept |
| An instance is destroyed from outside | Its asset handle, by instance id; it is never kept |
| The owner of a preload ends, or the root is destroyed | The lease, so the asset |
| A load is cancelled (withdrawn, owner ended, root destroyed) or times out | The late result, by the provider when it arrives |
| The root is destroyed | Open instances, kept instances and leases |
| The `AddressablesViewProvider` component is destroyed | Every instance and its asset handle, then every lease |

Removing a catalog leaves the open views of its rows open; they end when their own owner ends.

---

## The load timeout and the load indicator

Both are Inspector fields on the `ViewRoot`, in unscaled seconds on the root's clock:

| Field | Default | Minimum | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Load Timeout Seconds` | 15 | 0.1 | The longest a view may take to load. Then the token given to the provider is cancelled and the request ends as `NotShown` with `RejectReason.LoadTimedOut` ([UIDIRECTOR105](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector105)). |
| `Indicator Delay Seconds` | 0.4 | 0 | How long a load must run before the load indicator is shown. |
| `Load Indicator` | none | | An optional GameObject. It is activated when a load has run longer than the indicator delay, and deactivated when the loads end. |

The defaults come from the constants `DefaultLoadTimeoutSeconds` (15) and
`DefaultLoadIndicatorDelaySeconds` (0.4). The timeout counts from the moment the layer's runner starts
the load, not from the call, so time a request spends waiting behind another one is not part of it.
The indicator shows only while a load is running on a layer that shields input, so a load on a
layer without that rule shows no indicator. The clock advances by at most 0.1 s per frame, so after a
long hitch or a suspension the timeout and the delay are later than wall-clock time.

A short timeout is a good way to see the failure path; a long one hides a stalled download. If a
load legitimately takes longer, raise the field or preload the view before it is needed.

---

## When a load fails

A load that fails ends the request as not shown with `RejectReason.LoadFailed`. The package logs
[UIDIRECTOR104](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector104) as an error, puts the exception message in
`Detail`, and routes the exception itself to the root's error handler
(`ViewErrorSource.Provider`), or to `Debug.LogException` when none is set. For the Addressables
provider the message always names the key: `Addressables failed to load '<key>'.` for a failed load,
and `The parent for '<key>' was destroyed ...` when the staging parent is gone.

Common causes: the prefab is not marked addressable or the address differs from the row's key, the
Addressables settings do not exist, or the content is not built or not reachable in the player.
A key that Addressables cannot resolve fails at once; a load that never finishes ends as
`LoadTimedOut` after the load timeout.

The code that opened the view reads the failure from the result. The sample reports the setup
step that is usually missing:

<!-- source: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/AddressablesBootstrap.cs -->
```csharp
var result = await navigator.ShowAsync(
    RemoteViews.Gallery,
    navigator.RootToken,
    new OpenOptions { Source = "boot" });

// A gallery that was shown and later closed is not a failure.
if (result.Rejected == RejectReason.None)
    return;

Debug.LogWarning(
    $"The gallery did not open ({result.Rejected}): {result.Detail}. " +
    "Mark Prefabs/Gallery and Prefabs/Photo as addressable, as the sample README describes, " +
    "and create the Addressables settings if the project has none.");
```

When the addresses are missing in the sample, the gallery's open ends as `NotShown` with `LoadFailed`,
the bootstrap logs one warning that starts with `The gallery did not open (LoadFailed): `, and the
navigator logs its own error with `UIDIRECTOR104`. Fix the addresses and press Play again.

For a popup that fails to open from a view, check `Rejected` the same way. The gallery sets the status
`Photo '<title>' did not open: <reason>.` when `Rejected` is not `None`. See
[Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md#reject-reasons).

---

## The validator's UIDIRECTOR124 warning

`Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs` checks every row that has an asset key and no prefab. With
Addressables installed it looks the key up in the project's Addressables settings. When no entry
has that address, GUID or label, it reports
[UIDIRECTOR124](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector124) as a warning. The check runs in the editor only,
never at run time, and a batch run does not fail on it. When the key matches an address or a GUID,
the validator also checks the prefab it finds like any other row; a key that matches a label is
accepted without a prefab check.

Fix it by marking the prefab addressable with that address, or by correcting the key. **Ignore it when
the key is valid for something the validator cannot see:**

- the root uses a provider of your own, whose keys are not Addressables keys;
- the key is served by content built outside this project, which its settings do not list.

With Addressables not installed, the same rows report
[UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120) as a warning: the key only loads when the root has a
provider of your own.

---

## Write a provider of your own

Implement `IViewProvider` and pass it in `ViewRootSetup.AssetProvider`. The package relies on this
contract:

1. **`AcquireAsync` returns an inactive instance under the inactive parent.** The instance must be
   a child of `inactiveParent`, so `Awake` and `OnEnable` have not run when the package injects
   and prepares it. Its root needs a `ViewHost` and a view component for the key's types
   ([UIDIRECTOR103](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector103), [UIDIRECTOR102](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector102)).
   Return nothing or throw to fail the load; both end the request as `LoadFailed`, and a thrown
   message becomes the `Detail`. An instance that is already destroyed when the package prepares it
   fails the request as `LoadFailed` too.
2. **Respect the token.** It is cancelled by the load timeout, by a withdrawn request, by an owner
   that ended and by a destroyed root. Stop waiting at once, complete with
   `OperationCanceledException`, and release whatever you loaded, also when the load completes
   later. If a result does arrive after the token was cancelled, the stage hands it back to
   `Release`.
3. **`Release` releases exactly what `AcquireAsync` returned, and decides what happens to the
   instance.** Destroy it, or return it to a pool. When the package lets go of a provider's instance, it
   deactivates the instance if it is still active, calls `Release`, and does nothing else to it, so a
   pooling provider always receives it inactive.
   `Release` must not throw, and it must be safe on a Unity object that was already destroyed, because
   an instance destroyed from outside is still released. Key your bookkeeping by instance id, not by a
   reference you test with `null`. Doing nothing for a null or an unknown instance is correct. An
   exception from `Release` does not stop the package: the instance still counts as released, and the
   exception is routed to the root's error handler as `ViewErrorSource.Provider` with the view id
   (or logged with `Debug.LogException` when no handler is set).
4. **`PreloadAsync` loads without instantiating and returns a lease.** The asset stays loaded until the
   lease is disposed. `Dispose` must be safe to call twice. Throw or return `null` to fail; the
   preload then returns `false`. A lease and the instances of the same key must not depend on each
   other's release order.
5. **Complete on the main thread.** The package does not switch threads after an await
   ([Threading](Threading.md)).
6. **Own your lifetime.** The root reads the provider once and never disposes it. Release what you
   still hold when the provider goes away, as the Addressables provider does in `OnDestroy`.

Every release the package makes goes through `Release`, which is why the table in
[What is released when](#what-is-released-when) names it so often.

No sample shows a custom provider; the contract above comes from the interface and from how the
stage and the Addressables provider use it.

---

## Traps

- **An asset key and no provider.** The open fails as `LoadFailed` with
  [UIDIRECTOR120](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector120). Add the component, pass a provider, or fill in the
  row's `Prefab`.
- **A component added after `Initialize`.** The root does not see it. Add it before the root initialises.
- **An address that differs from the key by a character.** Addresses are compared exactly. The
  validator warns with [UIDIRECTOR124](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector124); the player fails with
  [UIDIRECTOR104](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector104).
- **Content that is not built.** "Use Asset Database" hides the problem in the editor; a player build
  fails to load until the Addressables content is built.
- **Releasing an instance yourself.** Never destroy a provider's instance by hand or call
  `Addressables.ReleaseInstance` on it (it returns `false` for the Addressables provider's instances);
  the provider owns the handle and the package calls `Release`.
- **Expecting a lease to keep an instance.** A lease keeps the asset loaded, not a view instance;
  keeping an instance is `KeepInstance`.
- **Forgetting that Trim spares leases and requests in flight.** It frees idle kept instances only. Low memory does not end a preload lease; only its owner token does, so end that owner from your own `Application.lowMemory` handler (see [Keep and trim](#keep-and-trim)).
- **Expecting the timeout to apply to a preload.** It does not.

---

## See also

- [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md): rows, `Asset Key`, `Retention` and the validator
- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md): kept instances and the prefab structure
- [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md): the result of a failed load
- [Threading](Threading.md): a custom provider completes on the main thread
- [Limitations](Limitations.md): the timeouts and what the package does not do

---

<!-- file: Documentation~/Zenject.md -->

# Zenject

[Back to index](index.md)

This page connects a `ViewRoot` to a Zenject or Extenject container. After it, the container injects
every view instance the root creates, and `INavigator` and `ViewRoot` can be injected into your own
classes. It covers turning the integration on, the call that wires the root and its overload that takes a
`ViewRootSetup`, what the call does while Zenject validates a scene, when a view is injected, which container a root belongs to, how to
set up the SceneContext, and where the EventSystem comes from.

The integration adds one class and no new concepts. Without it, the same job is one delegate,
`ViewRootSetup.Inject` ([Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md#initialize-with-viewrootsetup)).

The examples come from the Zenject Usage sample. Its catalog has a `scoreboard` screen and a
`reset-score` popup, and both receive a `ScoreService` from the container.

---

## Turn the integration on

The integration is its own assembly, `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection.Zenject`. Unity compiles
it only while the scripting define `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DI_ZENJECT` exists. How the define gets there
depends on how Zenject is installed:

- **Extenject as a package** (`com.svermeulen.extenject`, version 9.0.0 or newer, from UPM or
  OpenUPM): the assembly sets the define for itself. There is nothing to do.
- **Zenject copied under `Assets/`:** choose `Tools/UIDirector/Zenject Integration` once. The menu
  item adds the define to the Player Settings of every build target, and it is ticked while the
  integration is active. Commit the `ProjectSettings` change. Choosing it again removes the define.

The menu item refuses to turn the integration on when no assembly named `Zenject` exists in the
project, and says so. When Extenject is installed as a package at 9.0.0 or newer, it explains that
there is nothing to toggle.

If Zenject is removed while the define is still set, the integration assembly can no longer compile.
Turn the menu item off, or delete `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DI_ZENJECT` from the scripting define symbols
by hand.

Names and references:

- `NavigatorInstaller` is in the namespace `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection`.
- Code in an assembly definition references `Ecanakli.UIDirector`,
  `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection.Zenject` and `Zenject`.
- **Game code does not test the define.** With Extenject as a package, `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DI_ZENJECT`
  is set inside the integration's own assembly only, so an `#if ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DI_ZENJECT` in your
  code is false and would skip your installer. Use `NavigatorInstaller` directly: it is there whenever
  Extenject and the integration are installed.
- The integration assembly references the `Zenject` assembly and the precompiled `Zenject-usage.dll`
  by name, so the Zenject install must provide both.

---

## Wire the root in an installer

The whole integration is one static method with two overloads:

<!-- signature -->
```csharp
namespace Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection
{
    public static class NavigatorInstaller
    {
        public static void Install(DiContainer container, ViewRoot root);
        public static void Install(DiContainer container, ViewRoot root, ViewRootSetup setup);
    }
}
```

Call it from `InstallBindings` of an installer that holds a reference to the root. The installer is a
`MonoInstaller`, declared like this:

<!-- source: Samples~/ZenjectUsage/AppInstaller.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class AppInstaller : MonoInstaller
```

A Scene Context lists it under Mono Installers ([Set up the SceneContext](#set-up-the-scenecontext)).
This is the sample's installer, without the declaration:

<!-- source: Samples~/ZenjectUsage/AppInstaller.cs -->
```csharp
// "Initialize On Awake" must be off on this root: Install initializes it with the container as the injector, and throws otherwise.
[SerializeField] private ViewRoot _viewRoot;

public override void InstallBindings()
{
    // Before the root initialises, which warns when no EventSystem exists; never while validating.
    if (!Container.IsValidating)
        SampleEventSystem.EnsureExists();

    Container.Bind<ScoreService>().AsSingle();
    NavigatorInstaller.Install(Container, _viewRoot);
    Container.BindInterfacesTo<AppStart>().AsSingle();
}
```

What `Install` does, in order:

1. Binds the root: `ViewRoot` from the instance you passed, as a single.
2. Initializes the root with `ViewRootSetup { Inject = container.InjectGameObject }`. From now on every
   new view instance is injected by this container.
3. Binds `INavigator` to the navigator of that root, as a single.

After it, any class the container creates can take `INavigator` or `ViewRoot` in its constructor.

The two-argument overload passes an empty `ViewRootSetup`, so `ErrorHandler`, `ExtraLayers` and
`AssetProvider` keep their defaults: the root has the three default layers and logs errors itself. An
`IViewProvider` component on the root's object, such as the Addressables provider, is still found.

### Pass layers, an error handler or an asset provider

A project that needs a layer of its own, an error handler or an asset provider uses the overload that
takes a `ViewRootSetup`. Fill in `ExtraLayers`, `ErrorHandler` and `AssetProvider` as on
[Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md#initialize-with-viewrootsetup) and leave `Inject` null: the installer sets
`Inject` to the container itself. The same steps run, with your three members carried over, and the
`setup` object you pass is never changed, so one setup can be reused.

- A `setup` whose `Inject` is not null throws `ArgumentException`. The installer does not chain your
  delegate after the container's, because the order would be ambiguous.
- A null `setup` throws `ArgumentNullException`.

### Initialize On Awake must be off

`NavigatorInstaller.Install` initializes the root, and a root initializes once. Turn off `Initialize
On Awake` on the `ViewRoot` Inspector. If the root is already initialized when `Install` runs,
`Install` throws an `InvalidOperationException`. The message names the root and says what to do:

```text
The ViewRoot 'UIDirector Root' was initialised before NavigatorInstaller.Install ran, so its views
would not be injected. Turn off "Initialize On Awake" on it.
```

A root is initialized before `Install` when its own `Awake` ran first with the setting on, or when any
code read `ViewRoot.Navigator` first, because that read initializes the root with default settings.
Leaving the setting on makes the result depend on which `Awake` runs first. Keep it off.

`Install` also throws `ArgumentNullException` for a null container or a null root (and, in the
overload with a setup, for a null `setup`). Install each root once: a second `Install` for the same
root finds it initialized and throws.

### While the container validates

Zenject validates a scene without Play Mode and without constructing the bound classes. In that mode
`Install` binds `ViewRoot` and binds `INavigator` to a method that returns `root.Navigator`, and does
nothing else. The root stays uninitialized and nothing in the scene is created or changed. Because
Zenject never calls the method while validating, validation needs no running root.

The arguments are still checked: a null container, root or setup, and a setup with `Inject` set, throw
even while validating.

Anything else in `InstallBindings` that creates scene objects needs the same guard. That is why the
sample's installer creates the EventSystem only when `Container.IsValidating` is false.

---

## Open the first screen

Nothing opens a view by itself. `AppStart` is a plain class that the container creates and runs once
the container is built; it takes the navigator through its constructor:

<!-- source: Samples~/ZenjectUsage/AppStart.cs -->
```csharp
public sealed class AppStart : IInitializable
{
    private readonly INavigator _navigator;

    public AppStart(INavigator navigator)
    {
        _navigator = navigator;
    }

    public void Initialize()
    {
        // Owned by the root, so the scoreboard ends only when the root does.
        _navigator.Open(ZenjectViews.Scoreboard, _navigator.RootToken, new OpenOptions { Source = "boot" });
    }
}
```

The installer binds it with `BindInterfacesTo<AppStart>().AsSingle()`, so Zenject calls `Initialize`
after every installer has run. The owner is the root's token, as in the other samples: the screen
ends when the root does. See [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).

---

## Receive services in a view

A view is a `MonoBehaviour`, so it takes its services through an `[Inject]` method. The scoreboard
keeps the service in a field:

<!-- source: Samples~/ZenjectUsage/ScoreboardView.cs -->
```csharp
// Runs before Awake, while the new instance is still inactive; a kept instance is not injected again.
[Inject]
private void Construct(ScoreService scores)
{
    _scores = scores;
}
```

The reset popup does the same, and uses the service in `OnOpen`:

<!-- source: Samples~/ZenjectUsage/ResetScoreView.cs -->
```csharp
// Runs before Awake, while the new instance is still inactive.
[Inject]
private void Construct(ScoreService scores)
{
    _scores = scores;
}
```

When injection happens:

- **Every new instance is injected while it is inactive, before its `Awake` and `OnEnable`.** The
  package injects after the prefab is loaded and before it activates the instance, so `Awake`,
  `OnOpen` and every later callback see the injected fields.
- **The components on the instance's child objects are injected too,** before their own `Awake`.
- **A kept instance is injected once.** A catalog row with `KeepInstance` creates the instance on its
  first open and reuses it afterwards, and the reuse does not inject again. That is why
  `ScoreboardView` reads the score in `OnVisible` and not in the `[Inject]` method: the screen is
  kept, and the number changes between opens.
- **A released instance is a new instance.** A row that releases its view on close creates, and
  injects, a fresh instance on every open. `ResetScoreView` is such a popup.
- **A reopen in place does not inject.** It reuses the live instance
  ([Navigation and back](Navigation-and-Back.md#return-to-a-screen-that-is-already-open)).

If injection throws, for example because a service the view asks for has no binding, the open ends as
not shown with `RejectReason.LoadFailed`, logged as
[UIDIRECTOR104](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector104), and the exception goes to the root's error handler
with the source `ViewErrorSource.Inject`. The view is never shown half-injected. An instance that was
already destroyed when its turn to be injected came is skipped by injection and fails when the view is
resolved, as a `LoadFailed` with the source `Provider`.

---

## The root's scope

`Install` hands the root one container, and that container injects every view the root opens, from
whichever scene the call comes from. A view sees what that container sees: its bindings and those of
the containers above it.

- A root installed in a **SceneContext** sees the scene's bindings and the app-wide ones, because a
  scene container sits below the app-wide container.
- A root installed under an **app-wide context** (the ProjectContext) sees only app-wide bindings.
  A view opened from a scene cannot be injected with something that is bound only in that scene's
  context: with the root installed in the app-wide container, a view receives the app value and never
  the scene value.

Two ways out when a view needs something from a scene context:

- Use a scene-owned root, installed by that scene's installer, as the sample does.
- Keep the app-wide root and pass the data as the arguments of the open call: `ShowAsync(key, args,
  owner)` carries any value, and the view takes it in `OnOpen`. This also keeps the view free of the
  container.

Several roots can exist, each with its own container: every root injects through the container it
was installed in. The documented setup is one root per application ([Limitations](Limitations.md)).

A root keeps the container it was installed with for as long as it lives. Put a root that persists
across scenes under an app-wide context so the root and its container share a lifetime.

---

## Set up the SceneContext

The Zenject Usage sample ships a scene without a Scene Context, because Zenject's script GUIDs depend
on how Zenject was installed. Add it yourself, in the sample scene or in your own:

1. Make sure the integration is active (see above).
2. In the scene, have a root made with `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root`, with `Initialize On Awake`
   off and your catalogs assigned.
3. Create the installer object. In the sample it is an object named `Installers` that holds the
   `AppInstaller` component, with its `View Root` field pointing at the root.
4. Choose `GameObject > Zenject > Scene Context`.
5. Drag the `AppInstaller` component of the `Installers` object into the Scene Context's Mono
   Installers list.
6. Press Play. The scoreboard opens by itself. `Window > UIDirector` shows the stacks and the shield
   live.

The sample's scene has no EventSystem on purpose; the next section explains who creates it.

---

## The EventSystem

A root warns with [UIDIRECTOR116](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector116) when the scene has no EventSystem
at the moment it initializes, and a scene without one gives views no input. `Install` initializes the
root, so an EventSystem that the installer creates must exist before `Install` runs. The sample's
installer does it in the first lines of `InstallBindings`, behind `if (!Container.IsValidating)`:
validation must not create scene objects.

If your scene already has an EventSystem, none of that is needed. How the sample's `EnsureExists`
picks the input module is on [Input and platform](Input-and-Platform.md#give-the-ui-an-eventsystem).

---

## Traps

- **`Initialize On Awake` left on.** `Install` throws when the root was initialized first. Turn it
  off.
- **Reading `root.Navigator` before `Install`.** The read initializes the root with defaults and
  `Install` then throws. Take the navigator from the container.
- **A scene binding that a view cannot see.** The root belongs to the container it was installed in,
  not to the scene that opens the view. See [The root's scope](#the-roots-scope).
- **Creating scene objects in `InstallBindings` during validation.** Guard them with
  `Container.IsValidating`.
- **An EventSystem created after `Install`.** The root has already warned. Create it before.
- **Per-open data read in the `[Inject]` method of a kept view.** It runs once. Read it in `OnOpen` or
  `OnVisible`.
- **Missing binding in a view.** The open fails with
  [UIDIRECTOR104](Troubleshooting.md#uidirector104); the view does not appear.

## See also

- [Root canvas](Root-Canvas.md)

- [View authoring](View-Authoring.md)

- [Catalogs and keys](Catalogs-and-Keys.md)

<!-- file: Documentation~/API-Reference.md -->

# API reference

[Back to index](index.md)

Every public type of the package, with its namespace, its assembly and its public members. The guides
explain what the calls do and when to use them; this page is the list of names and shapes, written as
they are declared in the source. Each type has one line on what it is for, one block with its public
declarations and no bodies, and a link to the guide that teaches it.

The page covers 60 public types: 57 in the core assembly and one in each integration assembly. The
editor tools (the UIDirector window, Validate Catalogs, the integration menu items) are internal and
have no scripting API.

---

## How to read this page

- **Blocks show declarations, not bodies.** Attributes that tell the compiler or the Inspector
  something (`[Flags]`, `[RequireComponent]`, `[AttributeUsage]`) are kept; the `[SerializeField]`
  fields of the components are private and are not API. Their Inspector names are in the guides.
- **Caller-information parameters are declared on purpose and are never passed.** The methods that
  register work or open a view end with `[CallerMemberName] string member = null, [CallerLineNumber] int line = 0`.
  The compiler fills them in. `HoldInput` and `ViewQueue.Hold` show their call site (member and line)
  in UIDIRECTOR110 and UIDIRECTOR111, the UIDirector window and `Describe`; `ShowAsync` and `Open` put
  the calling member on the shield holders they take; `AddObserver`, `AddCatalog` and `PreloadAsync`
  take them for future use and do not show them in this version. The methods that have them are
  `ShowAsync`, `Open`, `HoldInput`, `AddObserver`, `AddCatalog` and `PreloadAsync` on `INavigator`, the
  `ShowAsync` and `Open` shortcuts in `NavigatorExtensions`, and `Hold` on `ViewQueue`.
- **Main thread.** Unless a line says otherwise, a member must be called on Unity's main thread. The
  calls that throw off the main thread, the calls that are posted to it, and the calls that are not
  checked at all are listed on [Threading](Threading.md). The ones that may be called from any thread
  are `ViewRegistration.Remove`, `INavigator.CloseAll`, `INavigator.Trim` and `ViewQueue.Clear`.
- **Nothing here throws for what happens to a view.** `ShowAsync` completes with a `ViewResult<TResult>`
  that says how the request ended, and `Open` returns a `ViewHandle`; a refusal, a failed load and an
  owner that ended are all data. What a member throws for a usage error is listed with the type. See
  [Opening and results](Opening-and-Results.md).
- **Diagnostic ids are not public constants.** A warning or an error in the console carries an id such
  as UIDIRECTOR101; the ids are listed under [Errors and diagnostics](#errors-and-diagnostics).

### Assemblies and namespaces

| Assembly | Compiled | Namespace of its public types |
|---|---|---|
| `Ecanakli.UIDirector` | Always | `Ecanakli.UIDirector` |
| `Ecanakli.UIDirector.Addressables` | When `com.unity.addressables` is installed (define `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_ADDRESSABLES`, set by the assembly) | `Ecanakli.UIDirector` |
| `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DOTween` | When DOTween is installed (`DOTWEEN`, or `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DOTWEEN` for a UPM package named `com.demigiant.dotween` or set by `Tools/UIDirector/DOTween Integration`) | `Ecanakli.UIDirector` |
| `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection.Zenject` | When `ECANAKLI_UIDIRECTOR_DI_ZENJECT` is defined: set by the assembly for Extenject 9.0.0+ as a package, or by `Tools/UIDirector/Zenject Integration` for Zenject under Assets/ | `Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection` |

One `using Ecanakli.UIDirector;` reaches everything that user code calls, including the Addressables
and DOTween types. An installer adds `using Ecanakli.UIDirector.DependencyInjection;`. How each
integration turns on is explained on [Assets and Addressables](Assets-and-Addressables.md#the-integration-turns-on-by-itself),
[DOTween](DOTween.md#turn-the-integration-on) and [Zenject](Zenject.md#turn-the-integration-on).

### Types from other libraries in the signatures

Snippets on these pages leave out their `using` lines; the sample files they are copied from under
`Samples~/` carry them in full. This table names the namespace of each outside type in the signatures
and of the ones the snippets use most.

| Type | Namespace | Library |
|---|---|---|
| `UniTask`, `UniTask<T>` | `Cysharp.Threading.Tasks` | UniTask |
| `CancellationToken` | `System.Threading` | .NET |
