<!-- signature -->
```csharp
public abstract class ViewTransition : MonoBehaviour
{
    public abstract UniTask PlayAsync(bool show, CancellationToken ct);
    public abstract void Snap(bool shown);
}
```

**The contract for a custom transition.**

- Use unscaled time. A transition on scaled time never finishes while `timeScale` is 0, and the
  watchdog snaps it after the transition timeout and reports `UIDIRECTOR106`.
- Start from the opposite end pose and stop when `ct` is cancelled. There is no "continue from the
  current pose" requirement, because the runner never interrupts a transition with another one
  ([ADR-002](Decisions/ADR-002-Strict-Serialization.md)).
- `Snap` is synchronous, idempotent and never throws. It writes the end pose. It must not complete the
  task of a play that is running from inside `Snap`: a play that `Snap` ends finishes one step later,
  because the runner would otherwise resume inside `Snap` and carry on as if the play had ended
  normally. The same holds for a play ended from a destroy or disable message.
- Do not call the navigator.

**The sequence.** Before the first show the runner calls `Snap(false)`, moves the request to `Opening`, runs the first
projection pass and plays the show. Before a hide it plays the hide. On a terminate cause or a watchdog it cancels `ct` and calls
`Snap` with the target pose if the instance survives. A transition that throws, in `PlayAsync` or in
`Snap`, is routed as `ViewErrorSource.Transition` with the view id, and a failed play is then
snapped. The stage does not swallow a `Snap` exception: the caller that holds the request routes it.

**Built-ins** (`FadeTransition`, `ScaleTransition`, `SlideTransition`) need no tween library. They run
on one internal loop, `UnscaledAnimation`: it waits one frame at a time, adds
`min(Time.unscaledDeltaTime, 1/30 s)` per frame so that a long frame does not make the animation
jump, checks its token after every frame so that no step runs after a cancel, and allocates nothing
per frame once warm. The clamp has a cost: below 30 fps a transition takes longer than its duration,
and the transition timeout, which counts on the navigator clock, can snap one that is still
animating. Defaults: 0.25 s, show `OutCubic` (`OutBack` for scale), hide `InCubic`. Easing is a
serialized internal enum with no public easing API. Sizes come from the layer rect in canvas units,
not from `Screen.width`. The backdrop's fade uses the same loop.

**`TweenTransition`** (the DOTween assembly) builds one `Sequence` of `DOTween.To` tweens per play from
serialized fade, scale and offset settings. It uses only the core DOTween library, because the module
extension methods live in assemblies a package cannot reference. It sets its own ease, auto-kill and
unscaled update explicitly, so project-wide DOTween defaults cannot compound the ease or stop the kill
callback from firing. The await ends in the tween's own kill callback, bridged by an internal
`TweenAwaiter`; a cancelled token kills the tween with `Kill(false)` and ends the await at once, even
when DOTween defers the kill inside its own update. The reference is dropped inside the callback, so a
recycled tween is never touched. A kill that the component makes itself, from `Snap`, from a newer
play or from `OnDestroy`, resumes the caller on the next player-loop step instead of inside that
call or inside Unity's destroy message. See [Transitions](../Transitions.md) and
the DOTween page for usage.

---

## 16. Editor tooling

The editor assembly is internal and compiles in the editor only. It reads state through structured
read-outs and never parses text.

**Read-outs.** `Navigator.CaptureState` fills a reused `NavigatorState`: layers (id, order, rules,
whether a runner is active, pending operations) with their requests (id, view, phase, slot, close
pending, latched outcome, priority, source, whether an owner is bound), shield holders (kind, request,
reason, age, call site), kept and preloaded view ids, and counts. `ViewQueue.CaptureState` does the
same for a queue: name, layer, held and holds, gates, the presenting item and the waiting items in
presentation order. Warm captures allocate nothing. The event ring of [section 10](#10-events-and-the-order-at-close)
is the third source.

**`Window > UIDirector`.** A UI Toolkit window (`CreateGUI`). A plain `UIDirectorWindowModel` holds
everything the window shows; the view updates rows in place four times a second in Play Mode and
keeps foldout states. A dropdown picks the root. The page shows a status line
(settled or busy, with the shield count), one foldout per layer with its requests, shield holders,
queues, kept instances, preload leases and the last 100 events newest first. "Copy state" puts the
navigator's text trace on the clipboard and "?" opens the documentation for the installed version.

**Validator.** `Tools > UIDirector > Validate Catalogs` checks every `ViewCatalog` in the project and
every static class marked `[ViewKeys]`. It logs one line per finding, with the id first and a link to
its Troubleshooting section, then a summary. The same checks run in the catalog's inspector, which has
a Validate button. `CatalogValidation.RunFromCommandLine` is the batch-mode entry point for
`-executeMethod`: it exits with code 1 when any error exists and 0 otherwise; warnings never fail a
run.

| Id | Severity | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| `UIDIRECTOR101` | Error | A key field in a `[ViewKeys]` class has no catalog row |
| `UIDIRECTOR102` | Error | The row's prefab root has no component implementing `IView<TArgs, TResult>` for the key |
| `UIDIRECTOR103` | Error | The row's prefab root has no `ViewHost` |
| `UIDIRECTOR108` | Error | Two rows share an id; the first wins |
| `UIDIRECTOR109` | Error | A row names a layer that does not exist |
| `UIDIRECTOR120` | Warning | A row has an asset key but Addressables is not installed |
| `UIDIRECTOR121` | Error | A row has neither a prefab nor an asset key |
| `UIDIRECTOR122` | Warning | `BackPolicy.Close` on a layer that does not take back |
| `UIDIRECTOR123` | Warning | The prefab contains a dropdown |
| `UIDIRECTOR124` | Warning | The asset key matches no Addressables address, GUID or label |
| `UIDIRECTOR125` | Error | A row has an empty id |

The root also reports `UIDIRECTOR125` at run time when a catalog is registered, and refuses the row.
Test assemblies are skipped when keys are collected. The validator is pure and deterministic: catalogs
in the given order, rows in order, then keys by type name and field name.

**Create menus.**

- `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root` creates, in the active scene, a canvas (screen space overlay)
  with a `CanvasScaler`, a `ViewRoot` and a `BackInput`, and an `EventSystem` if the scene has none.
  The root is built inactive and activated last, so `Awake` sees the final render mode and camera.
- `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root (Camera)` creates a scene-root `UIDirector` object that holds the
  root and a sibling `UI Camera` that draws the UI layer only. They are siblings because a
  camera-mode canvas that is a child of its own camera is not drawn. View prefabs must be on the UI
  layer, or the camera culls them.
- `Tools > UIDirector > Create Prefab UI Environment` writes a scene holding a canvas and scaler,
  copied from the selected root, for Prefab Mode. A view prefab whose root is a nested canvas has no
  scaler of its own and would otherwise open at the wrong size. The first root creation of an editor
  session offers it once, never in batch mode, and never saves the user's open scene.
- `Tools > UIDirector > DOTween Integration` and `Zenject Integration` toggle the scripting define
  that enables the optional assembly, on every build target.
- `Assets > Create > UIDirector/View Catalog` creates a `ViewCatalog`; `Tools > UIDirector >
  Documentation` opens the docs for the installed version.

---

## 17. Threading

The package is main-thread only. One internal seam, `IMainThread`, answers "am I on the main thread"
and "run this there"; the real implementation uses UniTask's main thread id and `UniTask.Post`.

| Call off the main thread | Result |
|---|---|
| `Open`, `ShowAsync`, `HoldInput`, `AddObserver`, `AddCatalog`, `PreloadAsync` | Throws `InvalidOperationException` at the call, and changes nothing |
| `ViewQueue.Enqueue`, `EnqueueAsync`, `Hold`, `AddGate`, `AddObserver` | Throws `InvalidOperationException`, also after the queue's lifetime ended |
| `Back`, `CloseTo` | Returns `false` |
| `CloseAll`, `Trim`, `ViewQueue.Clear` | Posted to the main thread |
| `ViewRegistration.Remove()` | Posted to the main thread |

After teardown nothing throws. **Owner cancellation** is the one place that foreign threads reach in:
a `CancellationToken` can be cancelled from a timer or a worker thread. The callbacks are registered
without capturing the execution context, and when one arrives off the main thread the package posts the
handling to the main thread and logs `UIDIRECTOR113`. The request, the registration, the queued item or
the queue (its lifetime token or the root token) then ends on the main thread, in the normal way. A cancellation that arrives after
the request ended posts nothing. See [Threading](../Threading.md) for the user-facing rules.

---

## 18. Allocation and idle cost

**Idle.** An idle root costs one call per frame and nothing else:

- `ViewRoot.Update` ticks the navigator clock. It allocates 0 B, and the clock keeps a timer list that
  is empty unless a watchdog, the load indicator, an input-hold warning or a queue-hold warning is pending.
- `BackInput` reads the back key, 0 B.
- The safe area and screen size are compared once per frame, only while a `SafeAreaFitter` is
  registered with the root; with none registered the comparison does not run.
- An idle backdrop runs no animation, an idle queue runs no timer, and nothing is scheduled per frame
  by the queue. A queue hold adds one timer for its 60 s warning: on the navigator clock when the
  queue is on the package's own navigator, which costs nothing per frame. A queue on any other
  `INavigator` waits for that warning with a UniTask delay, which polls once per frame for the first
  60 s of the hold.
- Each view carries a nested canvas and a graphic raycaster; the shield is one always-active graphic
  with an empty mesh.

**Queries.** `Back()` with nothing to do, `IsOpen`, `IsBusy` and `IsLayerClear` allocate nothing once
warm. A frame of a running built-in transition allocates nothing once warm. The editor read-outs
allocate nothing on a warm capture.

**Per open.** Opening is not a hot path, and the package does not claim zero allocation for it. An open
allocates a record with two awaiter lists, a handle, a context, an open scope (its token source is
created lazily), a visible scope per on-screen span, a cancellation source for each load or transition
step, and a completion source for each awaiter. The delegates that the terminator, the outbox and the
queue use are cached. Instance reuse is `KeepInstance`.

**Cover and reveal.** One hierarchy walk per cover and per reveal, into reused lists. `DisableCanvas`
is the default because reveal is the most frequent transition and `SetActive` rebuilds exactly there.

**Struct arguments.** Generic code over struct `TArgs` and `TResult` is instantiated once per
combination under IL2CPP, which costs code size. Small structs or classes keep that low.

---

## 19. Responsibility table

Public types are marked (P). Everything else is internal.

| Class | Owns | Does | Does not know |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Navigator` | Composition of the pieces | The `INavigator` facade: thread and root checks, delegation, registrations, teardown | Canvases, tweens, queues |
| `RequestIntake` | The request id counter | The acceptance checks in order, including the refusal of a queued row on another layer; creates records; registers owner callbacks | Unity objects |
| `ViewRegistry` | Rows by id; the root's layers | Lookup; refuses duplicate ids and unknown layers | Instances |
| `ViewRecord`, `ViewRecord<TArgs, TResult>` | One request: phase, row, owner registration, latched outcome, awaiters, scopes, instance | Holds state; completes awaiters | How anything is displayed |
| `LayerState` | The ordered records and the operation FIFO of one layer; slot numbers | Add, remove, order | Other layers |
| `LayerRunner` | The running step and its cancellation source | Executes operations through the stage; the watchdogs | Back and queueing decisions |
| `Projection` | Nothing (pure) | Hidden, interactive, order and backdrop placement from lists and phases | Unity types |
| `Terminator` | Nothing between calls | The one synchronous routine that ends a request | Loading |
| `Outbox` | Pending notifications | Runs them one at a time, isolated, in the defined order; holds events and notifications back while an observer dispatch is in progress | What a notification means |
| `InputShield` | The holder list | Raise and drop; the long-hold diagnostic | Views |
| `BackResolver` | Nothing (pure) | One back decision from a snapshot | Input devices |
| `RetainedInstances` | One idle instance per id | Stash, take, drop, trim | Why a view closed |
| `PreloadLeases` | Leases by owner | Acquire through the stage; dispose on owner end | Instances |
| `ObserverList`, `ErrorRouter`, `Diagnostics` | Observers; the handler; stable ids | Isolated dispatch; routes exceptions; logs diagnostics in the editor and development builds | Game types |
| `ViewScope` (P) | A token source and entries | Bind, subscribe, add, run; ends exactly once | The view it belongs to |
| `ViewContext<TResult>` (P) | A record reference | Complete, close, decline | Other requests |
| `IViewStage`, `UguiStage` | Layer rects, shield, backdrops, staging | What the logic needs from Unity; the uGUI implementation; routes the release of a late load result | Why something is shown |
| `ViewRoot` (P) | Serialized settings; the navigator | Initialise; tick the clock; forward destruction, low memory and safe-area changes | Navigation rules |
| `ViewHost` (P) | The view's presentation state and its handle | Reports loss; Inspector `Close()` | Layers and stacks |
| `QuitSignal` | The process-wide quitting flag | One `Application.quitting` subscription, renewed at subsystem registration | Views and roots |
| `Backdrop`, `ShieldGraphic` | A fade; a flag | Forward a tap; an empty-mesh raycast target | Counts and policies |
| `ViewTransition` and built-ins (P) | Serialized animation settings | Play, snap | The navigator |
| `BackInput`, `ViewButton`, `SafeAreaFitter` (P) | Nothing, a serialized action, edge flags | Back key; Inspector actions; fit a rect | The stack |
| `ViewQueue` (P) with `HoldSet`, `GateChain`, `QueueItem` | Waiting items, holds, gates | Pump; present through `INavigator` only | Layer contents |
| `AddressablesViewProvider` (P) | A handle per instance; preload leases | Instantiate, release, preload | Navigation |
| `TweenTransition` (P) | Tween settings | Play and kill a tween | Navigation |
| `NavigatorInstaller` (P) | Nothing | Bind and initialise through a Zenject container | Views |

---

## 20. Limits

Known limits of 0.1.0, as the code stands:

- The shield does not cover canvases sorted above it, including an open dropdown list and any
  interface the package does not own with a higher order ([section 7](#7-the-input-shield)).
- A kept instance is one idle instance per id, with no budget. A deep stack of heavy screens stays
  resident. `CloseTo` and return-to-existing keep stacks shallow.
- A cancelled `WaitForCloseAsync` waiter stays in the record's list until the request ends.
- An item that the navigator ended without showing is not retried by the queue.
- A queue on an `INavigator` other than the package's own is invisible to the editor tools, does not
  check its layer at construction, and waits for its hold warning with a delay that polls once per
  frame for the first 60 s of a hold ([section 18](#18-allocation-and-idle-cost)).
- A root destroyed from inside an observer callback removes the observers before the held-back
  terminal events drain, so observers and the event ring miss those events; awaiters still complete
  ([section 2](#2-the-root-and-its-layers)).
- A request whose owner token is the open scope of a screen that a reopen in place or a return
  replaces or pops ends with that screen ([Reopen in place](#reopen-in-place)).
- Unity 6000.0 or newer is required.

See [Limitations](../Limitations.md) for the user-facing list.

## See also

- [Concepts](../Concepts.md)
- [Performance](../Performance.md)
- [Threading](../Threading.md)
- [Diagnostics](../Diagnostics.md)
- [Troubleshooting](../Troubleshooting.md)

<!-- file: Documentation~/Design/Decisions/ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md -->

# ADR-001: Outcomes as data

- **Status:** Accepted, implemented in 0.1.0
- **Related:** [Architecture section 4](../Architecture.md#4-requests-and-phases),
  [Architecture section 11](../Architecture.md#11-exactly-once-outcomes),
  [ADR-005](ADR-005-Token-Owners.md), [Opening and results](../../Opening-and-Results.md),
  [Events and analytics](../../Events-and-Analytics.md)

## Context

Code that opens a view usually wants one thing back: how it ended, and the value if there was one.
The set of ways a view can end is large:

- the view closed itself with a value, or without one;
- the back key, a tap on the backdrop or a close call from code closed it;
- a screen change replaced it;
- the owner of the request ended;
- the instance was destroyed or deactivated from outside, or the root was destroyed;
- it never appeared: unknown id, a duplicate, a busy navigator, a gate that denied it, a failed or
  slow load, an `OnOpen` that declined or threw.

An API that reports some of these as a return value and the rest as exceptions makes every call site
a small decision tree. The exception route also has a worse problem. When the owner of a request
ends, a design that throws `OperationCanceledException` into the awaiting code assumes that the
awaiting code *is* the owner. It often is not: a flow that lives for the whole app can await a view
that is owned by one screen. When that screen goes away, the exception would unwind the app-wide
flow, and an `async` method that ends with a cancellation exception disappears without a message.

There is a second constraint from the async library the package is built on. A UniTask that is backed
by a pooled source can be awaited once. A handle that is a struct copy of an awaitable, passed around
and awaited twice or late, has undefined behaviour.

## Decision

**`ShowAsync` completes with a `ViewResult<TResult>` in every case. Outcomes are data.**

- The result carries `RequestId`, `WasShown`, `Reason` (a `CloseReason`), `Rejected` (a
  `RejectReason`), `Detail`, `HasValue` and `Value`. A request that never reached the screen reports
  `CloseReason.NotShown` and a `RejectReason` that says why. A shown view reports the `CloseReason` that
  ended it and `RejectReason.None`.
- `HasValue` is true only when the view was shown and closed with `Complete(value)`. `Value` is the
  default value otherwise. `TryGetValue` returns `HasValue`.
- The task does not fail for anything that happens to the view: the owner ending, the root being
  destroyed, a rejection, an exception inside `OnOpen`. `QueueItem` follows the same rule, so
  `ViewQueue.EnqueueAsync` completes with data also for an item that ended inside the queue.
- **The only exceptions are usage errors,** raised synchronously at the call: a call off the main
  thread, a null argument, an empty id in `ViewKey`. They are programming mistakes and never depend on
  what happens to a view later.
- **The owner token decides the life of the view and never cancels an awaiter.** When the owner
  ends, every awaiter completes with `OwnerEnded` as data, whether or not the awaiting code is the
  owner.
- **An awaiter is cancelled only by its own token.** `ViewHandle.WaitForCloseAsync(waiter)` throws
  `OperationCanceledException` for that waiter when `waiter` is cancelled, and leaves the view
  untouched. For the typed form the caller attaches a token to the task with UniTask's
  `AttachExternalCancellation`.
- **Handles are not awaitable.** `ViewHandle` is a read-only struct over the request record with
  `Phase`, `IsAlive`, `Close()`, `WaitForCloseAsync` and `TryGetInstance`. Every `ShowAsync` and
  `WaitForCloseAsync` call gets its own completion source, and records are never pooled, so a late or
  second wait returns the stored outcome at once.
- **Observers see the same facts untyped.** `ViewClosed` and the `Closed` and `NotShown` events carry
  `WasShown`, `Reason`, `Rejected` and `Detail`, with no arguments and no value.
- **Fakes need no test assembly.** `ViewResult.Completed`, `ViewResult.Closed` and
  `ViewResult.NotShown` are public factories, so a game can fake an `INavigator` without the package
  shipping a testing assembly.

A request ends exactly once and its awaiters complete exactly once. The first close cause is latched;
later causes, including the owner ending after a close was latched, do not change the outcome.

*Amendment, 2026-10-08:* the factories refuse combinations that are not outcomes. `ViewResult.Closed`
throws `ArgumentException` for `CloseReason.NotShown`, and `ViewResult.NotShown` throws it for
`RejectReason.None`. `Closed(CloseReason.Completed)` stays allowed: it is what a `ShowAsync` joined
with other argument or result types returns, a completion with `HasValue` false. `default(ViewResult<T>)`
is not an outcome the navigator returns. `RejectReason` gained `WrongLayer`, appended after `RootGone`. On
the package's navigator, a queued item whose row is on another layer than the queue's ends as `NotShown / WrongLayer`
(`UIDIRECTOR126`), also as data.

## Consequences

**Positive**

- A call site has one shape: await, then switch on `Reason` or check `HasValue`. There is no
  `try/catch` around an open to be forgotten, and no path on which the awaiting code stops without a
  trace.
- A flow that awaits a view owned by something else survives the owner ending and learns it from
  `OwnerEnded`.
- Analytics and the awaiter agree. Both read the same latched outcome, so the `Closed` event and the
  `ViewResult` never disagree about why a view ended.
- A late `await`, a second `await` and a join of a view that is already open are all well defined.
- A request that ends before it was shown, in any phase, still completes its awaiters, also during
  root teardown.

**Negative / accepted costs**

- **A caller can forget to look.** Code that ignores `WasShown` and `HasValue` treats a rejected open
  like a dismissal. The type makes the check easy, and it cannot force it.
- **No cancellation-driven control flow.** An awaiter that wants to stop waiting cannot cancel a
  `ShowAsync` call; it uses its own token on the wait, and the view lives on. To end the view, the
  caller closes it through its handle or cancels the owner.
- **A result is a message in memory.** It is not delivered if the process dies and an awaiter can be
  abandoned. A one-time side effect (a payment, a reward) must be performed by a service that persists
  it and is safe to repeat, and not by the awaiting continuation alone. The package offers no
  exactly-once delivery.
- **A joined request that was opened with other argument types shares the outcome but not the
  value.** `HasValue` is false for such a join.

**Enforced by tests**

- `AwaiterContractTests`: every close path completes `ShowAsync` exactly once with the reason as data;
  the owner ending succeeds and is never cancelled; many `WaitForCloseAsync` callers get one outcome;
  a cancelled waiter throws only for itself; late waits return the stored outcome; teardown completes
  every awaiter in every phase.
- `EventContractTests` and `CloseOrderContractTests`: the events and the awaiters agree and arrive in
  the defined order.
- `LifecycleTerminateTests`: a latched outcome survives a later terminate cause.
- `RandomInvariantTests`: a seeded random run checks after every step that every awaiter completed
  exactly once and that the event sequence per request id is one of the allowed shapes.

## Alternatives considered

### Throw `OperationCanceledException` when the owner ends

Rejected. It is the usual shape for cancellation, and it silently assumes the awaiter is the owner.
An app-wide flow that awaits a view owned by a screen would end without a message when that screen
goes away. Data is also easier to switch on than a catch block, and the distinction between "the
view ended because its owner ended" and "I stopped waiting" stays visible.

### An awaitable struct handle

Rejected. A UniTask-based handle that is copied, stored and awaited twice or late is undefined. The
package returns a task from `ShowAsync`, gives every call its own completion source, and keeps the
handle as an inert reference for `Close`, `Phase` and `WaitForCloseAsync`.

### One exception type per rejection reason

Rejected. A caller would catch a list of types for one operation, and a successful close with no value
would still need a second path. Reasons are enum values on one struct, which also flow unchanged into
events.

### A value-only return that is the default when the view did not complete

Rejected. It loses the reason, so a dismissal, a back press, a withdrawal and a rejected open all look
alike. The reason is what analytics and flow control need.

## See also

- [Architecture](../Architecture.md)
- [Opening and results](../../Opening-and-Results.md)
- [Events and analytics](../../Events-and-Analytics.md)
- [Concepts](../../Concepts.md)

<!-- file: Documentation~/Design/Decisions/ADR-002-Strict-Serialization.md -->

# ADR-002: Strict serialization

- **Status:** Accepted, implemented in 0.1.0
- **Related:** [Architecture section 5](../Architecture.md#5-the-per-layer-runner),
  [Architecture section 15](../Architecture.md#15-transitions),
  [ADR-001](ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md), [Transitions](../../Transitions.md),
  [Navigation and back](../../Navigation-and-Back.md), [Limitations](../../Limitations.md)

## Context

A view's life is a sequence of steps that take time: load, show transition, hide transition. The
requests that move a layer arrive from many places and not in a convenient order. A close arrives while
the view is still opening. Two opens arrive in the same frame. A pop-to arrives behind an open that has
not loaded yet.

The common answer is to let a new request interrupt the running one: stop the show transition where
it is and start the hide from the current pose. That answer has costs that show up late.

- Every transition must be written to start from any pose and to handle being superseded at any
  frame. A custom transition that does not is a bug that only shows when two requests collide.
- State is observable in between: a view that is half shown, a backdrop that has moved, a shield that
  was released by the superseded request and not yet taken by the new one.
- Most of the paths that create the overlap are not reachable by a person. The shield is raised when a
  request is accepted, so a user cannot tap into the middle of a transition. The overlap comes from
  code, and code can wait.

## Decision

**Each layer has one FIFO of operations and one runner. One operation runs at a time. A started step
is never interrupted.**

- The operations are open, close, pop-to and close-all. Every request that changes a layer becomes an
  operation on that layer's list. A close that is latched while the view is `Opening` runs after the
  open finishes.
- **Layers are independent.** Runners of different layers run concurrently, and the input shield count
  covers all of them. State that crosses layers is derived, not held: after every change the
  projection recomputes hidden, interactive and sort order for all layers
  ([section 6](../Architecture.md#6-projection)).
- **Two things cut a step short: a terminate cause and a watchdog.** A terminate cause is the owner
  token ending, the instance being lost from outside, or the root being destroyed. The terminator
  cancels the running step, snaps the view to its end pose, and finalizes the request at once. A
  watchdog is a timeout on a step.
- **Both snap.** A snap writes the end pose synchronously, so no step ever leaves a half-shown view
  behind. After a cut step the runner waits for the end routine to finish before it dequeues the next
  operation, so the next operation never runs inside it.
- **Every wait is bounded.** The load step has a timeout (default 15 s, `UIDIRECTOR105`). A show or
  hide transition has a timeout (default 3 s). On a transition timeout the package cancels the step,
  snaps and reports `UIDIRECTOR106`, then continues as if the transition had finished. Both timeouts
  are fields on the root. They count on the navigator clock, which `ViewRoot` advances by
  `min(Time.unscaledDeltaTime, 0.1 s)` per frame, so they run at `timeScale == 0` and a suspension adds
  at most one step.
- **The shield is released in a `finally`.** A faulted operation routes its exception, ends its
  request as not shown, releases its shield holder and lets the loop continue.
- **Immediate opens are accepted and serialized.** A burst of opens on one layer is shown in the order
  it was called. A layer accepts at most a waiting cap of requests in `Waiting` (default 4); the next
  one ends as `NotShown / Busy` with `UIDIRECTOR112`. `OpenOptions.RejectWhenBusy` is the per-call
  opt-in for tap handlers that must not stack.
- **A transition starts from the opposite end pose.** Because it is never interrupted, a transition has
  no "start from the current pose" obligation. `ViewTransition` asks for unscaled time, a stop on
  cancellation, and a synchronous, idempotent, non-throwing `Snap`.

## Consequences

**Positive**

- The superseded-transition bug class does not exist. At each step boundary the state is consistent,
  which is where the projection runs.
- A custom transition is simple: play from one pose to the other, stop when asked. A shared check
  (`TransitionConformance` in the tests) verifies the built-ins and `TweenTransition` against the same
  contract.
- One writer per layer. The list, the slots and the shield holders of a layer are only changed by its
  runner and by the terminator, and the two never overlap.
- A stall has a ceiling. A hung load, a transition on scaled time and a provider that never answers all
  end at a timeout, with a diagnostic that names the view.

**Negative / accepted costs**

- **Latency.** A close requested during a 0.25 s open waits for the open. Opens behind a slow load wait
  for the load. The input shield, the load indicator and back withdrawing a pending open are the
  mitigations, and the load timeout is the ceiling.
- **A custom transition on scaled time costs the whole transition timeout** on every play while the
  game is paused, before it is snapped.
- **At very low frame rates the two clamps differ.** The navigator clock advances at most 0.1 s per
  frame and the built-in animation loop at most 1/30 s per frame. Below 30 frames per second a built-in
  transition therefore takes longer than its duration. Timeouts are in clock seconds, so at 10 frames per
  second or fewer a built-in transition takes up to three times its duration on the clock, and one longer
  than a third of the transition timeout (1 s with the default 3 s) is snapped with `UIDIRECTOR106`.
- **The defaults are fields on the root.** The 15 s load timeout, the 3 s transition timeout, the 0.4 s
  load indicator delay and the waiting cap of 4 are set on `ViewRoot` and can be changed per project.
- **The queue and immediate opens can still meet.** Serialization is per layer; the queue handles
  cross-feature order ([ADR-004](ADR-004-Queue-Above-The-Navigator.md)).

**Enforced by tests**

- `LifecycleSerializationTests`: a close during `Opening` runs after the open; two and three opens on
  one layer run in call order while the first loads and while its transition runs; opens on different
  layers run concurrently; `CloseAll` withdraws waiting requests at call time.
- `LifecycleTerminateTests`: a terminate cause cuts the step, snaps before it finalizes and lets the
  next request run.
- `BuiltInTransitionTests` and the shared `TransitionConformance` check: every transition meets the
  contract.
- `RandomInvariantTests`: at most one operation runs per layer and a record has at most one running
  step, after every step of a seeded random run.

## Alternatives considered

### Interruptible transitions from the current pose

Rejected. The strongest alternative, and the common one. It puts a contract on every custom transition
(start from any pose, handle supersession at any frame) in exchange for a path that user input cannot
reach, because the shield is up from acceptance. The cost lands on every author of a transition; the
benefit is a shorter wait in a code-driven collision.

### A global lock across layers

Rejected. A popup that opens while a screen loads would wait for the screen, and the screen would
wait for the popup's load. Layers do not share list state, so they do not need to share a lock.

### Reject requests while busy by default

Rejected as the default. A tap handler that must not stack can ask for it per call with
`RejectWhenBusy`. As a global default it would drop opens that code issued in sequence on purpose,
for example a close followed by an open on the same frame. Accepting and serializing keeps calls
ordered, and the waiting cap bounds a runaway burst.

### Debounce at the call site

Rejected. It would hide a design problem in the caller and still need the layer to be consistent for
the calls that do get through.

## See also

- [Transitions](../../Transitions.md)
- [Navigation and back](../../Navigation-and-Back.md)
- [Architecture](../Architecture.md)
- [Troubleshooting](../../Troubleshooting.md)

<!-- file: Documentation~/Design/Decisions/ADR-003-Begin-Only-Hooks-And-Scopes.md -->

# ADR-003: Begin-only hooks and scopes

- **Status:** Accepted, implemented in 0.1.0
- **Related:** [Architecture section 8](../Architecture.md#8-back-resolution),
  [Architecture section 9](../Architecture.md#9-scopes),
  [ADR-005](ADR-005-Token-Owners.md), [View authoring](../../View-Authoring.md),
  [Navigation and back](../../Navigation-and-Back.md)

## Context

A view needs setup when it opens and cleanup when it ends. The usual shape is a pair of hooks:
`OnShow` and `OnHide`, with a subscription in the first and its removal in the second. Every such pair
is a line that someone has to remember to write, and nothing complains when the second half is
missing. A handler that stays subscribed to a long-lived publisher fires on a view that is gone, or
fires once per time the view was opened.

A "guaranteed close hook" does not fix this, because it cannot be guaranteed. A view's component can
be destroyed from outside before any hook runs. The owner of the request can end while the view is
shown. The root can be destroyed during a scene unload. In each case user code in the hook runs when
the objects it needs may already be gone, in an order that nobody chose.

There is also a span between "open" and "closed". A view that a fullscreen screen covers stays open,
and its animators, timers and listeners should stop and then start again when it is revealed. A single
open-to-close span does not describe that.

## Decision

**A view gets hooks that only begin something. Everything that has to end is registered on a scope
that the package ends.**

- **The hooks** are separate one-method interfaces on the view component:
  `IView<TArgs, TResult>.OnOpen(args, context)` (required), `IViewVisible.OnVisible(scope)` (optional)
  and `IViewBack.OnBack()` (optional, asked only for rows with `BackPolicy.HandledByView`). There is no
  `OnClose`, `OnHide` or `OnCovered`. `ViewBehaviour<TArgs, TResult>` is optional sugar over the same
  interfaces; a view can implement them directly.
- **The scopes.** The **open scope** is handed to `OnOpen` and ends when the request ends. A **visible
  scope** is handed to `OnVisible` for each span on screen and ends when the view is covered or the
  request ends. Per-open work (long-lived listening) goes on the open scope; per-span work (an
  animator, a timer) goes on the visible scope.
- **What a scope does.** `Bind` adds a listener to a `UnityEvent` now and removes it at the end.
  `Subscribe(add, remove, handler)` does the same for any event. `Add(IDisposable)`, `OnEnd` and
  `OnEnd<TState>` register cleanup. `Run` starts a task on the scope's token, swallows cancellation
  and routes any other exception. The registration call takes its cleanup in the same call, so there
  is no removal line to write.
- **Exactly once, on every path.** A scope's end routine runs once: the token is cancelled first, then
  the entries run newest first, each isolated so that a throw is routed and the rest still run. It runs
  when the view closes, when it was withdrawn before it was shown, when `OnOpen` declined or threw,
  when the owner ended, when the instance was lost from outside and when the root was destroyed. It
  never depends on the view component being alive.
- **Single-use and inert afterwards.** A registration on an ended scope is cleaned up at once: the
  listener is not added, the disposable is disposed, the action runs, the task does not start.
  `ViewContext.Open` after the end returns the ended scope, never `null`. A stale reference is
  harmless.
- **The package owns the scope.** User code cannot end or restart it.
- **Closing is not vetoed.** A code close (`ViewHandle.Close`, `CloseTo`, `CloseAll`), the owner
  ending and a loss from outside always take effect. Back is the one request that a view may answer:
  a row's `BackPolicy` (`LayerDefault`, `Close`, `Ignore`, `HandledByView`) and the optional
  `IViewBack.OnBack()`. A hook that returns `false` or throws lets the package close the view.
- **A minimal scope of the package's own.** `ViewScope` is small and single-use. The package does not
  depend on a general lifetime library to provide it.

## Consequences

**Positive**

- A forgotten removal line cannot exist. Cleanup is part of the call that registers the work.
- Cleanup does not need the view to be alive. It runs for a destroyed component, an ended owner and a
  torn-down root, because the package runs it, not the view.
- A covered view stops its per-span work and gets it back when revealed, without any code in the view
  that tracks being covered.
- A throwing cleanup cannot stop the others, and cannot stop the request from ending.

**Negative / accepted costs**

- **No code runs "when the view closes" except cleanup actions.** `OnEnd` actions run inside the
  terminate routine, where state is already consistent but the instance may be gone. They must not
  await and must not assume the view object is alive. Work that has to happen before the view goes
  away (saving a form) belongs before `Complete`.
- **Two scopes to learn.** Which work belongs on which scope is part of the guide.
- **A scope allocates.** An open has an open scope, and each span on screen has a visible scope. The
  token source of a scope is created lazily, so a scope that registers no task and reads no token
  creates none.
- **A view cannot veto a code close.** A project that wants a confirmation before closing asks for it
  in its own code before it calls `Close`, or uses `HandledByView` for the back key.
- **A scope cannot be used as a general lifetime** by user code: it cannot be ended by the user and it
  is not reusable.

**Enforced by tests**

- `ScopeContractTests`: bind, subscribe, add, end and run semantics, duplicates, an ended scope,
  ordering (token first, entries newest first), isolation of throwing cleanups and the errors that are
  routed.
- `ScopeOnNavigatorContractTests`: both scopes end exactly once on every close path, including a
  declined and a throwing `OnOpen`; the visible scope ends before the open scope and both end before
  the instance is released; a context stays readable after the end.
- `ReentrancyContractTests`: a navigator call from a hook or a cleanup is legal; `Complete` or `Close`
  inside `OnOpen` is latched and reported with `UIDIRECTOR118`.
- `NavigationBackTests`: `BackPolicy` and the `OnBack` hook.

## Alternatives considered

### Paired open and close hooks

Rejected. Each pair is a line that can be forgotten, and the second half cannot be guaranteed to run
on a destroyed component, during a root teardown or after the owner ended. A package that promises a
close hook promises something it cannot keep.

### A close veto: `CanClose(reason)`

Rejected. The strongest alternative to the back policy. An unscoped veto lets a view survive a code
close with its services already gone. A policy enum plus `IViewBack` covers the real need (the back
key may mean something to a view) and leaves every other close unconditional.

### A mandatory base class

Rejected. A view that has to derive from a package class cannot derive from the project's own. The
hooks are interfaces on the view component, and the base class is optional.

### One scope for the whole life of a view

Rejected. A view that stays open while it is covered would keep its animators and timers running under
a fullscreen screen. The visible scope is the span that stops when the view stops being seen.

### A hard dependency on a general lifetime library for the scope

Rejected. The package must stand alone, and the scope it needs is a small object: a token, a list of
entries and one end routine. A dependency would also bind the package's release cycle to another
project's.

### User-owned scopes

Rejected. A scope that user code can end or reuse can end while the view is still open, or be reused
for a second view, and the guarantee "ends exactly once, on every path" would no longer hold.

## See also

- [View authoring](../../View-Authoring.md)
- [Navigation and back](../../Navigation-and-Back.md)
- [Concepts](../../Concepts.md)
- [Architecture](../Architecture.md)

<!-- file: Documentation~/Design/Decisions/ADR-004-Queue-Above-The-Navigator.md -->

# ADR-004: The queue sits above the navigator

- **Status:** Accepted, implemented in 0.1.0
- **Related:** [Architecture section 13](../Architecture.md#13-the-queue-above-the-navigator),
  [Architecture section 10](../Architecture.md#10-events-and-the-order-at-close),
  [ADR-001](ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md), [ADR-005](ADR-005-Token-Owners.md),
  [Queue](../../Queue.md)

## Context

Several features of one app want to show a popup at about the same time: a maintenance notice, a
what-is-new card, a request for feedback, a tip that belongs to a tutorial. Nobody owns the decision of
which one comes first, and each feature knows only about itself. What an app needs is a small set of
rules that sit outside every feature:

- present them one at a time, the most important first;
- do not present anything while a flow is running (a tutorial, a purchase);
- do not present an item whose condition no longer holds when its turn comes;
- never open on top of a screen change, a modal that is already up, or a load in flight.

Most projects need none of this. A project with one confirm dialog should not pay for it, and the
navigator that runs every view should not carry state for it. The navigator's state is already subtle:
a list per layer, one operation at a time, shield holders, derived visibility. A second holder of
"what is allowed to be shown now" inside it would have to stay consistent with that state.

## Decision

**The queue is a separate public class, `ViewQueue`, that talks to the navigator through `INavigator`
only. The navigator knows nothing about queues.**

- **What it needs from the navigator is a few facts and one call.** `IsLayerClear(layer)` says whether
  the layer has no request, no modal layer above it has a request, and the navigator is not busy.
  `ReserveRequestId()` gives an id before the request exists. `ShowAsync` with `OpenOptions` carrying
  that id, the priority and the source tag presents the item. `AddObserver` delivers the navigator's
  `Settled`, `Closed` and `NotShown` events. A queue on a fake navigator in a test works the same way.
- **Per layer, by priority.** `new ViewQueue(navigator, layer, lifetime, name)` presents on one layer.
  Higher `QueueOptions.Priority` goes first and equal priorities keep enqueue order. A game can have
  several queues. The layer must exist on the navigator: a queue on the root's own navigator throws
  `ArgumentException` for a layer it does not have.
- **Holds pause it.** `Hold(reason, owner)` takes a counted hold that ends with its owner or on
  `Remove()`. While any hold exists nothing is presented. A hold has no automatic timeout; a hold older
  than 60 s warns once with `UIDIRECTOR111`. An atomic flow over the queue is an async method that takes
  a hold for its duration and opens its own views immediately.
- **Gates decide.** An `IViewGate` is a synchronous rule that answers `Allow` or `Deny(reason)`. Gates
  run in ascending order, at enqueue and again right before presentation, and the first deny ends the
  item as `NotShown / Denied` with the gate's reason. A gate that throws counts as a deny and is
  reported (`UIDIRECTOR119`).
- **The pump is coalesced and runs on the next tick.** Triggers are an enqueue, a hold removed, a gate
  added or removed, an item ending, and a navigator `Settled`, `Closed` or `NotShown`. Same-frame
  enqueues are therefore ordered by priority, and the continuation of a view that just closed runs
  before the queue presents the next item. The clear check, the gates, the re-check and the `ShowAsync`
  call happen in one synchronous block, so no other open can slip in between.
- **`Closed` and `NotShown` are triggers as well as `Settled`.** A request that ends without an
  operation (its owner ended, it was lost from outside, a screen change closed it) publishes no
  `Settled`, yet the layer it held may now be clear. Listening to those two events keeps the queue from
  waiting for a signal that never comes.
- **One id from enqueue to close.** The queue publishes `Enqueued`, and `NotShown` for items that never
  reached the navigator, to its own observers. Everything after presentation is the navigator's, with
  the same request id.
- **A queue has a lifetime, and it ends with the root.** When the lifetime token ends while the root still
  exists, waiting items end as `NotShown / Cancelled`, every registration ends, and the queue is inert.
  When the navigator's `RootToken` is cancelled, including when it is the lifetime itself, the same
  happens with `NotShown / RootGone` as the result. A view that is already
  presented is left to its own owner; it ends once through the navigator.
- **Immediate opens bypass it.** A direct `ShowAsync` ignores the queue and its holds. An immediate
  popup makes the layer busy, and the queue waits for it.

## Consequences

**Positive**

- A project that does not use a queue pays nothing: no state, no checks, no allocation in the
  navigator.
- One holder of "what is shown": the navigator. The queue reads facts and never writes layer state.
- The queue is testable against a fake navigator and a manual ticker, and the navigator is tested
  without it.
- Features register their own gates and holds with their own owners, and the registrations end with
  those owners.

**Negative / accepted costs**

- **Two systems to learn.** A reader has to know both what the navigator does and what the queue adds.
- **The queue sees only what `INavigator` exposes.** A rule that needs game state is a gate that reads
  that state; the package cannot provide a vocabulary for it.
- **Gates are synchronous.** A gate cannot await a server. A flow that must wait for something takes a
  hold, then releases it.
- **A tick of latency.** An item that could be shown now is shown on the next `Update` tick.
- **No expiry, no de-duplication and no re-evaluation while an item waits.** Gates run at enqueue and at
  presentation, and nothing runs in between. An item that should not wait forever is given an owner
  token that the game cancels.
- **An item that the navigator ended without showing is not retried.** The queue reports the navigator's
  result and moves on.
- **A queue on an `INavigator` other than the package's own is invisible to the editor tools.**

**Enforced by tests**

- `ViewQueueOrderTests`: priority and enqueue order, the next-tick rule, the layer-clear rule, the
  pump triggers including a layer that clears without `Settled`, the reserved id and the options handed
  to `ShowAsync`, and the events of the queue.
- `ViewQueueRulesTests`: counted holds and their owners, the 60 s warning, gates at enqueue and at
  presentation, ordering, a throwing gate, `Clear`, the lifetime, the root token ending, calls off the
  main thread, and that every enqueued item ends exactly once on every path.
- `ViewQueueNavigatorTests`: the layer check at construction.
- `ViewQueueOnRealRootTests`: a queue on a real root ends its waiting items as `NotShown / RootGone`
  when the root is destroyed, whatever its lifetime, and leaves the presented item to the navigator.
- `CloseOrderContractTests`: an awaiting continuation runs before the queue presents the next item.
- `RandomInvariantTests`: a seeded random run with queue steps checks that at most one item is
  presenting, that nothing is presented while a hold exists or the layer is not clear, that the
  presented item has the highest priority, and that no item waits forever.

## Amendment 2026-10-08

Two rules were tightened before 0.1.0 shipped. Neither changes the decision above; both follow from the
queue holding no navigator state of its own.

- **The queue also ends with its root.** A queue built on a navigator now reads `RootToken` once and
  ends when that token is cancelled, whatever its own lifetime is. Waiting items end as
  `NotShown / RootGone` with the detail "The root was destroyed.", later `Enqueue` and `EnqueueAsync`
  calls complete the same way, and the queue's registrations on both tokens are disposed, so neither
  token keeps a dead queue alive. A queue whose lifetime is `RootToken`, the usual case, therefore ends
  its waiting items as `RootGone` and not as `Cancelled`. A queue built after the root is gone is inert
  from the start. When both tokens end, the reason comes from the state of `RootToken`, not from which
  callback ran first. The presented item is the navigator's, so it ends once through the navigator,
  possibly after the queue's waiting items.
- **The layer is checked.** A queue on the package's own navigator throws `ArgumentException` at
  construction for a layer the navigator does not have. A queue on another `INavigator` cannot be
  checked that way. At presentation, a key whose catalog row is on a different layer than the queue's
  is refused by the navigator as `NotShown / WrongLayer`
  ([UIDIRECTOR126](../../Troubleshooting.md#uidirector126)).

## Alternatives considered

### Queueing as a layer policy inside the navigator

Rejected. The strongest alternative: give each layer an admission mode (immediate, queued, replace) and
let the navigator order requests. Every user would pay for it, the navigator would hold two copies of
the state of a layer (what is open and what is waiting), and the queue's rules would be tangled with
the operation list. A separate class keeps the navigator's contract small.

### A declarative rules engine

Rejected. A set of named conditions such as "not during a tutorial" or "at most once a day" is a
vocabulary, and the vocabulary is the structure of one particular game under another name. A
synchronous gate that the game implements covers every condition without the package guessing them.

### Automatic release of holds after a timeout

Rejected. An auto-release lets popups through in the middle of a flow that is merely slow. A hold is
tied to its owner, and the package only reports a hold that has lasted too long.

### Extras: a resolver, an awaitable "turn", a de-duplication key, expiry, interruption

Rejected for 0.1.0. Each one makes the queue a second scheduler. Interrupting the view that is
presented loses that view. An awaitable turn is a hold taken by an async method. Expiry is an owner
token that the game cancels. A de-duplication key is a gate that checks the game's state.

## See also

- [Queue](../../Queue.md)
- [Events and analytics](../../Events-and-Analytics.md)
- [Architecture](../Architecture.md)
- [Troubleshooting](../../Troubleshooting.md)

<!-- file: Documentation~/Design/Decisions/ADR-005-Token-Owners.md -->

# ADR-005: Token owners

- **Status:** Accepted, implemented in 0.1.0
- **Related:** [Architecture section 4](../Architecture.md#4-requests-and-phases),
  [Architecture section 17](../Architecture.md#17-threading),
  [ADR-001](ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md), [ADR-003](ADR-003-Begin-Only-Hooks-And-Scopes.md),
  [Opening and results](../../Opening-and-Results.md), [Threading](../../Threading.md)

## Context

Every request has to end somehow. Usually the view closes itself or the user dismisses it. But the code
that asked for the view can go away first: a screen is closed while the popup it opened is still up, a
feature is torn down while its notice waits in a queue, a scene unloads. If nothing says who the view
belongs to, a view outlives the code that knew what to do with its answer, and the answer goes nowhere.

The same question comes up for everything else that a caller registers with the navigator or a queue: a
shield hold, an observer, a catalog, a preload, a gate, a queue hold. A registration that has to be
removed by a call that the owner remembers is the forgotten removal line again.

The package is built on UniTask and runs in an engine whose async code already speaks one currency for
"until this ends": `CancellationToken`. Objects that provide such a token are everywhere: the destroy
token of a component, the token of a scope, the application's own. A package-defined owner type would
need adapters to each of them, and an optional owner would make "no owner" the default.

## Decision

**Every request and every registration takes a required `CancellationToken` as its owner.**

- **Positional and required.** `ShowAsync` and `Open` take `owner` right after the key and the arguments
  (the no-argument forms take it right after the key). `HoldInput`, `AddObserver`, `AddCatalog`, `PreloadAsync` and the queue's `Enqueue`,
  `EnqueueAsync`, `Hold`, `AddGate` and `AddObserver` take one too, and so does the queue's lifetime.
  There is no overload without it.
- **`CancellationToken.None` is the explicit "until someone closes it".** `INavigator.RootToken` is the
  recommended long-lived owner: it is cancelled when the root is destroyed, as the last step of the
  teardown, so it means "as long as the UI exists".
- **The owner decides the life of the view and never cancels an awaiter.** When it ends while the view
  is on screen, the request is terminated at once: the running step is cancelled, the view snaps, and
  the request is finalized with `CloseReason.OwnerEnded`. A request that is not shown yet is withdrawn
  with `RejectReason.OwnerEnded`. In both cases every awaiter completes with that outcome as data
  ([ADR-001](ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md)). An outcome that was already latched wins over the owner
  ending. An owner that is already cancelled at the call ends the request as not shown, with no shield
  and no load.
- **A popup can be owned by the open scope of the screen that opened it.** Passing the scope's `Token`
  as the owner closes the popup when the screen goes away, and the popup reports `Closed` before the
  screen does ([ADR-003](ADR-003-Begin-Only-Hooks-And-Scopes.md)). A `ViewButton` that opens a view
  uses `RootToken`, so the view outlives the screen that holds the button.
- **The callback is cheap and cleaned up.** The package registers its callback with
  `RegisterWithoutCaptureExecutionContext`, after the `Requested` event, so a token that fires during
  registration cannot reorder events or leak a shield holder. On every normal end the registration is
  disposed, which unregisters without invoking, so a long-lived owner does not accumulate entries. A
  token that cannot be cancelled registers nothing.
- **Registrations end with their owner and nothing restarts.** A hold, an observer, a catalog, a
  preload lease, a gate and a queue's registrations are removed when their owner ends or when
  `ViewRegistration.Remove()` is called, whichever is first. `Remove()` is safe to call twice and from
  any thread. A registration whose owner is already cancelled comes back empty. The game registers
  again if it wants the effect again.
- **A queue also ends with its root.** A queue watches the navigator's `RootToken` as well as its own
  lifetime. When either ends, its waiting items complete as `NotShown`, with `RootGone` if the root is
  gone and `Cancelled` otherwise, and later `Enqueue` calls complete the same way. A queue whose
  lifetime *is* `RootToken` therefore reports `RootGone`. The presented item is left to the navigator,
  which ends it once, possibly after the queue's waiting items. A queue built after the root is gone is
  inert from the start. Both registrations are disposed when the queue ends, so neither token keeps a
  dead queue alive.
- **A foreign thread can cancel.** A token may be cancelled from a timer or a worker thread. The
  callback then posts the handling to the main thread and logs `UIDIRECTOR113`; the request or
  registration ends on the main thread, in the normal way.
- **The scope tokens are different.** A `ViewScope.Token` belongs to the package and ends with the
  scope. It is never the request's owner token.

| Token | Cancelled by | When it fires |
|---|---|---|
| Request owner | The caller | The request is withdrawn, or the shown view is terminated; awaiters get `OwnerEnded` |
| Registration owner (hold, observer, catalog, preload, gate) | The caller | The registration is removed |
| Queue lifetime | The game | Waiting items end as `NotShown / Cancelled`, or `NotShown / RootGone` when the root is already gone; a presented view is left to its own owner |
| `RootToken` | The package | The root is destroyed, as the last step of the teardown; a queue also ends with it |
| Scope token | The package | The open or visible scope ends |
| `WaitForCloseAsync` waiter | The awaiting caller | That one await throws; the view is untouched |

## Consequences

**Positive**

- A request cannot outlive the code that can handle its answer without that being a visible choice at
  the call: the caller wrote `CancellationToken.None` or `RootToken`.
- The type is the one that every async API in the engine and UniTask already accepts. A destroy token,
  a scope token or a service's token is a valid owner with no adapter.
- A registration needs no removal line. The owner ends and the package removes it.
- Teardown is uniform. The root ending cancels `RootToken` and every request, hold, observer and lease
  ends through the same paths.

**Negative / accepted costs**

- **`CancellationToken.None` is easy to type.** A request owned by `None` lives until somebody closes it;
  a view that waits for an answer nobody gives stays up. `RootToken` and the shield make the failure
  visible, and the guide says which to pass.
- **Ending by owner snaps.** A view whose owner ends is not animated out. It is snapped and finalized,
  because the code that owned it is already gone.
- **The owner is a token, not an object.** A diagnostic can name the caller's member and line, but not
  "the screen" that owns the request.
- **Cross-thread cancellation costs a post and a warning.** A project that cancels from a worker thread
  gets `UIDIRECTOR113` each time.
- **Nothing restarts by itself.** A hold or gate registered with a token that ended must be registered
  again by the game.

**Enforced by tests**

- `AwaiterContractTests`: the owner ending succeeds and is never cancelled, whether or not the awaiting
  code is the owner; every awaiter completes with data.
- `LifecycleAcceptanceTests` and `LifecycleTerminateTests`: an owner that is already cancelled is
  rejected at the call; the owner ending terminates a shown view and withdraws a waiting one; a latched
  outcome survives the owner ending.
- `ThreadingContractTests`: an owner cancelled off the main thread is posted and logs `UIDIRECTOR113`;
  a registration removed off the main thread is posted; a cancellation after the end posts nothing.
- `ViewQueueRulesTests`: a hold or an item owner that ends, a queue lifetime that ends, and the removal
  of registrations.

## Alternatives considered

### An optional owner

Rejected. A default of "no owner" is how views outlive the code that opened them. A required parameter
makes the choice appear at the call, and `CancellationToken.None` is a deliberate way to say it.

### A package-defined owner or lifetime object

Rejected. A new owner type would need an adapter to every token source a project already has, and it
would be one more concept to learn. A token carries exactly the information the package needs: "this
ended".

### A dependency on an external lifetime or scope library

Rejected. The package must install and work alone, and its owner type should not bind it to another
project's release cycle. Any lifetime library that exposes a token works with the package unchanged.

### An implicit owner: the calling component or the active scene

Rejected. The package has no knowledge of scenes or of the caller's object, and a hidden default owner
is how work silently outlives what it belonged to. The explicit `RootToken` says "as long as the UI
exists" in one word.

### The awaiter as the owner

Rejected. Throwing into the awaiting code when the owner ends assumes the two are the same. See
[ADR-001](ADR-001-Outcomes-As-Data.md).

## See also

- [Opening and results](../../Opening-and-Results.md)
- [Threading](../../Threading.md)
- [Events and analytics](../../Events-and-Analytics.md)
- [Architecture](../Architecture.md)

<!-- file: Samples~/AddressablesUsage/README.md -->

# Addressables Usage

Core plus the Addressables integration: the views are not prefab references in the catalog, they are loaded by
address. Needs the Addressables package (`com.unity.addressables`; the sample's assembly compiles only when it is
installed), the uGUI package (`com.unity.ugui`, which includes TextMeshPro) and UniTask.

## Setup

1. Import TextMeshPro's Essential Resources once: `Window > TextMeshPro > Import TMP Essential Resources`.
   The texts stay blank until then.
2. Make the two prefabs addressable, with exactly these addresses: `Prefabs/Gallery` as `uidirector-samples/gallery`
   and `Prefabs/Photo` as `uidirector-samples/photo`. Either way works:
   - Menu: `Tools/UIDirector/Samples/Make Addressables Usage Prefabs Addressable`. It creates the Addressables
     settings if the project has none, and only when you click it; nothing runs on import. It puts both prefabs in
     the default group and sets the two addresses.
   - By hand: open `Window > Asset Management > Addressables > Groups`, create the settings if asked, drag
     `Prefabs/Gallery` and `Prefabs/Photo` into a group, and set the two addresses.
3. Open the scene `AddressablesUsage.unity` from the folder the Package Manager imported the sample into:
   `Assets/Samples/UIDirector/<version>/Addressables Usage/`. The scene has no Event System on purpose: the right
   input module depends on your project's input handling, so the bootstrap creates one when Play starts.
4. Press Play. Optionally open `Window > UIDirector` to watch the stacks, the shield and the queues live (it shows
   something in Play Mode only).

In the editor the default play mode script, "Use Asset Database", loads the prefabs directly, so no build step is
needed. A player build needs the Addressables content built first.

The view ids in this sample (`gallery`, `photo`) differ from the ids in the other samples, so importing several
samples into one project never makes `Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs` report a duplicate.

## What to do

The catalog rows carry an address instead of a prefab. `gallery` is a screen that keeps its instance, with the
address `uidirector-samples/gallery`; `photo` is a popup that closes on a tap on the backdrop, with the address
`uidirector-samples/photo`. The scene's root has "Initialize On Awake" off and an `AddressablesViewProvider`
component on its own GameObject; the root's asset provider field stays empty, so that component loads and releases
every view.

- **Play** opens the gallery on its own (`source=boot`). The status line first shows nothing, then reads "Photo
  popup preloaded." once the preload below finished. The gallery has three photo buttons, "Trim kept views" and the
  status line.
- **What happens when the addresses are missing**: the load of the gallery fails and the navigator turns the
  request away with `NotShown` and the reason `LoadFailed` (after the 15 second load timeout, `LoadTimedOut`). The
  bootstrap then logs one warning that starts with `The gallery did not open (LoadFailed): ` and the reason's
  detail, followed by "Mark Prefabs/Gallery and Prefabs/Photo as addressable, as the sample README describes, and
  create the Addressables settings if the project has none." The navigator also logs its own error with the
  diagnostic ID `UIDIRECTOR104`. Fix the addresses, then press Play again.
- **Sunrise**, **Harbor**, **Glacier** each open the photo popup with that word as its title and a "Close"
  button (`source=gallery.photo`). While the gallery is visible the photo asset is already loaded, so the first
  photo opens without a load wait. "Close", or a tap on the backdrop, closes the popup and the gallery is
  usable again. If the popup cannot open, the status line reads `Photo '<title>' did not open: <reason>.`
- **Trim kept views** calls `Trim()` and sets the status "Trimmed: hidden kept instances were released." Trim
  frees kept instances that are not on screen. The gallery is open, so it stays. Nothing else in this sample is
  kept (the photo popup is destroyed when it closes), so you see only the status line change; the call matters in
  a project with several kept screens.
- **A photo address that is missing while the gallery address is right**: the gallery opens, the status reads
  "Photo popup could not be preloaded, see the console.", and a photo button sets the status to
  `Photo '<title>' did not open: LoadFailed.`

## What to look at

- The preload: [GalleryView](GalleryView.cs) asks `PreloadAsync` for the photo view from `OnVisible`, on the
  visible scope. The asset stays loaded for as long as the gallery is on screen, and the lease ends when the gallery
  is covered by another screen or closed. A photo popup does not cover the gallery, so the lease stays while the
  popups open and close.
- Trim: the same file, the "Trim kept views" handler.
- Catalog rows with an address and no prefab: select `AddressablesUsageCatalog.asset` and read the `gallery` and
  `photo` rows.
- The Hierarchy: the root made with `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root` has "Initialize On Awake" off and carries
  the `AddressablesViewProvider`; the `Bootstrap` object holds `AddressablesBootstrap`. The prefabs are in
  `Prefabs/`: Gallery and Photo.
- `Window > UIDirector`: the gallery in `screens` and a photo popup in `popups` while it is open.
- [AddressablesBootstrap](AddressablesBootstrap.cs) - the root initialised in `Awake` with an empty setup, the
  gallery opened with the root as the owner, and the warning that names the setup step when the result carries a
  reject reason.
- [GalleryView](GalleryView.cs) - the preload on the visible scope, photo popups owned by the open scope, the
  `Rejected` check on the result and `Trim`.
- [PhotoView](PhotoView.cs) - a popup with typed arguments that closes on a button.
- [RemoteViews](RemoteViews.cs) - the two keys and the argument struct.
- [MarkSampleAddressables](Editor/MarkSampleAddressables.cs) - the menu helper from step 2, editor only.
- [SampleEventSystem](Support/SampleEventSystem.cs) - the event system creation.

<!-- file: Samples~/BasicUsage/README.md -->

# Basic Usage

Core only: no DOTween, no Zenject, no queue. Needs the uGUI package (`com.unity.ugui`, which includes TextMeshPro)
and UniTask.

## Setup

1. Import TextMeshPro's Essential Resources once: `Window > TextMeshPro > Import TMP Essential Resources`.
   The texts stay blank until then.
2. Open the scene `BasicUsage.unity` from the folder the Package Manager imported the sample into:
   `Assets/Samples/UIDirector/<version>/Basic Usage/`. The scene has no Event System on purpose: the right input
   module depends on your project's input handling, so the bootstrap creates one when Play starts.
3. Press Play. Optionally open `Window > UIDirector` to watch the stacks and the input shield live (it shows
   something in Play Mode only). Click the Game view once so it has keyboard focus: device back is the Escape key
   in the editor.

The view ids in this sample (`home`, `library`, `item-detail`, `settings`, `confirm`, `rename`, `saving`, `toast`)
differ from the ids in the Queue Usage sample, so importing both samples into one project never makes
`Tools/UIDirector/Validate Catalogs` report a duplicate.

## What to do

Every request writes `[views]` lines to the Console (see "What to look at"). The lines named below are the ones
that matter for each action.

- **Play** opens Home on its own: `[views] Requested #1 view=home layer=screens source=boot`, then `Shown`, then
  `Settled`. Home has two buttons, "Library" and "Settings". The bootstrap owns Home with the root's token, so it
  ends only when the root does.
- **Library** (on Home) opens the library screen. The label reads "3 items", written when the screen becomes
  visible. Home is still in the stack under it. Source tag: `home.library`.
- **Settings** (on Home) opens the settings screen the same way. Source tag: `home.settings`.
- **Getting started** and **Release notes** (on Library) each open the item detail screen with that item's title
  (`library.item`). Detail has three buttons: "Rename", "Back to the library" and "Home".
- **Archive** (on Library) opens the same detail screen with the title "Archive". Archive cannot be renamed, see
  **Rename** below.
- **Back** (on Library) calls `Back()` from code. Library closes with `reason=Back` and Home is revealed again,
  without its open code running a second time.
- **Rename** (on an item detail) opens the rename popup, owned by that detail screen's open, with the current
  title in a text field and the buttons "Cancel" and "Save". For Getting started and Release notes the popup
  appears. For Archive the popup declines inside its open code: nothing is shown, the screen stays as it is, and
  the Console logs `Requested` and then
  `[views] NotShown #n view=rename layer=popups source=item.rename rejected=Declined detail=This item cannot be renamed.`
- **Rename > type a new name > Save** closes the popup (`reason=Completed`). A moment later, once the popup is
  gone, the detail screen's title changes: the screen subscribed to the library's `Renamed` event on its open
  scope, and the event fired when the popup's answer reached the screen. The buttons on the Library screen keep
  their fixed labels; open the item again and the detail screen shows the new title, because the item list kept it.
- **Rename > Save with an empty field** keeps the popup open and shows "Enter a name first." Nothing is renamed.
- **Rename > Cancel** closes the popup without a value (`reason=Dismissed`). The title does not change.
- **Rename > type something, then Escape**: the popup asks its own back hook first, so it does not close. A hint,
  "Press back again to discard the change.", appears. A second Escape closes the popup with `reason=Back` and the
  title does not change. Escape without having typed anything closes the popup at once. Typing and then restoring
  the original text still counts as an edit.
- **Back to the library** (on an item detail) calls `CloseTo` for the library: the detail screen closes with
  `reason=Code` and the library is revealed.
- **Home** (on an item detail) opens `home` while Home is already in the stack. That is a return, not a new
  screen: no `Requested` line for Home, Home's open code does not run again, and everything above it closes with
  `reason=Navigated` (the detail screen with its hide transition, the library at once). Only Home is left.
- **Reset settings** (on Settings) opens the confirm popup "Reset settings" / "All settings return to their
  defaults." with "No" and "Yes". "No" closes it with a false answer and nothing else happens. "Yes" closes it,
  then the Console shows `[settings] reset to defaults`, the Settings label reads "Settings were reset." and a
  toast with the same text slides in at the top, on its own layer, and leaves by itself after 2 seconds
  (`Closed ... view=toast layer=toasts ... reason=Dismissed`). A toast never blocks a tap: the layer has no input
  shield and no back.
- **Reset settings, double click**: the first click opens the confirm popup at once and raises the input shield
  in the same call, so the second click lands on the shield. One popup opens and no extra line is logged.
- **Reset settings while a toast is sliding in or out** is the case the "Busy, try again." text is for. The call
  asks not to wait, the navigator is busy with the toast's transition, and the request is refused at once:
  `[views] NotShown #n view=confirm layer=popups source=settings.reset rejected=Busy detail=The navigator is busy and the call asked not to wait.`
  No popup opens and the Settings label reads "Busy, try again." The window for this is short (the toast's slide
  in right after "Yes", and its slide out 2 seconds later). While the toast sits still, Reset opens the popup as
  usual.
- **Save** (on Settings) opens the "Saving..." overlay on the system layer and keeps it for 1.5 seconds
  (unscaled time) while the fake save runs. The overlay blocks input and swallows back for that time: Escape does
  nothing, it neither closes anything nor opens the quit confirm. After 1.5 seconds the overlay closes
  (`Closed ... view=saving layer=system ... reason=Code`) and only once it is gone the Settings label reads
  "Saved." Source tag: `settings.save`.
- **Back** (on Settings, a Back button with no code behind it) calls `Back()`: Settings closes with
  `reason=Back` and Home is revealed. The label is cleared the next time Settings opens.
- **Escape on a screen above Home** (Library, an item detail, Settings) does the same as the Back button of that
  screen. With a popup open, Escape goes to the popup first (the confirm popup closes with `reason=Back` and
  counts as "No"). Escape while a view is still opening is swallowed.
- **Escape on Home**: nothing in the stack handles it, so `Back()` returns false and the bootstrap's handler
  opens the "Quit" / "Close the application?" confirm (`source=back.root`). "Yes" calls `Application.Quit()` and,
  in the editor, leaves Play Mode. "No" or Escape closes it and keeps the app running.

## What to look at

- The Console. Each line is `[views] <Kind> #<request> view=<id> layer=<layer> source=<tag>`. `Shown` adds
  `waited=`, `Closed` adds `reason=` and `open=`, `NotShown` adds `rejected=` and `detail=`, and `Settled` (the
  navigator went from busy to idle) has no request and no view. The `source` tags (`home.library`, `item.rename`,
  `settings.reset`, `back.root` and so on) say which line of code asked. The log is [ViewEventLog](ViewEventLog.cs),
  added in [AppBootstrap](AppBootstrap.cs) with the root's token as its owner.
- `Window > UIDirector`: one section per layer (`screens`, `popups`, `system`, `toasts`) with its requests and
  phases, `Shield holders (n)` (open it during a transition or while the popup opens), and the newest events.
  Home, Library and an item detail stack up in `screens`; the confirm and rename popups appear in `popups`; the
  saving overlay in `system`; the toast in `toasts`.
- The Hierarchy: the root made with `GameObject > UI > UIDirector Root` has "Initialize On Awake" off and carries
  `BackInput`; the `Bootstrap` object holds `AppBootstrap`. The prefabs are in `Prefabs/` (Home, Library,
  ItemDetail, Settings, Confirm, Rename, Saving, Toast) and `BasicUsageCatalog.asset` lists them with their layers
  and policies.
- [AppViews](AppViews.cs) - every key of the sample: the id, the argument type and the result type in one place.
- [AppBootstrap](AppBootstrap.cs) - the setup in `Awake` (event system, services, `Initialize` with the inject
  seam, the error handler and the extra layer), Home opened in `Start`, and the quit confirm behind the unhandled
  back press.
- [AppLayers](AppLayers.cs) - the `toasts` layer: above the system layer, no history, no back, no input shield.
- [HomeView](HomeView.cs), [LibraryView](LibraryView.cs), [ItemDetailView](ItemDetailView.cs) - screens that open
  other screens with the root as the owner, return to a screen already in the stack, and subscribe to a C# event on
  the open scope.
- [ConfirmView](ConfirmView.cs) - a popup with typed arguments and a bool result, written on the base class.
- [RenameView](RenameView.cs) - the same kind of popup written on the interfaces only (`IView` and `IViewBack`),
  with `Decline` inside the open code and a back hook.
- [SettingsView](SettingsView.cs) - a popup awaited with `ShowAsync` (with `RejectWhenBusy` and the `Rejected` check), a toast opened with the root as the owner, and a system overlay closed in a `finally`.
- [SavingOverlay](SavingOverlay.cs) and [ToastView](ToastView.cs) - an overlay with work on the visible scope, and
  a view that closes itself after a delay.
- [PopTransition](PopTransition.cs) - a custom transition on unscaled time, the example for writing your own.
- [HardwareBackRouter](HardwareBackRouter.cs) with [LegacyPopup](Support/LegacyPopup.cs) - the recipe for a
  project that still has an older UI above the package: ask it first, then call `Back()`. It replaces `BackInput`
  and is not wired into the scene.
- [ViewArgs](ViewArgs.cs), [AppServices](AppServices.cs), [SettingsStore](Support/SettingsStore.cs),
  [ItemLibrary](Support/ItemLibrary.cs), [SampleEventSystem](Support/SampleEventSystem.cs) - the stand-ins for
  your own code: argument structs, the services views receive, a fake settings store and item list, and the
  event system creation.
